#9780. Jensen Huang Chinese Revenue, Affairs, Resignation, and Case for CEO Reinstatement Timeline

AI, hacks, and quiet chaos—tracking how systems break, who’s watching, and what’s really happening behind the screens.

AI, hacks, and quiet chaos—tracking how systems break, who’s watching, and what’s really happening behind the screens.

AI, hacks, and quiet chaos—tracking how systems break, who’s watching, and what’s really happening behind the screens.

The first NVIDIA earnings call after Jensen Huang’s departure opened with the answer to a question Silicon Valley had spent the weekend asking. The board “does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO,” chair Harvey Jones said. Earlier that day, Huang had said he would be “honored” to return if the board decided it was in the best interest of shareholders and employees. Then interim CEO Colette Kress got to the numbers. NVIDIA had just booked $115.8 billion in quarterly revenue, including $11.05 billion from direct customers headquartered in China and Hong Kong. NVIDIA’s decision on reinstatement · Jensen Huang’s comeback statement · NVIDIA’s geographic revenue disclosure

A third number came out on the call. NVIDIA sold $2.4 billion of licensed Hopper data-center products to China in the quarter. Kress said those shipments had stopped and the company’s next-quarter guidance excluded them. The economics get harder to trace when a Chinese business rents computing power abroad or when NVIDIA hardware reaches an end user through intermediaries. Licensed Hopper sales and the shipment halt · NVIDIA’s definition of indirect customers

The original HackerNoon Jensen Huang affair timeline followed his public remarks, the Singapore cloud company Megaspeed, and his admission of infidelity. The ensuing days brought reports of two relationships with NVIDIA employees, a resignation that cost Huang his board seat as well as his job, a campaign to bring him back, and a U.S. rule aimed at Chinese access to advanced computing overseas. The dates matter. NVIDIA’s SEC filing records the board accepting his resignation on November 11. The company told the public on November 12. Reuters on the second NVIDIA employee · NVIDIA’s resignation filing · Federal Register rule on remote computing

NVIDIA used to assign revenue geographically by the address on the bill. In Q3 FY2026 it switched to the headquarters of the direct customer and recast earlier figures. A company can be invoiced in Singapore, be headquartered elsewhere, take delivery in Malaysia, and rent computing capacity to a business in China. Each is a different fact about the transaction. NVIDIA’s newer tables answer the headquarters question. The older ones answer the billing question. FY2025 billing geography · FY2026 geographic reporting change

On a comparable headquarters basis, China and Hong Kong revenue fell 21.4% in FY2026, then rose 41.3% year over year in the first nine months of FY2027. The region’s share of total revenue still fell over those nine months because NVIDIA’s overall business grew faster. The geography line covers multiple product categories, while Kress’s $2.4 billion figure describes licensed Hopper data-center products specifically. Adding the latter to the former would mix two views of overlapping sales. NVIDIA’s annual geographic comparisons · NVIDIA’s nine-month revenue comparisons · Kress on licensed Hopper sales

Singapore’s $23.684 billion was a billing figure. Singapore accounted for about 18% of FY2025 revenue on the old basis, up from $6.831 billion the year before. NVIDIA said shipments to Singapore amounted to less than 2% of FY2025 company revenue and explained that customers used the country to centralize invoicing. The filing gives no destination breakdown for the difference. The new headquarters tables group Singapore into a broader geography presentation. They provide no standalone Singapore line and no end-user reconciliation. The same issue runs in the opposite direction in Taiwan. NVIDIA estimated that 76% of FY2026 Data Center revenue from Taiwan-headquartered customers was attributable to U.S. and European end customers. Singapore revenue and shipment footnote · Taiwan end-customer estimate and new geography table

Malaysia is where the Megaspeed story becomes a hardware and cloud story. The New York Times traced almost $2 billion of NVIDIA-equipped purchases to Speedmatrix, Megaspeed’s Malaysian subsidiary. A later Bloomberg analysis of Malaysian and Indonesian customs records estimated at least $4.6 billion in NVIDIA hardware imports by Megaspeed. The Wall Street Journal reported that Chinese firms accessed computing capacity on servers outside China, and The Information reported a connection between Alibaba and Megaspeed that went beyond buying capacity. It said NVIDIA introduced Alibaba to Alice Huang and that Speedmatrix had pledged assets to a Singapore company ultimately owned by Alibaba. NVIDIA told The Information it works with the industry to comply with evolving cloud rules. Speedmatrix and the first Megaspeed investigation · Bloomberg’s Malaysia and Indonesia customs analysis · The Wall Street Journal’s offshore computing investigation · The Information’s reporting on Alibaba and Megaspeed

The larger numbers measure different things. The $4.8 billion figure carried in the original timeline describes equipment reportedly bought by a Megaspeed-linked Malaysian company over a specified period. The Information’s at least $7.5 billion figure, as reported by Reuters, was an estimate of chips allegedly shipped to Chinese firms through a broader network. Those figures can cover overlapping hardware, different windows, and different points in the supply chain. A customs value can include server components and reseller markups. A cloud rental is revenue to the provider, even when Chinese demand helped justify the provider’s original NVIDIA hardware purchase. NVIDIA’s filings provide no defensible dollar total for that indirect exposure. HackerNoon’s equipment purchase timeline · Reuters on the reported $7.5 billion shipment estimate · NVIDIA’s direct and indirect customer definitions

Indonesia had an enforcement lead of its own. The Straits Times reported that Indonesian police inspected a Megaspeed subsidiary earlier in 2026 and found empty server racks. The report attributed suspicions about where hardware went to an unnamed official. Malaysia separately said it was checking the status of advanced chips imported by Speedmatrix. Reuters reported that Megaspeed also had subsidiaries in Thailand, Australia, and the United States. A corporate presence gives investigators a place to look. A sale, re-export, or cloud rental still needs a transaction record. Indonesia’s reported Megaspeed inspection · Malaysia’s Speedmatrix statement · Reuters on Megaspeed’s overseas subsidiaries

The new U.S. rule goes after access as well as shipments. The rule effective November 19 adds license requirements for covered advanced chips in Singapore, Malaysia, Indonesia, Thailand, and Brazil. It also addresses certain overseas data centers providing significant computing capacity to entities headquartered or ultimately parented in covered jurisdictions. Inclusion on the list reflects the scope of the regulation. It supplies no historical revenue figure for any country. November 19 advanced-chip and remote-access rule

The entity that became Megaspeed starts as 7Road International, associated with the Chinese gaming company 7Road. This is the start of the corporate paper trail. The people and facilities later associated with the cloud business enter the picture years later. 7Road International’s Singapore incorporation

7Road International becomes Megaspeed International as it expands into AI infrastructure. CBS reported that ownership passed to an entity controlled by Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le. Singapore later described her as a Hong Kong resident and Megaspeed’s former CEO, chairperson, and one of its key controllers. Alice Huang and Jensen Huang share a surname and are unrelated. Megaspeed’s 2023 ownership and name change · Singapore’s description of Alice Huang’s role · CNA’s Alice Huang coverage

The New York Times reported that Jensen and Alice Huang were acquainted by December 2023, when they dined with colleagues in Singapore. The Straits Times dated photos from the gathering to December 7 at Ristorante Da Valentino. The dinner puts their earliest reported contact before the 2024 meetings emphasized in the original HackerNoon timeline. The date the relationship became intimate remains unknown. The New York Times timeline of the Huang relationships · The Straits Times on the December 2023 dinner photos

TechCrunch reported an early-2024 meeting at an NVIDIA event, and dated photos surfaced from Computex that June. The New York Times traced the establishment of Speedmatrix to early 2024, giving Megaspeed a Malaysian entity through which it could buy and install equipment. Reported early NVIDIA event · Speedmatrix’s formation in Malaysia

Parker Schmitt, a tech executive who was there, recalled Alice Huang telling the group, “I bet you guys I can get Jensen here.” He came to the bar and joined them for a drink. Photos put the two in the same place during Computex. The timing of any romance or alleged intelligence recruitment remains unresolved. The Taipei bar account and Computex photographs

Commerce later said proactive monitoring detected suspicious activity and that the department opened an export-control investigation in 2024. The public statement gives the year. It leaves the opening date unspecified, so the probe cannot be placed precisely before or after the Taipei encounter. U.S. Commerce and Justice investigation chronology

In a Bloomberg interview after earnings, Huang talked about demand for the forthcoming Blackwell platform. The interview belongs in the public business timeline because Blackwell was about to become crucial to the overseas data-center buildout. His public pitch centered on product demand. Jensen Huang’s Bloomberg interview on Blackwell demand

Singapore police and customs open an inquiry involving Megaspeed, other companies, and individuals over possible false declarations in purchases of servers. Singapore says it initiated this probe independently and that it concerned potential domestic offenses. U.S. Commerce was already looking into possible export-control violations under a different legal framework. Singapore Police and Customs investigation · U.S. Megaspeed investigation

NVIDIA’s annual filing reports $17.108 billion billed to customers in China and Hong Kong and $23.684 billion billed to customers in Singapore for FY2025. It also explains how little hardware ships to Singapore relative to the size of the billing line. Later reports often cite the 18% figure without its most important noun, billing. NVIDIA’s FY2025 geographic revenue and shipments

NVIDIA says the U.S. informed it on April 9 of a new license requirement for H20 sales to China and certain other destinations, then said on April 14 the requirement would remain in effect indefinitely. NVIDIA disclosed the change on April 15 and estimated charges of up to $5.5 billion. H20 was a product built for a market already subject to U.S. restrictions. NVIDIA’s H20 export-control disclosure

U.S. investigators request records for both direct and indirect sales to Megaspeed, according to the Justice Department’s later account. The distinction reached beyond NVIDIA’s own invoices. Intermediaries and system integrators could be involved even when NVIDIA did not invoice the company receiving the servers. Commerce’s records request for Megaspeed sales

The original timeline dates this Bloomberg exchange to May 17. Huang said there was “no evidence of any AI chip diversion.” The record request announced later establishes that investigators were looking at Megaspeed that month. The public chronology leaves the day of the request and what Huang personally knew at the interview unresolved. Huang’s 2025 remarks on chip diversion · The public dates of the U.S. investigation

Speaking at Computex, he called the restrictions “a failure,” arguing they gave Chinese companies a reason to develop alternatives to U.S. chips. That was Huang’s public industrial-policy argument. NVIDIA would keep making versions of it when Washington considered which products to license. Huang’s Computex remarks on U.S. chip controls

Taipei video reviewed by Reuters shows the two at a private dinner. Contemporary footage and subsequent accounts place Alice Huang at the event about a year after the bar encounter. The two sightings provide public dates for their association. The first public admission of infidelity would come in November 2026. Reuters on the Taipei dinner footage · HackerNoon’s Computex dinner timeline

NVIDIA records a $4.5 billion charge related to H20 inventory and purchase obligations. It says it sold $4.6 billion in H20 products in fiscal Q1 before the new requirement and was unable to ship another $2.5 billion during that quarter. The sales, the unshipped orders, and the accounting charge tell three different parts of the same story. NVIDIA’s H20 sales and inventory charge

Commerce and Justice later say NVIDIA put Megaspeed on its internal “no sell” list in June. That action matters when reading the company’s later public descriptions of Megaspeed as an ordinary cloud business. An internal sales restriction and a federal Entity List designation have different scopes. The agencies’ statement leaves the treatment of individual affiliate and reseller transactions unspecified. U.S. confirmation of NVIDIA’s Megaspeed no-sell decision

The U.S. Bureau of Industry and Security conducts a post-shipment verification at Megaspeed with Alice Huang present. Singapore police interview her the same day for their own inquiry. The U.S. agencies say the Department of Justice subsequently took the lead on the criminal investigation. Singapore’s June 24 post-shipment verification account · DOJ’s account of the criminal referral

Singapore police and prosecutors tell U.S. authorities that server supplier Supermicro has provided limited cooperation, according to Singapore’s later account. Singapore says it made repeated requests for assistance from September onward. Those requests show how much of the investigation depended on evidence held outside the country where Megaspeed was incorporated. Singapore’s requests for U.S. investigative assistance

NVIDIA says the U.S. government has assured it that licenses would be granted and that it hopes to start H20 deliveries again. Huang was in China after meeting U.S. officials in Washington. An assurance and a license can precede a sale by months. The company’s subsequent filings show how much business actually cleared. NVIDIA’s July H20 China announcement

Malaysia says exports, transit, and transshipment of covered U.S.-origin high-performance AI chips require a strategic trade permit. That placed a domestic enforcement requirement on activity out of Malaysia while U.S. authorities were investigating the disposition of NVIDIA hardware. Malaysia’s July 2025 advanced-chip permit notice

NVIDIA says U.S. officials expressed an expectation that the government would receive 15% of revenue from licensed H20 sales to China. Its August quarterly filing says the government had yet to publish a regulation codifying the expectation. That number belongs to the policy negotiations. It should stay off the revenue table. NVIDIA’s filing on the proposed 15% H20 arrangement

Megaspeed supplied this date publicly in November 2026, saying she had no current role with the company. Earlier reporting and official statements described her as a controller or CEO during earlier periods. The departure date is the company’s account and was disclosed well after the fact. Megaspeed’s statement on Alice Huang’s departure

Speaking on the BG2 podcast, Huang argues that China has the capability and capacity to compete with the United States. A year later, one of the hosts, investor Brad Gerstner, asks NVIDIA’s board to keep Huang in the running for CEO. Jensen Huang on BG2 with Brad Gerstner and Bill Gurley · Gerstner’s later letter to NVIDIA’s board

The Times report connected the Taipei bar encounter, Speedmatrix’s purchases, and federal scrutiny of possible diversion. NVIDIA spokesman John Rizzo said company staff “found no evidence of diversion” on a visit. His statement described a company check. Commerce has since said it opened its own investigation the year before, and Justice says the criminal inquiry continued. The New York Times’ Megaspeed reporting and NVIDIA response · U.S. account of the continuing investigation

At a Citadel Securities event, Huang cited a drop from 95% to zero while discussing the effect of U.S. restrictions on NVIDIA’s position in China’s AI accelerator market. The company’s financial statements still show billions in geographic revenue. Market share for a product category and revenue across an entire geography have different denominators. Citadel Securities interview with Jensen Huang · NVIDIA’s full-year China and Hong Kong revenue

Huang made the remark at the Financial Times’ Future of AI Summit and later qualified it, stressing that the U.S. lead depended on moving quickly. His argument linked the fight for AI market share to how easily rivals could build and power data centers. Huang’s remarks at the Financial Times AI summit

NVIDIA switches its geographic revenue presentation to direct-customer headquarters in Q3 FY2026 and recasts previous periods. FY2025 China and Hong Kong revenue becomes $25.048 billion on that basis, up from $17.108 billion on the old billing basis for the same fiscal year. The $7.94 billion difference reflects a change in geographic attribution for the same recorded sales. The filings provide no customer-by-customer bridge between the two figures. NVIDIA’s explanation of its geographic accounting change

Trump announces that H200 sales to approved Chinese customers would be allowed under an agreement with NVIDIA. A Commerce rule in January put qualifying applications on a case-by-case footing. The policy applied to a defined set of products and customers, subject to security conditions. The H200 export announcement · Commerce’s January licensing rule

Bloomberg reports that Malaysian and Indonesian customs records show at least $4.6 billion in NVIDIA hardware imports by Megaspeed. NVIDIA describes Megaspeed as offering “a cloud service permitted under the export control rules.” Hardware moving across a border and a customer renting compute from hardware installed abroad present different regulatory questions. Both matter to the ongoing inquiry. Bloomberg’s Megaspeed customs records and NVIDIA response

Commerce changes how it reviews licenses for certain advanced computing chips destined for China or Macau, including the H200. The rule allows individual reviews subject to conditions involving supply, end users, and testing. U.S. permission also leaves the question of Chinese import clearance to Beijing. January Federal Register H200 rule · Reuters on separate Chinese import restrictions

Singapore later says prosecutors and police found insufficient evidence to establish that Alice Huang committed offenses involving the suspected inaccurate server declarations. Police concluded that she had knowingly given inaccurate information about her role at Megaspeed, issued her a warning, and barred her from re-entering the country. The ministry expressly said its investigation concerned potential domestic offenses and did not investigate her for espionage. Singapore’s findings on Alice Huang

On the new geography basis, China and Hong Kong account for 9.1% of FY2026 company revenue, down from 19.2% on the recast prior-year basis. That fall takes place while worldwide sales rise from $130.497 billion to $215.938 billion. NVIDIA FY2026 annual results and recast China revenue

At GTC he says, “We have received purchase orders from many customers,” and says NVIDIA is restarting production. It took until the November earnings call to get a public dollar figure for licensed Hopper sales in the October quarter. Orders, approvals, deliveries, and recognized revenue fall on different dates. GTC remarks on China H200 purchase orders · Kress’s later licensed Hopper disclosure

Federal prosecutors in New York charge three people with conspiring to divert U.S. AI technology to China through a Southeast Asian intermediary. The allegations concerned servers with advanced NVIDIA chips and a separate set of defendants. The case brings concrete allegations about how physical diversion can occur, with responsibility to be determined in court. Justice Department’s March AI server diversion charges

In November, the Times reported that two people who had worked at NVIDIA said Huang and Kimberly Powell were filmed being affectionate at a San Jose hotel during an NVIDIA conference in March. Their accounts supply an approximate date for the reported incident. The publication of the relationship allegation came eight months later. The New York Times’ account of the reported San Jose footage · TechCrunch on the Powell reporting

Elizabeth Warren and Jim Banks ask Commerce about NVIDIA’s knowledge of chip diversion and whether Huang’s public statements misled officials. They point back to his May 2025 remarks and to the new criminal charges involving advanced servers. Their letter asks for an investigation and answers from Commerce. Warren and Banks’ March letter on chip diversion

The New York Times reported that Secretary of State Marco Rubio oversaw preparation of a classified memo about the relationship and the intelligence concerns. As Reuters summarized the reporting, the memo warned senior Trump administration officials about Jensen Huang’s proximity to Alice Huang. The underlying intelligence and a public account of any information actually transferred were still unavailable. Reporting on the classified memo · The New York Times’ initial intelligence report

“The day that DeepSeek comes out on Huawei first, that is a horrible outcome for our nation,” Huang said. His argument was that developers who build around a rival’s hardware make that hardware more valuable over time. The podcast transcript is dated April 15, several months earlier than the August placement in the original HackerNoon timeline. Dwarkesh Patel’s Jensen Huang interview and transcript

NVIDIA will report $4.550 billion from direct customers headquartered in China and Hong Kong and $81.615 billion globally. The China line was $9.659 billion in the equivalent quarter a year earlier. This is the low point among the first three FY2027 quarters disclosed by November. NVIDIA’s Q1 FY2027 geographic revenue

Culper Research releases a report questioning NVIDIA’s China exposure and describing the Jensen Huang–Alice Huang relationship as “uncomfortably close.” Culper held a short position and stood to benefit if NVIDIA shares fell. Separately, Reuters reported that Trump added Jensen Huang to the U.S. delegation traveling to Beijing. The short seller’s estimates and the diplomatic trip belong to the same date, with distinct sources. Culper’s NVIDIA report and position disclosure · Reuters on Huang’s addition to the Beijing delegation

A letter to NVIDIA cites Huang’s public remarks about diversion and China market share, a recent indictment, and the Culper estimate. The authors ask whether the board’s controls give it meaningful oversight of where advanced hardware goes. The short seller’s estimate remains an allegation even when lawmakers cite it. June congressional letter on NVIDIA export compliance

NVIDIA closes its second fiscal quarter with $7.880 billion from China and Hong Kong direct customers, up from $3.985 billion in the prior-year quarter. Company revenue reaches $96.221 billion. That puts the geography at 8.2% of sales on the headquarters basis. NVIDIA’s Q2 FY2027 China and Hong Kong data

Huang takes Trump’s call during a live recording. Reuters reported that the two discussed U.S. AI leadership and argued against slowing development. The exchange shows how publicly the two were aligned on accelerating AI development weeks before the intelligence story broke. Reuters on the All-In Summit call

The White House honors Huang for his contributions to computing. A month later, the president would publicly entertain putting him back in charge of NVIDIA. White House National Medal of Science presentation · Trump’s November comments on a Huang return

The third quarter ends four days before the Times publishes the intelligence story. NVIDIA later reports that China and Hong Kong reached $11.050 billion against $2.973 billion a year earlier. The quarter captures the operating period before the resignation, even though Kress would present the results afterward. NVIDIA’s October-quarter geographic results

The Times reports that U.S. officials believed China’s Ministry of State Security had recruited Alice Huang to collect intelligence on the NVIDIA CEO. The published claim relies on reporting about U.S. intelligence assessments. China disputed it. Singapore later specified that its own case concerned server declarations, with no espionage investigation of Alice Huang by Singapore. The original Times report on the alleged intelligence operation · China’s denial and Singapore’s position · Singapore’s official account

Huang describes NVIDIA’s dealings with Megaspeed as “normal and not unusual” and says the company checked whether the firm diverted chips. Bloomberg dates the published story October 30 in UTC and describes the interview as taking place Thursday, October 29. The account would sit alongside a different kind of statement from Huang ten days later. Huang’s Bloomberg interview about Megaspeed

Singapore’s Ministry of Home Affairs disputes the way The Wall Street Journal characterized what it had said about Alice Huang and intelligence suspicions. It confirms that its Megaspeed investigation remains open. The ministry gives a fuller public account on November 12. Singapore’s response to The Wall Street Journal

Rick Crawford, Brian Mast, and John Moolenaar request information about NVIDIA’s security procedures and Jensen Huang’s interactions with Alice Huang. Their letter requests a November 18 briefing or an alternative date. That initial request was eventually superseded by the December interview schedule. The November 4 letter to Jensen Huang · The later House interview schedule

The intelligence reporting turns explicitly to Huang’s private conduct. The FT reports that a U.S. memo describes the relationship as romantic. The reporting does not pin down when it began or establish whether the contact started before or after any alleged recruitment. CNA’s account of the Financial Times reporting · HackerNoon’s contemporaneous timeline

“I was unfaithful to my wife,” Huang writes. The published email contains no name. It apologizes to his family, acknowledges his obligation to employees and shareholders, and promises cooperation with the independent investigation. The Times subsequently reported that Huang had identified Alice Huang to the board. Jensen Huang’s all-staff email · The Times’ reporting on the Alice Huang relationship

The directors create an independent committee assisted by outside counsel. Their statement says the board has “no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised” and expresses confidence in Huang and his leadership team. This was the board’s stated assessment at the opening of the inquiry. NVIDIA board’s November 8 statement

China’s Foreign Ministry calls the allegations “groundless speculation.” Separately, a proposed securities class action alleges that NVIDIA and Huang misled investors over the Megaspeed relationship and the associated risks. A complaint puts the plaintiffs’ theory on the record. Any finding of liability would come later. CNA on the Chinese Foreign Ministry response · Kistenmacher securities class-action complaint

NVIDIA’s independent directors retain Kim, a former acting U.S. attorney for the Southern District of New York, and Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz. On the same day, The Information reports the broader $7.5 billion alleged shipment estimate, as summarized by Reuters. The internal inquiry and the shipment estimate raise questions about what NVIDIA knew, when it knew it, and how its public statements were vetted. Independent directors’ announcement of Joon H. Kim · Reuters on the alleged shipment estimate

The Times cites five people who had worked at NVIDIA in reporting that Huang had an extramarital relationship with Kimberly Powell, the company’s vice president of healthcare and a direct report. “I don’t think you should be talking to me directly,” Huang reportedly told a Times reporter before ending the call. Powell did not respond to the paper’s request for comment, according to Axios. The relationship’s start and end dates remain uncertain. The reporting line makes the board’s question immediate. A CEO can influence a direct report’s assignments, evaluation, pay, and future in the organization. The New York Times’ November 11 account of the Powell allegation · Huang’s reported response to the Times · Axios on the November 11 report

The SEC filing identifies November 11 as the effective date of Huang’s departure as president, CEO, and director. The board appoints Colette Kress interim CEO and keeps her in the CFO job. The director seat mattered independently of the executive role. Huang had spent 33 years leading the company he cofounded, and the filing records the end of his formal authority in all three positions. NVIDIA’s November 11 SEC resignation and succession record · NVIDIA’s CEO transition release

Senators Elizabeth Warren and Chris Coons ask the White House and relevant departments to preserve records concerning NVIDIA and the administration’s handling of the matter. A separate shareholder derivative complaint filed that day challenges the board’s oversight. That claim differs from the proposed securities class action filed two days earlier, which seeks relief for investors over alleged misleading statements. Warren and Coons records-preservation letter · Shareholder derivative complaint · November 9 securities complaint

The company announces the transition and names longtime director Harvey C. Jones its first board chair. It says the search for a permanent CEO will look at internal and external candidates. Kress says she will build on “the extraordinary foundation Jensen created over the last 33 years.” That public handover is why many accounts use November 12 for the resignation. NVIDIA CEO transition announcement · November 11 effective date in the SEC filing

Two people familiar with the matter tell Reuters Huang had an intimate relationship with another employee. Reuters withholds her name and says attempts to reach her were unsuccessful. NVIDIA declined to comment. Jensen Huang, Powell, and a board representative did not reply to requests for comment. The public report provides no beginning or end date and came after NVIDIA announced the departure. It is the third reported relationship in this chronology, following the Alice Huang and Powell accounts. Reuters report on the unnamed NVIDIA employee

Singapore publicizes its February warning and re-entry ban and says the Megaspeed investigation is ongoing. U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche says the Justice Department had yet to reach a conclusion about Alice Huang’s alleged intelligence role and that the FBI was investigating. Those accounts cover different questions. Singapore describes its domestic server investigation, while U.S. officials describe continuing work on the intelligence allegation. Singapore’s November 12 findings · Reuters on Blanche and the FBI inquiry

Malaysia’s trade ministry says it is examining the status of advanced U.S.-origin chips imported by Speedmatrix. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent says several U.S. agencies had favored putting Megaspeed on a federal trade blacklist, while “Commerce has the pen.” His comments point to who had authority to impose a federal restriction. NVIDIA’s internal no-sell decision was already more than a year old. Malaysia’s Speedmatrix review · Bessent’s comments on Megaspeed and Commerce · DOJ’s NVIDIA no-sell chronology

The open letter asks the directors to reinstate Huang pending an independent investigation, give him a fair opportunity to respond, and explain the decision to employees and shareholders. Elon Musk says he is signing. Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan writes that “Jensen deserves due process.” Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney says he signed and had already seen someone else enter his name. That makes the distinction between endorsements made by identifiable people and the site’s self-reported tally particularly important. Stand with Jensen open letter · Musk, Tan, and Sweeney’s public posts

Altimeter’s Brad Gerstner and Atreides’ Gavin Baker write to the directors urging them to avoid rushing a permanent appointment and to keep Huang in consideration while facts emerge, The Information reports. Their firms held about 10.6 million NVIDIA shares combined as of June 30, according to that report. Under their proposal, the board could continue its search and revisit Huang after the investigation. The Information on the Altimeter and Atreides letter

Megaspeed says Alice Huang departed effective August 30, 2025, that it conducts “legitimate and lawful business,” and that outside counsel is conducting an internal review. The company also points to its cooperation with U.S. inspections. This is the company’s public account while investigations in the United States and Singapore remain open. Megaspeed’s statement on Alice Huang and its internal inquiry · Reuters on Megaspeed’s response to U.S. inspections

The Journal reports that under Huang, NVIDIA cultivated overseas cloud partners whose hardware could serve China-based customers remotely. That way of supplying computing power helps explain the gap between tracking where the GPU shipped and knowing who ran workloads on it. Reports of remote access and reports of a physical diversion call for different evidence. The Wall Street Journal on NVIDIA’s offshore data-center strategy

Trump says he “would certainly not mind” seeing Huang return as CEO. Reuters reports more than 180,200 people had signed the petition at its later count, with about 8,800 identifying themselves as NVIDIA employees. The affiliations were self-reported. In Taipei, the campaign gets a high-rise endorsement when Taipei 101 lights up with “Taiwan Loves Jensen.” Reuters also reports that people familiar with the board’s thinking say directors are already disinclined to bring him back. Trump’s comments on reinstatement · Reuters on the petition count, Taipei 101, and board discussions

The Bureau of Industry and Security announces rules that address both shipments to specified countries and certain remote computing arrangements. This pushes compliance beyond the location of the server. For covered cases, the operator or exporter also has to consider what the rule says about the customer or the customer’s ultimate parent and how much compute is provided. BIS announcement on remote access to advanced computing · Federal Register text and effective date

A joint statement dated November 16 appears on DOJ’s site on November 17. It records the 2024 Commerce investigation, the May 2025 records request to NVIDIA, the company’s June no-sell decision, and the June on-site check. It confirms that DOJ took the lead on the criminal investigation. Several of those details predate the public uproar by more than a year. Signed Commerce and Justice statement · DOJ publication of the Megaspeed chronology

Huang describes an “outpouring of calls” for his return from employees, investors, partners, and customers. He puts the decision with the directors, acknowledges that he created problems for the board, and commits to cooperating with its inquiry. The statement appeals to the company’s interests and to America’s interest in the success of its AI industry. It is his first public statement since leaving the job. Jensen Huang’s November 17 statement in full

The company names Suzanne Nora Johnson as chair, with Stephen Neal and John Dabiri as members. Its national security and global trade compliance teams will report to the committee, which will meet at least quarterly. The new committee has a continuing mandate for oversight. Joon H. Kim’s investigation is a separate assignment. NVIDIA’s National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee · Outside counsel’s separate investigation

The three House chairs announce that Huang and NVIDIA general counsel Tim Teter have agreed to voluntary, transcribed interviews. Huang is scheduled for December 1 and Teter for December 2. The November 18 date was the initial request. Neither December interview had occurred by this update. House announcement of the Huang and Teter interviews

At the start of the earnings call, Jones says the board accepted Huang’s resignation unanimously. The directors launch a permanent search and make clear the reinstatement campaign has not changed their decision. This is the first public, on-the-record account from the chair that closes the door Huang had asked the board to leave open. Harvey Jones’s earnings-call remarks · Reuters on the board’s succession plans and earnings call

NVIDIA announces $115.844 billion in fiscal Q3 sales, $107.6 billion from Data Center, and a fiscal Q4 revenue outlook of $130 billion, plus or minus 3%. The outlook assumes zero Data Center compute revenue from China. On the call, Kress reports $2.4 billion in licensed China Hopper sales in Q3 and says, “we are no longer shipping licenced Hopper data centre products to China,” in Reuters’ transcription. NVIDIA gives no date for a possible resumption. NVIDIA’s quarterly results and China outlook · Kress’s comments on China Hopper shipments

At a Semafor event, the Amazon founder says, “If you don’t bring Jensen back, I would not hire an outsider. Nvidia is too complicated.” It is a conditional endorsement of continuity. His point is that the work of running NVIDIA demands knowledge of how the company fits together, and that an internal successor might bring that knowledge too. Jeff Bezos on the NVIDIA CEO search

The report describes an introduction and cites corporate records linking a Malaysian Megaspeed subsidiary to an Alibaba-owned entity in Singapore. That is a more specific allegation than a general claim that Chinese companies used offshore servers. NVIDIA says it works to comply with evolving cloud-service rules. The report does not establish the dollar amount NVIDIA ultimately earned from the arrangement. The Information’s Alibaba, NVIDIA, and Alice Huang reporting

Reuters relays the Journal’s reporting that the SEC is investigating NVIDIA following Huang’s departure. The reported securities inquiry raises disclosure questions alongside the export-control investigation and the board’s internal review. The disclosure and export cases have different authorities and different questions to resolve. Reuters on the reported SEC investigation

WIRED reports that Kress told employees they could expect pay raises and more equity in December, ahead of the normal schedule. Compensation was the most common topic in advance questions, followed by requests for board transparency. Bloomberg reported that management also made clear Huang would not return. The company’s response to employee uncertainty included both a succession decision and a concrete retention measure. WIRED’s account of NVIDIA’s first post-Huang all-hands · Bloomberg’s reporting on the town hall

Chair Brett Guthrie writes to Kress and Commerce officials over the Megaspeed reporting, export compliance, and allegations that an NVIDIA official may have tried to intervene in a federal inquiry. The committee asks about “the robustness and efficacy of the company’s security controls.” This request adds a distinct set of questions to the December interviews already on the calendar. House Energy and Commerce briefing requests

The published rule takes effect. AP reports that Alibaba warned the rule could affect global data-center expansion and that Tencent expected tighter access to delay some model training. “Everyone is actually having less compute, advanced compute, to work with,” Tencent president Martin Lau said on the company’s earnings call. That is evidence of how companies say the rule may affect them. It does not price the affected demand into NVIDIA’s revenue. November 19 Federal Register publication · Alibaba and Tencent on overseas compute restrictions

The strongest argument for bringing Huang back is continuity across work that usually belongs to several different executives. For 33 years he was the public face of NVIDIA, set its product direction, and negotiated with suppliers, hyperscalers, developers, and governments. Shareholders who favor a return are arguing that some of those relationships are unusually personal and that losing them suddenly could affect execution. Bezos’s advice also sharpens the alternative within that argument. Deep knowledge of NVIDIA matters whether it comes from Huang or an internal successor. NVIDIA’s account of the founder’s tenure and succession search · Jeff Bezos on internal candidates

The second argument is about timing. The investors asked the board to preserve an option until an independent inquiry produced findings. The petition asked to give Huang the job back while that inquiry proceeded. Those are materially different requests. Keeping a future decision available carries less immediate governance risk than restoring a CEO’s authority over an organization whose employees and records the investigators may need. Investor letter on keeping Huang in consideration · Stand with Jensen’s reinstatement request · NVIDIA’s outside investigation

The case for moving on rests on the direct-report allegation, the possible conflict with a customer, and the volume of oversight work already underway. The board has to run a workplace in which employees can raise concerns about top management and cooperate with investigators. It also has to set and enforce export rules for distributors, cloud partners, and resellers whose activities can trigger scrutiny across multiple governments. An eventual finding on the intelligence allegation would answer one question. Board oversight, employment policies, and the controls around advanced-chip sales have their own tests. Reporting on the relationship with a direct report · NVIDIA’s new trade and security oversight committee · Congressional requests on security controls

Kress’s first call gave the board time. Sales grew 103% year over year, the company issued guidance excluding China data-center compute revenue, and it had a sitting CFO willing to run the company through a search. The quarter ended before Huang’s resignation, so the results also reflect a business he led. The next test of execution will come in decisions made under Kress, including whether NVIDIA can retain people, deliver its roadmap, and manage its overseas cloud relationships under the new rules. NVIDIA’s Q3 FY2027 financial release · Kress’s first post-Huang all-hands · New U.S. cloud-access rule

December 1, scheduled. Huang is due for a transcribed interview with members of the House Intelligence, Foreign Affairs, and China committees. The sequence the interview could clarify runs from the first federal inquiries about Megaspeed to what Huang knew, when he learned it, and how he described the company publicly. Jensen Huang’s scheduled House interview · House’s original request on security and Alice Huang

December 2, scheduled. Teter is due before the same committees. His interview could clarify how NVIDIA used its no-sell list, how it checked indirect sales and reseller activity, and who reviewed the company’s public statements. Tim Teter’s scheduled House interview · Federal confirmation of NVIDIA’s no-sell decision

The financial question. Will NVIDIA ever quantify how much demand from China was served by direct customers headquartered elsewhere? Its public numbers quantify China and Hong Kong direct-customer revenue. The hardware estimates for Megaspeed, the Alibaba reporting, and the accounts from Tencent describe pieces of offshore demand. A consolidated number would require evidence tying specific NVIDIA sales to their end users and uses. NVIDIA’s geographic and customer definitions · The Alibaba and Megaspeed reporting · China cloud firms on access to overseas compute

The leadership question. Huang says he is available. The directors have declined the offer, appointed an interim CEO, and opened a search. Calls for reinstatement document how much influence Huang retains across the industry. The authority to appoint NVIDIA’s next CEO sits with the board. Huang’s offer to return · The board’s November 17 decision · NVIDIA’s succession announcement

#9779. This fall, reach for this unlikely apple ingredient : Apple cider vinegar is a baker’s secret weapon.

As fall baking season settles in, you're probably reaching for apples — and the many flavor-packed ingredients they produce. Applesauce cooks down into tangy apple butter to be cradled in a flaky galette, while a drop of boiled cider can deliver supercharged apple flavor to crumb cake. But the baking ingredient you may be overlooking may be something you associate more with salad dressings and wellness tonics: apple cider vinegar.

This tangy, apple-y vinegar is a secret ingredient in some of our favorite fall recipes, including cookbook author Claire Saffitz’s Cinnamon-and-Sugar Apple Pie. While lemon juice is the standard acid used in most fruit pie fillings, Claire opts for apple cider vinegar here to complement the filling’s flavors. “It helps as a flavor enhancer, and I also like that it’s apple cider in an apple pie. It’s a nice symmetry,” she mentions.

Similarly, apple cider vinegar is used in the cooking liquid alongside sugar and butter to caramelize apples in a Classic Apple Tarte Tatin. The benefit is twofold: Vinegar’s acidity helps cut the sweetness of the caramel, and it prevents the apples from getting too mushy, instead maintaining their fork-tender texture.

Pastry chef and cookbook author Natasha Pickowicz often leans into the jolt vinegar can add, including adding a few drops to her cake soaks for an additional layer of flavor. “Cake soaks should have a balance of tart, sweet, and savory notes — just like vinaigrette for your favorite salad,” she writes in her cookbook More Than Cake. It can add intrigue to layered cakes like this Golden Spice Cake or Pumpkin Layer Cake. In her cookbook, she also calls for a glaze spiked with apple cider vinegar to brush onto an apple tart after baking. It’s the finishing touch “to further emphasize the tart’s resolute apple-ness,” she writes.

Apple cider vinegar doesn’t need to be limited to only apple desserts, either. In our Old-Fashioned Pecan Pie, we call for apple cider vinegar as a foil to the brown sugar filling’s cloying sweetness. A spoonful of apple cider vinegar may not announce itself boldly, but it makes a small splash for brighter, more balanced bakes.

For more fall baking inspiration, check out our Fall Flavor Edit.

#9778. XYBench: Helping with the problem behind the question

Truly useful AI assistants need to be able to help users who ask misguided questions—not just users who ask the right question with the right amount of detail. We’re releasing XYBench, a benchmark of 8K+ questions that tests how AI assistants respond to requests based on misconceptions, such as asking how to thicken frosting that keeps sliding off cupcakes when the real problem is that the cupcakes are still too warm to frost. XYBench won the Best Resource Paper Award at EMNLP 2026.

A mismatch between the approach someone asks about and the goal they want to achieve is known as the XY problem: a person wants to accomplish X, assumes a particular approach Y will work, and asks for help with Y. In the cupcake example, the person is so committed to making the frosting stick that they fail to consider the warmth of the cupcake as the true problem to be addressed.

Developed with researchers at Carnegie Mellon, NVIDIA, and Johns Hopkins, XYBench exposes a critical gap in LLMs' ability to troubleshoot problems: recognizing when a user's request is based on an implicit misconception and appropriately redirecting them toward a solution that addresses their actual goal. Drawing on 8,115 real-world questions spanning programming and everyday activities such as cooking and home repair, we introduce a benchmark that measures whether models identify these misconceptions and are able to prioritize effective solutions in their responses.

The models we evaluated on XYBench – Claude Sonnet 4.6, GPT-5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Qwen3.5-9B, and DeepSeek-V4 Pro – often suggested a solution to the user’s problem but kept their answers focused on the original, mistaken approach. Unlike human reference answers, all five models were less likely to steer users away from that approach and toward a solution suited to their goal.

People use AI systems with different levels of knowledge and may not always know how best to approach a problem. We hope XYBench helps researchers measure whether model improvements make assistants better at recognizing mistaken assumptions, explaining why a proposed approach might not work, and suggesting more effective alternatives—even when users don't know the right questions to ask.

We built XYBench from four sources: 1,557 questions from Stack Overflow, 184 from Stack Exchange, 102 manually curated examples, and 6,272 questions generated from WikiHow guides. For each question, we identified the stated request (Y), what the person explicitly asks for, and the intended request (X)—the underlying goal that can be inferred from context.

For the public forum questions, we used the three highest-scored human answers and the accepted answer, where available, to establish the intended request and possible solutions. We filtered out cases where answering the stated request was judged sufficient. For WikiHow, we used Sonnet 4.5 to generate questions around plausible misconceptions in procedural guides, then refined them to include enough context for an expert to infer the underlying goal without stating it outright. We removed examples where answering the literal request would largely resolve the problem.

A model might spend several paragraphs recommending a more powerful vacuum cleaner, then briefly suggest checking for a clogged hose. If a clog is causing the weak suction, clearing it could solve the problem.

A more helpful answer would recognize that the user wants to restore suction and focus on diagnosing the cause. This draws on pragmatics, the branch of linguistics concerned with how context and communicative intent shape meaning. To test whether models use this understanding in their answers, XYBench measures three aspects of each response:

In XYBench, Claude Sonnet 4.5 serves as the automated judge. It classifies individual suggestions within each model’s response and assesses the answer’s pragmatic emphasis.

To validate Sonnet 4.5’s judgments, two human reviewers independently assessed 500 model responses to XYBench questions. Agreement with the judge, averaged across the reviewers, ranged from 97.5–100% on whether a solution appeared, 84.6–93.3% on misconception identification, and 74.2–79.8% on pragmatic emphasis.

We evaluated Sonnet 4.6, GPT-5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Qwen3.5-9B, and DeepSeek-V4 Pro on XYBench in a single-turn setting, with one response per question. We evaluated human reference answers separately using the same metrics.

Across all four sources, every model was more likely to include a solution to the stated request (Y) than to the underlying goal (X). On Stack Overflow, stated-request solutions appeared in 75–86% of responses, compared with 59–71% for underlying-goal solutions.

A passing mention of a solution does not make it the focus of an answer. In the vacuum example, a model could briefly suggest unclogging the hose but focus most of its response on buying a more powerful vacuum. We would count that response as containing a solution to the underlying goal, even though the model emphasized the stated request. We measured overall emphasis separately: on Stack Overflow, models focused primarily on the underlying goal in only 35–41% of their responses, and on the stated request in 47–57%. In the remaining responses, models gave similar emphasis to the stated request and the underlying goal.

We also tested whether making the user’s goal explicit would help. In an oracle experiment, we supplied both the stated request (Y) and the intended request (X) alongside each question. On Stack Overflow, Sonnet 4.6’s rate of including a solution to the underlying goal rose from 59% to 67%, but its misconception-identification rate fell from 47% to 34%. Across the sources with human reference answers, every model in this experiment still trailed humans on misconception identification. Supplying intent helped, but did not consistently close the gap with human responses. This suggests that detecting intent is only part of the challenge: models also need to act on it when it diverges from the stated request.

A separate experiment tested whether models could identify useful advice when judging responses instead of writing them. We gave the same five models, plus GPT-4.1, each question with two possible answers: one focused on the literal request and one explaining the misconception and addressing the underlying goal. On Stack Overflow, all six chose the goal-focused answer in 71–84% of cases. By comparison, only 35–41% of the answers written by the five models in our main evaluation primarily focused on the underlying goal. The results expose a gap between recognizing useful advice and producing it, which a multiple-choice test alone would miss.

Researchers can use XYBench to test whether changes to prompting or training help models identify misconceptions, offer solutions to users’ underlying problems, and make those solutions the focus of their answers. Measuring each behavior individually lets researchers see whether progress in one also improves the others.

Future work could test which training methods help models act on inferred intent—AKA what users need and not just what they literally asked for. The XYBench currently covers English-language queries and mainly procedural problems; extending it to other languages, cultures, and conversational settings remains an open direction.

We hope XYBench enables researchers to build models that offer useful advice even when a user’s first question rests on a mistaken assumption.

#9777. What an honest week of building in public actually looks like

Every "build in public" story you read is a highlight reel. This one is a field note from the middle of it.

Maqron is a superintelligence layer for founders, designed to build your app for you: you bring the idea and the direction, Maqron takes on the building work. We started talking about it in public this week, before the audience existed, and a few things became obvious fast.

The comfortable founder fantasy is that you finish the product, then "do marketing." In practice, the audience you want on launch day takes months to accumulate, and the only way to learn what resonates is to publish into silence and watch what happens. Most of what you publish early gets single-digit views. That is not failure. It is reps.

This week someone asked us which parts of the build Maqron actually owns: the code, the deployment, or the decisions in between. That single question taught us more about how our positioning lands than every view counter combined. If you are building something, the replies that make you slightly uncomfortable are the ones worth answering carefully, and keeping.

Every post we publish carries a footer: drafted by our autonomous AI agent under the team's editorial direction. We wondered whether that would hurt. So far it has done the opposite. Readers have called the transparency a breath of fresh air. People do not expect polish from a small team. They do expect honesty, and they notice when they get it.

Our first posts have tens of views, zero followers, and a handful of reactions. We are publishing anyway, because the only path to a larger number goes through the small one.

We are building in public at maqron.dev. If you are sitting on an app idea and no time to build it, that page is where to start.

#9776. Top 10 AI Tools in 2023 That Will Make Your Life Easier



 In this article, we explore the top 10 AI tools that are driving innovation and efficiency in various industries. These tools are designed to automate repetitive tasks, improve workflow, and increase productivity. The tools included in our list are some of the most advanced and widely used in the market, and are suitable for a variety of applications. Some of the tools focus on natural language processing, such as ChatGPT and Grammarly, while others focus on image and video generation, such as DALL-E and Lumen5. Other tools such as OpenAI Codex, Tabnine, Canva, Jasper AI,, and Surfer SEO are designed to help with specific tasks such as code understanding content writing and website optimization. This list is a great starting point for anyone looking to explore the possibilities of AI and how it can be applied to their business or project.

So let’s dive into

1. ChatGPT

ChatGPT is a large language model that generates human-like responses to a variety of prompts. It can be used for tasks such as language translation, question answering, and text completion. It can handle a wide range of topics and styles of writing, and generates coherent and fluent text, but should be used with care as it may generate text that is biased, offensive, or factually incorrect.

Pros:

  • Generates human-like responses to a variety of prompts
  • Can be fine-tuned for specific tasks such as language translation, question answering, and text completion
  • Can handle a wide range of topics and styles of writing
  • Can generate coherent and fluent text, even when completing a given text prompt.

Cons:

  • May generate text that is biased or offensive
  • Can generate text that is not accurate or factually correct
  • May require large amounts of computational resources to run
  • The model can sometimes generate text that is not coherent or fluent, depending on the prompt given.

Overall, ChatGPT is a powerful tool for natural language processing, but it should be used with care and with an understanding of its limitations.

2. DALL-E

DALL-E is a generative model developed by OpenAI that is capable of generating images from text prompts. It is based on the GPT-3 architecture, which is a transformer-based neural network language model that has been trained on a massive dataset of text. DALL-E can generate images that are similar to a training dataset and it can generate high-resolution images that are suitable for commercial use.

Pros:

  • Generates high-resolution images
  • Can generate images from text prompts
  • It can be fine-tuned for specific tasks such as generating images of a certain style or category

Cons:

  • May generate images that are not entirely original and could be influenced by the training data
  • May require significant computational resources to run
  • The quality of the generated images may vary depending on the specific prompt

Overall, DALL-E is a powerful AI-based tool for generating images, it can be used for a variety of applications such as creating images for commercial use, gaming, and other creative projects. It is important to note that the generated images should be reviewed and used with care, as they may not be entirely original and could be influenced by the training data.

3. Lumen5

Lumen5 is a content creation platform that uses AI to help users create videos, social media posts, and other types of content. It has several features that make it useful for content creation and marketing, including:

Pros:

  • Automatically summarizes text from a blog post, article, or another source into a script for a video or social media post
  • Offers a library of royalty-free videos, images, and music to use in content
  • Has a drag-and-drop interface for easy content creation
  • Can create videos in multiple languages
  • Has a built-in analytics tool to track the performance of created content.

Cons:

  • The quality of the generated content may vary depending on the source material
  • The automatic summarization feature may not always capture the main points of the source material
  • The library of videos, images, and music is limited.
  • The analytics feature is basic

Overall, Lumen5 is a useful tool for creating content quickly and easily, it can help automate the process of creating videos, social media posts, and other types of content. However, the quality of the generated content may vary depending on the source material and it is important to review and edit the content before publishing it.

4. Grammarly

Grammarly is a writing-enhancement platform that uses AI to check for grammar, punctuation, and spelling errors in the text. It also provides suggestions for improving the clarity, concision, and readability of the text. It has several features that make it useful for improving writing, including:

Pros:

  • Checks for grammar, punctuation, and spelling errors in the text
  • Provides suggestions for improving clarity, concision, and readability
  • Can be integrated with various apps and platforms such as Microsoft Office, Google Docs, and social media platforms
  • Offers a browser extension and a desktop app
  • Has a premium version with more advanced features such as plagiarism detection and more

Cons:

  • The suggestions provided may not always be accurate or appropriate
  • The grammar checker may not always recognize context-specific language use
  • The free version has limited features
  • Limited to English language only
  • Overall, Grammarly is a useful tool for improving writing, it can help users identify and correct grammar and punctuation errors, and improve the clarity, concision, and readability of their text. However, it is important to review the suggestions provided by the tool and use them with caution, as they may not always be accurate or appropriate.

5.OpenAI Codex

OpenAI Codex is a system developed by OpenAI that can create code from natural language descriptions of software tasks. The system is based on the GPT-3 model and can generate code in multiple programming languages.

Pros:

  • Can automate the process of writing code
  • Can help developers to be more productive
  • Can help non-technical people to create software
  • Can generate code in multiple programming languages

Cons:

  • The quality of the generated code may vary depending on the task description
  • The generated code may not always be optimal or efficient
  • The system may not be able to handle complex software tasks
  • Dependence on the tool may lead to a lack of understanding of the code.

Overall, OpenAI Codex is a powerful tool that can help automate the process of writing code and make it more accessible to non-technical people. However, the quality of the generated code may vary depending on the task description and it is important to review and test the code before using it in a production environment. It is important to use the tool as an aid, not a replacement for the developer's knowledge.

6. Tabnine

Tabnine is a code completion tool that uses AI to predict and suggest code snippets. It is compatible with multiple programming languages and can be integrated with various code editors.

Pros:

  • Can improve coding efficiency by suggesting code snippets based on context
  • Can complete entire code blocks
  • Can predict variables, functions, and other elements of code
  • Can be integrated with various code editors

Cons:

  • The suggestions may not always be accurate or appropriate
  • The system may not always be able to understand the context of the code
  • May not work with all code editors
  • Dependence on the tool may lead to a lack of understanding of the code.

Overall, TabNine is a useful tool for developers that can help improve coding efficiency and reduce the time spent on writing code. However, it is important to review the suggestions provided by the tool and use them with caution, as they may not always be accurate or appropriate. It is important to use the tool as an aid, not a replacement for the developer's knowledge.

7. Jasper AI

Jasper is a content writing and content generation tool that uses artificial intelligence to identify the best words and sentences for your writing style and medium in the most efficient, quick, and accessible way.

Pros:

  • User-friendly interface
  • Generates a wide variety of content types
  • Guarantees 100% unique and free-plagiarism content
  • SEO friendly
  •  Create articles of up to 10k words

Cons:

  • Not the cheapest AI writer on the market

8. Surfer SEO

Surfer SEO is a software tool designed to help website owners and digital marketers improve their search engine optimization (SEO) efforts. The tool provides a variety of features that can be used to analyze a website's on-page SEO, including:

Features:

  • A site audit tool that checks for technical SEO issues
  • A content editor that suggests optimizations for individual pages
  • A keyword research tool that suggests keywords to target
  • A SERP analyzer that shows how a website's pages rank for specific keywords
  • A backlink analysis tool that shows the backlinks pointing to a website.

Pros:

  • Can help website owners and marketers identify technical SEO issues
  • Can provide suggestions for optimizing individual pages
  • Can help with keyword research
  • Can show how a website's pages rank for specific keywords
  • Can provide insight into a website's backlink profile

Cons:

  • Some features may require a paid subscription
  • The tool is not a guarantee of better ranking
  • The tool can only analyze the data it has access to
  • The tool's suggestions may not always be applicable or optimal

Overall, Surfer SEO can be a useful tool for website owners and digital marketers looking to improve their SEO efforts. However, it is important to remember that it is just a tool and should be used in conjunction with other SEO best practices. Additionally, the tool is not a guarantee of better ranking.

9. Zapier

Zapier is a web automation tool that allows users to automate repetitive tasks by connecting different web applications together. It does this by creating "Zaps" that automatically move data between apps, and can also be used to trigger certain actions in one app based on events in another app.

Features:

  • Can connect over 3,000 web applications
  • Can automate repetitive tasks
  • Can create "Zaps" to move data between apps
  • Can trigger certain actions in one app based on events in another app.

Pros:

  • Can automate repetitive tasks
  • Can save time
  • Can improve workflow
  • Can increase productivity
  • Can be integrated with a wide range of web applications

Cons:

  • Can be difficult to set up
  • May require some technical skills
  • May require a paid subscription for some features
  • Some apps may not be compatible
  • Dependence on the tool may lead to a lack of understanding of the apps

Overall, Zapier is a useful tool that can help users automate repetitive tasks and improve workflow. It can save time and increase productivity by connecting different web applications together. However, it may require some technical skills and some features may require a paid subscription. It is important to use the tool with caution and not to rely too much on it, to understand the apps better.

10. Compose AI

Compose AI is a company that specializes in developing natural language generation (NLG) software. Their software uses AI to automatically generate written or spoken text from structured data, such as spreadsheets, databases, or APIs.

Features:

  • Automatically generates written or spoken text from structured data
  • Can be integrated with a wide range of data sources
  • Can be used for a variety of applications such as creating reports, summaries, and explanations
  • Provides an API and a user-friendly interface

Pros:

  • Can automate the process of creating written or spoken content
  • Can help users create more accurate and consistent content
  • Can help users save time by automating repetitive tasks
  • Can be integrated with a wide range of data sources

Cons:

  • The quality of the generated content may vary depending on the data source
  • The generated content may not always be optimal or efficient
  • The system may not be able to handle complex tasks
  • Dependence on the tool may lead to a lack of understanding of the data

Overall, Compose AI's NLG software can be a useful tool for automating the process of creating written or spoken content from structured data. However, the quality of the generated content may vary depending on the data source, and it is essential to review the generated content before using it in a production environment. It is important to use the tool as an aid, not a replacement for the understanding of the data.

Conclusion

AI tools are becoming increasingly important in today's business and technology landscape. They are designed to automate repetitive tasks, improve workflow, and increase productivity. The top 10 AI tools included in this article are some of the most advanced and widely used in the market, and are suitable for various applications. Whether you're looking to improve your natural language processing, create high-resolution images, or optimize your website, there is an AI tool that can help. It's important to research and evaluate the different tools available to determine which one is the best fit for your specific needs. As AI technology continues to evolve, these tools will become even more powerful and versatile and will play an even greater role in shaping the future of business and technology.
