#9775. International Men’s Day: Anthropic IPOs, Trump Meets Putin and Xi, and GTA 6 Is Released

Amplifying words and ideas to separate the ordinary from the extraordinary, making the mundane majestic.

Amplifying words and ideas to separate the ordinary from the extraordinary, making the mundane majestic.

Amplifying words and ideas to separate the ordinary from the extraordinary, making the mundane majestic.

November 19, 2026. Three of the world’s most powerful men meet to discuss nuclear weapons. An artificial intelligence company raises more money in a single IPO than most countries spend on technology. And millions of men finally get to steal fictional cars in Vice City.

An ⁠excellent Venn diagram circulating on X captured the extraordinary coincidence of three events occurring on November 19, 2026.

Someone in our HackerNoon Slack channel pointed out the final coincidence: it’s International Men’s Day.

The joke is funny enough on its own. But the more you investigate the actual news, the stranger the connections become.

Elon Musk thinks AI might eventually generate games like GTA without traditional developers. Anthropic’s CEO believes advanced AI chips should be kept away from China. Trump thinks whoever wins the race to superintelligence wins everything. Meanwhile, the leaders of the world’s largest nuclear powers are discussing how not to destroy civilization.

And Rockstar Games has just released a video game about committing crimes.

Let’s examine this particularly remarkable day in the history of men.

On November 18, Anthropic announced that it had ⁠priced its initial public offering at $83 per share.

The offering comprised 980 million shares, representing approximately $81.34 billion in gross proceeds before expenses and excluding any additional shares sold through the underwriters’ option.

Not all of that money goes to Anthropic. Approximately 23.6 million shares were being sold by existing stockholders.

Nevertheless, it was an extraordinary amount of money.

When Anthropic began trading on the Nasdaq under the ticker ANT on November 19, shares opened at $111.50.

That’s approximately 34% above the IPO price.

As ⁠Barron’s reported when trading began, investors who received shares at the offering price immediately found themselves holding something worth considerably more.

The $83 price also happens to be almost identical to the price of GTA VI.

For approximately $80, Rockstar gives you a fictional world where you can do almost anything.

For $83, Anthropic gives eligible IPO investors a tiny ownership stake in a company trying to build artificial intelligence that might eventually do almost anything.

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has spent years arguing that increasingly powerful artificial intelligence could fundamentally transform society.

Now public investors get to bet on that argument.

In an ⁠interview following the IPO, Amodei reflected on how rapidly the technology’s economic implications had become real:

“I don’t think we really believed it until it actually happened.”

His sister, Anthropic cofounder and president Daniela Amodei, characterized the IPO as another milestone rather than the destination:

“it’s like one stop on the journey, right?”

The company has also warned investors that its commitments to AI safety may sometimes conflict with maximizing profits.

What happens when shareholders want Anthropic to make more money, but Anthropic’s leadership believes making more money would create unacceptable risks?

Senator Elizabeth Warren has already raised concerns about exposing investors and retirement savings to the risks surrounding advanced AI.

In a statement ahead of the offering, she argued:

“The SEC must protect investors and Congress must act quickly to put in place safeguards on advanced AI development.”

The broader contradiction is difficult to ignore.

Anthropic was founded partly because its creators believed advanced AI required extraordinary caution.

Now it is participating in one of the largest financial spectacles in stock-market history.

Apparently, protecting humanity is extremely capital-intensive.

While Anthropic was making financial history in New York, Donald Trump, Xi Jinping, and Vladimir Putin were making diplomatic history in Shenzhen, China.

The three leaders held an unprecedented trilateral summit on November 19 during the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation gathering.

According to ⁠Reuters’ account of the meeting, nuclear weapons and the war in Ukraine were among the major subjects.

Xi described the gathering as a historic opportunity for cooperation.

Putin emphasized that the three countries shared interests in resolving regional conflicts, including Ukraine.

There is something extraordinary about three men collectively representing such enormous military and economic power sitting around a table to discuss whether they can trust one another.

Especially when you read what they actually said.

During the summit, Trump offered a remarkably straightforward explanation of why nuclear disarmament is difficult.

According to the ⁠published transcript of his remarks:

“Once you have the nuclear weapons, it’s very hard to not have them.”

“It’s very hard to give them up as the leader of a country.”

They are also the sort of statements that sound like a man explaining why he still has a garage full of things he purchased fifteen years ago.

Except the garage contains nuclear warheads.

Trump also praised Shenzhen, telling the gathering:

“They have a major city, one of the biggest cities anywhere in the world, and it’s flawless.”

The president of the United States was discussing global security while also delivering what sounded like a five-star hotel review.

Before the trilateral meeting, Trump greeted Putin warmly.

According to ⁠ABC News’ coverage, Trump referred to the Russian president as:

He also praised their longstanding relationship.

That friendship is politically consequential, given Russia’s continuing war against Ukraine and the enormous disagreements between Washington and Moscow.

Trump’s remarks illustrate the central tension of the summit: personal relationships between leaders are being presented as a potential route toward resolving conflicts involving millions of people.

Whether those relationships produce meaningful agreements remains another question.

The leaders endorsed a declaration emphasizing the importance of reducing nuclear risks.

“a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought”

It is also a principle the major nuclear powers have endorsed before.

The declaration did not establish a specific schedule for eliminating nuclear weapons, end the war in Ukraine, or resolve the major strategic disagreements among the three countries.

As ⁠the Associated Press observed in its analysis of the summit, the meeting’s symbolism appeared more substantial than its immediate policy achievements.

The world’s most powerful men agreed that peace is good.

Humanity will now wait to see what they do about it.

The overlap between Anthropic’s IPO and the international summit is arguably the most important part of the meme.

Advanced artificial intelligence requires enormous computing resources.

Those resources depend heavily on sophisticated semiconductors, including Nvidia’s most advanced chips.

And access to those chips has become a central dispute between the United States and China.

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has been particularly outspoken about this issue.

In his ⁠essay about DeepSeek and American export controls, Amodei argued:

“Export controls serve a vital purpose: keeping democratic nations at the forefront of AI development.”

His argument is that restricting access to advanced computing hardware can help preserve America’s technological advantage.

China, unsurprisingly, sees restrictions on access to advanced technology rather differently.

During his visit to China, Trump discussed the competition to develop superintelligence.

His summary was characteristically direct:

SI refers to superintelligence: artificial intelligence that exceeds human capabilities across a broad range of intellectual tasks.

Trump’s statement captures the geopolitical stakes in six words.

The economy? Military superiority? Scientific progress? Control over the future?

At APEC, Trump also rejected international restrictions that could constrain American AI development.

As ⁠ABC News reported, Trump opposed what he called globalist regulation of advanced AI.

Meanwhile, Xi emphasized international cooperation and human oversight.

The Chinese government’s account of his position called for countries to:

“ensure that AI is always under human control”

These competing positions reveal a remarkable situation.

The United States wants to maintain its lead in artificial intelligence.

China wants greater access to advanced computing and a meaningful role in setting global rules.

Anthropic wants to develop increasingly capable AI while maintaining its safety commitments.

And investors want all of these companies to make money.

These objectives are not necessarily compatible.

Yet they are increasingly shaping the same global economy.

While world leaders were discussing nuclear weapons and investors were buying shares in Anthropic, Rockstar Games finally released Grand Theft Auto VI.

The company confirmed the launch in its ⁠official November 19 announcement.

The game is available on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S.

Its standard edition costs $79.99 in the United States.

That is $3.01 less than Anthropic’s IPO price.

Unlike an Anthropic share, however, the game comes with an entire fictional criminal economy.

Players return to Vice City and the fictional state of Leonida, following the story of Jason and Lucia.

It has been more than thirteen years since Grand Theft Auto V arrived in September 2013.

Rockstar delayed GTA VI several times before settling on November 19, 2026.

In its ⁠final major delay announcement, the company explained:

“these extra months will allow us to finish the game with the level of polish you have come to expect and deserve.”

Apparently, building a realistic simulation of American criminality takes longer than building some forms of artificial intelligence.

Rockstar’s parent company, Take-Two Interactive, is publicly traded.

Its CEO, Strauss Zelnick, has repeatedly emphasized the enormous commercial significance of GTA VI.

“a lot of people will be calling in sick on November 19”

That is a remarkable prediction from the CEO of a publicly traded company.

Imagine Anthropic’s CEO announcing that the company’s next AI model would cause millions of employees to stop showing up for work.

Actually, that’s not too far from what some people in the AI industry have been predicting.

Take-Two previously forecast approximately $8 billion to $8.2 billion in net bookings for fiscal 2027.

Those figures cover the company’s broader business, not just GTA VI.

Nevertheless, they demonstrate the scale of the expectations surrounding the launch.

The connections become even stranger when Elon Musk enters the story.

Musk has repeatedly argued that generative artificial intelligence will eventually transform video game development.

Instead of spending years and billions of dollars building a game, developers might eventually describe the world they want and let AI generate it.

In January 2026, Vercel CEO Guillermo Rauch suggested:

“There’s definitely a non-zero chance we get ‘generate your own GTA 6 in a few minutes’ before GTA 6.”

Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney also entertained the possibility of AI-generated games.

The broader discussion concerned whether systems capable of generating images, video, and software could eventually generate entire interactive worlds.

That possibility would fundamentally change the economics of the video game industry.

Rockstar has spent more than a decade building GTA VI.

An AI system that could generate comparable experiences in minutes would represent an extraordinary technological achievement.

But generating a playable environment is not the same as creating a coherent, polished game with compelling characters, sophisticated systems, and a consistent artistic vision.

GTA VI is a particularly useful test case because its value depends on more than the number of buildings, vehicles, or characters an AI could generate.

It depends on how all those pieces work together.

Zelnick has also challenged sweeping claims about artificial intelligence replacing human workers.

Responding to Musk’s predictions about automation, Zelnick reportedly asked:

“If AI was going to take anyone’s job, wouldn’t it take his job?”

“Maybe Elon Musk is indeed a simulation, it’s possible.”

The exchange illustrates a disagreement that extends well beyond video games.

Musk believes increasingly capable AI could dramatically reduce the need for human labor.

Zelnick runs a company whose most important product depends on thousands of people coordinating their creative and technical work over many years.

Both men have enormous financial interests in their respective visions of the future.

And both are discussing a technology that could transform the businesses they operate.

On International Men’s Day, the argument is particularly appropriate.

One billionaire thinks AI might eventually generate the work of another billionaire’s employees.

The other billionaire wonders why the first billionaire still needs to work.

There is a deeper connection between Anthropic and GTA VI.

Both companies are building systems that simulate aspects of the world.

Rockstar builds a fictional environment with characters, vehicles, economies, police departments, and social systems.

Anthropic develops AI systems designed to understand and interact with the real world through language, software, and other tools.

GTA VI’s characters exist inside a fictional world.

Claude’s outputs can influence decisions outside the computer.

But both businesses depend on the ability to represent increasingly complex aspects of human behavior.

The comparison becomes more interesting when considering the economics.

Rockstar spends years developing a world that millions of people will pay to enter.

Anthropic spends billions developing intelligence that businesses hope will make work more efficient.

Rockstar wants people to spend more time inside its product.

Anthropic’s customers often want to spend less time completing tasks.

The other sells a tool for changing reality.

And on November 19, 2026, both are asking consumers and investors to pay approximately $80 for a piece of the future.

The final overlap in the Venn diagram reads:

It is attached to GTA VI and the Trump–Xi–Putin summit.

Grand Theft Auto is a video game built around criminal activity, reckless driving, violence, and increasingly elaborate ways to behave badly.

International diplomacy, meanwhile, involves leaders making decisions with consequences for millions or billions of people.

The difference is that GTA VI has a reset button.

There is also a revealing contrast in how the two events are evaluated.

Rockstar’s success will be measured through sales, reviews, player engagement, and the quality of its game.

The summit’s success will be measured through changes in international relations, nuclear risks, military conflicts, and economic cooperation.

Rockstar can release a patch when something goes wrong.

Perhaps the most absurd part of the day is that the fictional criminal world might offer a more predictable set of rules than the real geopolitical one.

The observance was established to recognize positive male role models, celebrate men’s contributions to families and communities, and raise awareness of issues affecting men’s health and well-being.

Its stated objectives include recognizing:

“everyday, working-class men who are living decent, honest lives.”

Those men are largely absent from the Venn diagram.

There are no circles for fathers taking their children to school.

No circles for men caring for aging parents.

No circles for teachers, nurses, construction workers, or friends helping one another through difficult times.

Instead, the world’s attention is focused on billionaires, presidents, nuclear weapons, artificial intelligence, and a video game about stealing cars.

There is something appropriate about that.

International Men’s Day is partly about recognizing the positive things men contribute to society.

The day’s biggest headlines offer an unusually vivid illustration of how much power men still exercise over its future.

Some of that power produces extraordinary technological achievements.

Some produces entertainment enjoyed by millions.

And some creates risks that everyone else must live with.

The International Men’s Day organizers have emphasized that improving men’s lives benefits society more broadly.

That is a more useful principle than treating masculinity as a competition to accumulate the most money, military power, or technological influence.

There are also important women in these stories.

Anthropic cofounder Daniela Amodei helped lead the company to its public-market debut.

GTA VI features Lucia Caminos as one of its two protagonists.

And the consequences of decisions made by the three presidents in Shenzhen will affect women and men alike.

The Venn diagram is funny because it compresses three enormous stories into one ridiculous coincidence.

But the stories are connected by something more consequential than their shared date.

They are all about who gets to control the future.

Anthropic wants to build increasingly powerful artificial intelligence.

Trump, Xi, and Putin want to shape the international rules under which that technology develops.

Rockstar wants to create a fictional world so compelling that millions of people will voluntarily disappear into it.

And ordinary people are left trying to figure out what all of this means for their lives.

And if he doesn’t answer, don’t rule out Vice City.

#9774. RAG vs GraphRAG vs Knowledge Graphs: Choosing the Right Enterprise Knowledge Architecture

Microsoft now reports sub-second retrieval with GraphRAG Zero. Yet independent benchmarks show graph-based systems can lose to ordinary RAG. RAG vs GraphRAG vs Knowledge Graphs isn't a race to add nodes. It's a decision about where your enterprise's answers actually live.

RAG retrieves relevant evidence, usually text passages, to ground an LLM's response. GraphRAG augments retrieval with relationships, graph neighborhoods, or graph-derived summaries to connect information across sources. A knowledge graph stores entities and explicit relationships as reusable enterprise data; applications can query it without generating text. RAG and GraphRAG are retrieval-grounded answering approaches. A knowledge graph is an information asset that either approach can use.

Important: An automatically extracted GraphRAG index is not necessarily an authoritative enterprise knowledge graph.

The deciding factor is the question your application must answer.

Consider a procurement assistant connected to supplier contracts, purchase orders, incident reports, and operational data.

GraphRAG is worth testing when answers require several connected documents, entity disambiguation, or a summary of patterns across a large collection. Graph traversal can bring related evidence together; community summaries can improve corpus-wide coverage. It is not automatically more accurate than hybrid RAG for one-document lookups. Benchmark actual enterprise questions because extraction errors, missing links, and maintenance costs can erase the benefit.

Microsoft's GraphRAG documentation describes local, global, and DRIFT search.

Its newer GraphRAG Zero research reports 0.93-second average context retrieval in a specific evaluation, not a universal production latency guarantee.

Meanwhile, AWS's September 2026 reference architecture combines GraphRAG and LightRAG on shared infrastructure, allowing developers to select retrieval methods per query.

The architectural shift is toward selective retrieval, not replacing every vector index with a graph.

Build a governed knowledge graph when relationships must remain consistent across multiple applications, not merely help one chatbot answer questions. Supplier dependencies, customer identities, ownership hierarchies, and data lineage often require stable identifiers, typed relationships, source provenance, and change history. Query those facts deterministically where possible; use RAG to explain them. A graph inferred solely from documents needs verification before it drives high-stakes decisions.

Supplier → supplies → Component → used_in → Product

Each relationship should have a source, owner, validity date, and access policy.

A practical implementation should follow six stages:

The intent-detection functions require validation against real queries. This example illustrates routing logic, not a complete production implementation.

Quokka Labs' eight-stage RAG retrieval failure ladder provides a practical framework for diagnosing chunking, retrieval ranking, and context assembly failures before introducing another architecture.

Don't choose an architecture based on a vendor demonstration.

Build an evaluation set of 50 representative enterprise questions:

Use the same documents, model, and evaluation criteria across competing retrieval approaches.

Decision rule: Add graph complexity only when it improves relevant answer quality enough to justify additional engineering and operating costs.

This distinction matters. Independent GraphRAG-Bench research, published at ICLR 2026, reports that graph-based approaches frequently underperform standard RAG on certain real-world tasks.

For more implementation detail, explore Quokka Labs' Graph RAG vs Vector RAG comparison.

At Quokka Labs, 15+ years of product engineering experience informs how we design AI-native applications around measurable workflows and governed data.

For Run The Day, Quokka Labs integrated a knowledge-connected AI assistant to help race directors access operational guidance and event information.

The implementation illustrates a practical principle: solve the document retrieval and workflow integration problem before introducing graph complexity.

The same discipline applies when adding entity relationships, agent workflows, or new knowledge sources.

Not universally. GraphRAG can provide stronger context for relationship-intensive or corpus-wide questions. Traditional or hybrid RAG can be more efficient for straightforward document retrieval.

GraphRAG approaches generally use graph structure or graph-derived information. Some construct graphs from documents; others use existing knowledge graphs or lightweight graph representations.

No. Knowledge graphs improve relationship traceability, but incorrect edges, stale data, and unsupported generation can still produce inaccurate answers.

RAG is a strong baseline for document-based enterprise AI. GraphRAG becomes valuable when connecting evidence across sources matters. Knowledge graphs are worth maintaining when verified business relationships must serve multiple systems.

The best architecture may combine all three but only where each contributes measurable value.

#9773. Build a Robot Pick-and-Place Simulation with SimReady Assets

This walkthrough showcases a beverage can pick-and-place task that uses the UR17G arm, Robotiq 2F-140 gripper, and beverage can to compose a scene in Isaac Sim, check their behavior, and run a pick-and-place example with agent-generated controls.

For robotics workflows, SimReady means an OpenUSD asset has been prepared with the properties needed for a defined simulation use case, such as collisions, mass, joints, and joint drives. SimReady Central, an open asset library on Hugging Face, lets you reuse robot and object assets with authored simulation properties and profile-validation evidence. For more about the library and its launch, read the announcement blog.

SimReady Foundation defines what features the OpenUSD asset needs for a simulation use case. Its specifications connect three levels:

For this task, those properties include the arm and gripper’s joints and a beverage can asset collisions and mass. Validation checks these settings against the profile’s requirements. The simulation then tests whether the assembled robot can use them to pick up and move the can.

The UR17G, Robotiq 2F-140, and beverage can packages include the models and their simulation settings. You assemble the scene and add task code to define the arm–gripper assembly, work surface, starting positions, and controls for moving the arm and opening and closing the gripper.

Figure 2. SimReady Central supplies the asset models and simulation settings and the example scene and controls define the pick-and-place task.

A robot can look visually correct while stationary in Isaac Sim but move or interact with objects incorrectly when the simulation runs. Before running pick-and-place, test its joints, movement, and contact behavior. You can ask the agent to perform these tests or do them manually in Isaac Sim.

During pick-and-place, watch whether a beverage can stay in the gripper as the arm moves. Asset structures vary, so use the settings in your loaded scene as your starting point. We will be going through the overall process of downloading the assets and composing the scene in the steps below.

This example combines the UR17G arm, Robotiq 2F-140 gripper, and beverage can in Isaac Sim. The task is to grasp the can, lift it, move it to a target, and release it. You can also leverage SimReady Central Space search service endpoint to look for OEM curated content.

We will also use a frontier AI model to help create and run the task code in an open Isaac Sim scene. For this example, we use GPT-6 Sol, but another agent and model combination may work if it can load the required skills and execute Python against Isaac Sim (generated code and results can vary). The prompt provides a starting point. Inspect the generated code and check the resulting behavior before adapting the task.

Open SimReady Central and find the UR17G arm, Robotiq 2F-140 gripper, and beverage can used here. Select Download on each asset, then use Save to folder or the supplied Hugging Face command. Keep all three complete asset folders intact so Isaac Sim can find their supporting files.

Use the asset versions linked in this example and provide your agent with the local USD file paths for the arm, gripper, and beverage can. An example gripper path is shown below; your download location may differ.

Figure 3. SimReady Central search and interactive previews help identify the Robotiq 2F-140 gripper and beverage can used in this example.

Figure 4. The beverage can’s download options include saving the asset package to a folder or using the Hugging Face CLI.

The arm validation report uses the Robot-Body 4.0.0 profile and the gripper validation report uses Robot-Gripper 3.0.0. Both record passing PhysX driven-joint checks, which inspect joint-drive settings.

SimReady profile validation provides a shared baseline for reusing these assets. The pick-and-place run then tests how the arm, gripper, can, and controller work together in the assembled scene.

With the assets downloaded, use your agent with Isaac Sim skills to help assemble the robot, run validation tools, and create the pick-and-place controls. You can also perform these steps manually using the linked documentation.

Start Isaac Sim from its installation directory with the remote Python server enabled so the agent can interact with the simulation through Python:

If you are using an agent, make sure you start it from the Isaac Sim directory so that it can access the skills needed while going through the steps below.

Confirm that all three assets appear without missing-file errors. Ask the agent to inspect the arm and gripper’s joint limits and drive settings, or review them yourself in Isaac Sim. The robot and the gripper contain physics joints which can be tested and validated in the Isaac Sim GUI as well. We will now assemble the arm and the gripper next so that we can control the assembly as a single articulation.

You can follow the Robot Assembler tutorial for manual assembly. Here we will ask our agent to complete the assembly and validate it for us:

The agent ends up using the ‘isaac-sim-remote’ and ‘usd-articulation’ skills packaged with Isaac Sim to complete the assembly and validate the physics of the robot. We now have all the assets needed for running pick and place; the assembled robot and the soda can. We will now proceed with the final portion of the workflow.

Figure 5. Joint settings for the UR17G arm and Robotiq 2F-140 gripper in Isaac Sim.

With the assembled robot and can in the scene, ask the agent to run the task. Evaluate the simulation behavior using the checks in the next step.

Now that the assets include simulation properties and profile validation, we can now test in an assembled scene and controller. The controller coordinates the UR17G arm’s movement with the Robotiq 2F-140 gripper’s opening and closing. Use the behavior checks below to evaluate the agent-generated task. To understand or adapt the controller yourself, see the Adding a Manipulator Robot tutorial.

Skills used: ‘isaac-sim-remote’, ‘manipulaiton-ik’ and ‘physics-simulation’

The full task tests whether the gripper holds the can during movement and releases it at the target. Reset the scene, then run the approach, grasp, lift, hold, transfer, and release sequence. Compare your run with the opening video and the success criteria below.

Figure 6. The UR17G arm and Robotiq 2F-140 gripper move the beverage can from the yellow pickup marker to the green target in Isaac Sim. Shown at 4× speed.

If your run differs, note where the sequence fails and ask the agent to inspect the scene and generate controls. Reset the can and robot to the same starting state before retrying so you can compare the results.

These results apply to this scripted setup. They do not establish robustness to uncertain object positions, different payloads, or real hardware.

#9772. Exploring a week of live game show results with pandas (500,510 rounds, 42 games)

LiveCasinoRadar publishes a small open dataset: one CSV per week with round counts, bonus round shares and top multipliers for 42 live casino games. It is a nice size for practising pandas: 42 rows, 11 columns, real missing values. This post loads the week of 9–15 November 2026 and answers three questions.

Each row is one game. The columns that matter here are rounds_recorded, bonus_round_share_pct and zero_share_pct. The last two are empty for games that have no bonus round or no zero.

Only 12 of the 42 games have a bonus share, so dropna first:

Nine of the 54 wheel segments are bonus segments, so the expected share is 9/54. With 12,002 rounds we can check how far 17.1% is from that:

A z-score of about 1.3 is inside the usual ±1.96 range (16.0% to 17.3%), so this week is consistent with the wheel layout. The share in the CSV is rounded to one decimal, so treat z as approximate.

A single-zero wheel has 37 pockets, so zero should come up 1/37 = 2.70% of the time.

Twelve roulette tables, 131,865 spins, weighted zero share 2.66%. Individual tables range from 2.5% to 2.9%.

The CSV is CC BY 4.0 and lives at github.com/livecasinoradar/live-casino-weekly-stats. Figures are rounds recorded by LiveCasinoRadar and cover 96.4% of the rounds played that week. One week is a small sample. Past results do not predict future rounds.

#9771. Hugging Face and OpenRouter join forces to make open-weight models easy to run

Hugging Face and OpenRouter are teaming up to make open-weight models easy to run. Every major open-weight release is already being published on the Hugging Face Hub, and OpenRouter serves those models at scale, routing each request across 80+ providers based on live measurements of each one. Together, every open-weight model on the Hub that a provider serves can be called with your Hugging Face token, through the same API, with the best provider picked for each request.

Today, we are switching Inference Providers from our own custom router to OpenRouter's. Requests made to language models now go through OpenRouter, which picks the best provider for each call based on live price, speed and reliability, and retries on another provider if the first one fails. Your code stays the same.

The router supports OpenAI's Chat Completions and Responses APIs and Anthropic's Messages API for every chat model, whatever the provider behind it. Pick your coding agent or SDK and a model, then copy the steps, or copy the whole setup as a prompt for your agent:

Setup guides for Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Pi and Hermes Agent

The same Hugging Face token also gives you storage with Storage Buckets, compute with Jobs and dedicated inference with Inference Endpoints. PRO, Team and Enterprise plans include monthly credits for compute and inference.

On OpenRouter, open-weight models went from 26.8% of the tokens served in October 2025 to 71.7% at the end of September 2026, after peaking at 77.5% in July (OpenRouter, October 2026). Over the same period, weekly open-weight volume grew more than 60-fold, against almost tenfold for closed models. This week, the most used model on OpenRouter is an open-weight one, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017, with 59.2 trillion tokens (rankings).

Open-weight models cost about four times less on average: $0.28 per million input tokens and $1.62 per million output tokens, against $1.27 and $6.36 for closed models.

The best open-weight models still trail the best proprietary ones on the hardest benchmarks. On the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, Kimi K3.1 Pro, the best open-weight model, scores 46 against 65 for Claude Fable 5.2, at about a seventh of the cost per task ($3.68 against $26.54). For a lot of workloads, that trade-off is worth it.

OpenRouter serves more than 800 trillion tokens a month to over 10 million users, across 600+ models from 80+ providers. Its routing is based on live measurements of every provider across that traffic.

OpenRouter recently rebuilt its provider routing: instead of only looking at the lowest list price, it sends each request to the provider with the best mix of price, speed and reliability.

When a provider slows down or starts failing, traffic moves away from it until it recovers, and a failed try is retried on the next best provider inside the same call. In OpenRouter's measurements, the new routing cut capacity errors by 46% and improved time to first token by 16.9% and throughput by 16.3%.

Before, Inference Providers picked one provider for your request and returned its error if it failed. Now, the request is retried on another provider. You can still choose a policy or a provider with a suffix on the model id:

Routing is also cache-aware: a conversation stays on the provider that holds its prompt cache. To make it explicit, send a stable UUID per conversation in the X-HF-Session-Id header (see the prompt caching guide).

Pricing doesn't change: you pay the provider's price on your Hugging Face bill, and Hugging Face doesn't add a markup on top of it. PRO users get $2 of credits every month, and Team and Enterprise organizations get $2 per seat. See Pricing and Billing for the details.

Image, video, and audio generation continue to work exactly as before, directly through Hugging Face Inference Providers without going through OpenRouter. You can keep using the same token and API, and access tens of thousands of LoRAs.

On model pages, you can chat with the model right away in the widget. Two new tabs show what's behind it: Providers lists every provider OpenRouter can route the model to, with its input and output price, speed and uptime over the last 24 hours, and Metrics shows the best price, throughput, time to first token, context length and uptime among them:

Your usage overview breaks your spend down by the provider each request went to:

In your settings, you can turn off any provider you don't want: the router never sends your requests there. Organizations have the same settings, and they apply to every request billed to the organization.

Requests to language models now go through OpenRouter and are billed to your Hugging Face account or organization, so you can no longer use your own API key for a provider with these models. You can still pick a provider with a suffix on the model id (model:provider) or turn providers off in your settings, and your code stays the same. Custom keys for image and video providers keep working.

This is the first step of our partnership with OpenRouter. Next:

Try a model, or read the Inference Providers docs to get started.

#9769. Rumble-2-Flash: an open 0.5B speech model for 40+ languages

Today we're open sourcing Rumble-2-Flash under the Apache 2.0 license. It's a 0.5B-parameter speech recognition model for 40+ languages that competes with models 3-60x its size.

audio accepts a local path, a URL, a NumPy array, or a list of these.

Rumble-2-Flash uses the Qwen3-ASR architecture for day-0 support. If your stack runs Transformers or vLLM, it runs Rumble-2-Flash, with no forked runtime or trust_remote_code.

To find out how small a model could get before accuracy dropped off, we distilled Rumble-2, our larger production model, into it with on-policy distillation. The student doesn't train on transcripts the teacher wrote. It transcribes the audio itself, and the teacher grades that transcript token by token: at every position, it gives its own probability for what should come next, and the student learns to match it. Because the student learns from its own outputs, it gets corrected on exactly the mistakes it makes, with feedback on every token instead of one score per clip.

On-policy distillation normally requires teacher and student to share a tokenizer, and ours don't: choosing Qwen3-ASR meant taking its vocabulary too. GOLD removes that restriction. It merges tokens where the two tokenizers split the text differently, so both models are compared over the same text. Tokens that exist in both vocabularies are compared directly, and the rest by their sorted probabilities.

On the Open ASR Leaderboard multilingual track, Rumble-2-Flash averages a 6.96% error rate across Chinese, German, French, Italian, Spanish, Portuguese, Hindi, Dutch and English. That's better than Meta's omniASR-LLM 7B, a model 15x larger, and ahead of Whisper large-v3. On the English track it averages 6.6% WER.

Rumble-2-Flash is also fast. Its throughput depends on how full the batches are: on the larger datasets in HF's Open ASR Leaderboard, where batches stay full, it reaches over 7,000 RTFx. That's an hour of audio in about half a second.

Clean audio is easy. Phone calls are compressed and noisy, and often have speakers with very different accents. On AppTek's call-centre benchmark (302 hours of helpline calls, 14 English accents, scored with AppTek's own script), Rumble-2-Flash reaches 7.86% WER, on par with NVIDIA's Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe (30B) at 7.78%. That's well ahead of Qwen3-ASR 0.6B (8.7%), from the same model family, and close to Qwen3-ASR 1.7B (7.4%), the only model in the comparison that does better.

The weights are on the Hub at Reson8/Rumble-2-Flash. It's also available through our API.

We're very curious what you'll build with it. Tell us in the Discussions tab what you've made, what you like, and what you'd like to see changed in a next version.

#9768. LimeWire AI Studio Review 2023: Details, Pricing & Features

 

In the rapidly advancing landscape of AI technology and innovation, LimeWire emerges as a unique platform in the realm of generative AI tools. This platform not only stands out from the multitude of existing AI tools but also brings a fresh approach to content generation. LimeWire not only empowers users to create AI content but also provides creators with creative ways to share and monetize their creations.


As we explore LimeWire, our aim is to uncover its features, benefits for creators, and the exciting possibilities it offers for AI content generation. This platform presents an opportunity for users to harness the power of AI in image creation, all while enjoying the advantages of a free and accessible service.


Let's unravel the distinctive features that set LimeWire apart in the dynamic landscape of AI-powered tools, understanding how creators can leverage its capabilities to craft unique and engaging AI-generated images.


Introduction


LimeWire, a name once associated with the notorious file-sharing tool from the 2000s, has undergone a significant transformation. The LimeWire we discuss today is not the file-sharing application of the past but has re-emerged as an entirely new entity—a cutting-edge AI content publishing platform.

This revamped LimeWire invites users to register and unleash their creativity by crafting original AI content, which can then be shared and showcased on the LimeWire Studio. Notably, even acclaimed artists and musicians, such as Deadmau5, Soulja Boy, and Sean Kingston, have embraced this platform to publish their content in the form of NFT music, videos, and images.


Beyond providing a space for content creation and sharing, LimeWire introduces monetization models to empower users to earn revenue from their creations. This includes avenues such as earning ad revenue and participating in the burgeoning market of Non-Fungible Tokens (NFTs). As we delve further, we'll explore these monetization strategies in more detail to provide a comprehensive understanding of LimeWire's innovative approach to content creation and distribution.


LimeWire Studio welcomes content creators into its fold, providing a space to craft personalized AI-focused content for sharing with fans and followers. Within this creative hub, every piece of content generated becomes not just a creation but a unique asset—ownable and tradable. Fans have the opportunity to subscribe to creators' pages, immersing themselves in the creative journey and gaining ownership of digital collectibles that hold tradeable value within the LimeWire community. Notably, creators earn a 2.5% royalty each time their content is traded, adding a rewarding element to the creative process.


The platform's flexibility is evident in its content publication options. Creators can choose to share their work freely with the public or opt for a premium subscription model, granting exclusive access to specialized content for subscribers.


LimeWire AI Studio

As of the present moment, LimeWire focuses on AI Image Generation, offering a spectrum of creative possibilities to its user base. The platform, however, has ambitious plans on the horizon, aiming to broaden its offerings by introducing AI music and video generation tools in the near future. This strategic expansion promises creators even more avenues for expression and engagement with their audience, positioning LimeWire Studio as a dynamic and evolving platform within the realm of AI-powered content creation.


AI Image Generation Tools



The LimeWire AI image generation tool presents a versatile platform for both the creation and editing of images. Supporting advanced models such as Stable Diffusion 2.1, Stable Diffusion XL, and DALL-E 2, LimeWire offers a sophisticated toolkit for users to delve into the realm of generative AI art.


Much like other tools in the generative AI landscape, LimeWire provides a range of options catering to various levels of complexity in image creation. Users can initiate the creative process with prompts as simple as a few words or opt for more intricate instructions, tailoring the output to their artistic vision.


What sets LimeWire apart is its seamless integration of different AI models and design styles. Users have the flexibility to effortlessly switch between various AI models, exploring diverse design styles such as cinematic, digital art, pixel art, anime, analog film, and more. Each style imparts a distinctive visual identity to the generated AI art, enabling users to explore a broad spectrum of creative possibilities.


The platform also offers additional features, including samplers, allowing users to fine-tune the quality and detail levels of their creations. Customization options and prompt guidance further enhance the user experience, providing a user-friendly interface for both novice and experienced creators.


Excitingly, LimeWire is actively developing its proprietary AI model, signaling ongoing innovation and enhancements to its image generation capabilities. This upcoming addition holds the promise of further expanding the creative horizons for LimeWire users, making it an evolving and dynamic platform within the landscape of AI-driven art and image creation.

Sign Up Now To Get Free Credits

Automatically Mint Your Content As NFTs



Upon completing your creative endeavor on LimeWire, the platform allows you the option to publish your content. An intriguing feature follows this step: LimeWire automates the process of minting your creation as a Non-Fungible Token (NFT), utilizing either the Polygon or Algorand blockchain. This transformative step imbues your artwork with a unique digital signature, securing its authenticity and ownership in the decentralized realm.


Creators on LimeWire hold the power to decide the accessibility of their NFT creations. By opting for a public release, the content becomes discoverable by anyone, fostering a space for engagement and interaction. Furthermore, this choice opens the avenue for enthusiasts to trade the NFTs, adding a layer of community involvement to the artistic journey.


Alternatively, LimeWire acknowledges the importance of exclusivity. Creators can choose to share their posts exclusively with their premium subscribers. In doing so, the content remains a special offering solely for dedicated fans, creating an intimate and personalized experience within the LimeWire community. This flexibility in sharing options emphasizes LimeWire's commitment to empowering creators with choices in how they connect with their audience and distribute their digital creations.


After creating your content, you can choose to publish the content. It will automatically mint your creation as an NFT on the Polygon or Algorand blockchain. You can also choose whether to make it public or subscriber-only.


If you make it public, anyone can discover your content and even trade the NFTs. If you choose to share the post only with your premium subscribers, it will be exclusive only to your fans.


Earn Revenue From Your Content

Additionally, you can earn ad revenue from your content creations as well.

When you publish content on LimeWire, you will receive 70% of all ad revenue from other users who view your images, music, and videos on the platform.


This revenue model will be much more beneficial to designers. You can experiment with the AI image and content generation tools and share your creations while earning a small income on the side.


LMWR Tokens

The revenue you earn from your creations will come in the form of LMWR tokens, LimeWire’s own cryptocurrency.

#9767. Building MCP Servers for My Own Products: Introducing the Workflow

I’m a full-stack engineer specialising in front-end development & design engineering

I’m a full-stack engineer specialising in front-end development & design engineering

I’m a full-stack engineer specialising in front-end development & design engineering

I used to manage my products through dashboards. Check analytics here, schedule posts there, pull metrics from another tab. Constant context-switching.

Now, I do all of it by talking to Claude.

Not through some hacked-together integration: through MCP servers I built for my own products. Model Context Protocol is the standard Anthropic published for giving AI assistants structured access to external tools. I built servers for both Spellcast and Lunary. Here's how, and why it changed everything.

MCP is a protocol that lets you define a set of "tools", which are functions with typed inputs and outputs that Claude can call during a conversation. Instead of copy-pasting data into a chat window, Claude calls your API directly and works with the live result.

The architecture: your MCP server exposes tools over stdio (or HTTP). Claude Code discovers them and can call them when relevant. You write the server once; it works in any MCP-compatible client.

Spellcast is my social scheduling platform. The MCP server exposes the full API as typed tools:

What I can do from a Claude conversation:

The practical workflow: I describe what I want, and Claude calls the tools. "Optimize the hooks on my scheduled tweets" becomes Claude reading every post, identifying weak openers, and rewriting them in batches.

Lunary is my astrology platform. The MCP exposes product analytics and content tools:

Me: "Check Lunary metrics and tell me what's changed since last week."

Claude calls get_dashboard, get_dau_wau_mau, get_cohort_retention. Returns a summary. Surfaces what moved.

Me: "Schedule a thread about the SEO growth for the sammii account."

Claude calls list_account_sets to find the right persona, get_brand_voice to load my voice profile, generate_content to write five thread variations, presents them, waits for my pick, then calls create_post to schedule it.

Me: "Those tweets from February with weak hooks, fix them."

Claude calls list_posts for the date range, reads each one, identifies weak openers, writes improvements, calls update_post in batches.

No dashboards. No tab-switching. Just conversation with full product access.

Your product's API is now accessible from any Claude conversation.

The power isn't just convenience. Claude can operate across your entire product context in a single conversation: read your analytics, read your content queue, read your brand voice, and produce work that's coherent across all of them without you manually bridging the gap.

I estimate MCP saves me 5-8 hours a week in dashboard time and manual data-pulling.

More importantly, it removes the friction that stops small tasks from getting done. If checking metrics requires three tabs and a copy-paste, you do it less. If it's one sentence, you do it constantly and catch things early.

#9766. Your LLM Wiki Remembers Facts. Teach It How You Work, Too.

Most LLM wiki setups I've seen are very good at one kind of memory and have almost none of the other.

Karpathy's LLM Wiki pattern is the one everyone copies now: raw sources go in, the model writes linked Markdown pages, and answers come back with sources. That's great for facts. What the release process looks like, which service owns sync, what we decided about the queue.

What it doesn't store is how you work. The fifth time my agent wrote release notes, it did the same five things it did the first four times: read the git log, searched the wiki for our changelog style, read that page, drafted, proposed the page for review. It rediscovered that path from scratch every time, burning context to do it.

That's procedural memory, and it was all over my feed this week:

Same idea three times: watch what the agent actually does, find what repeats, and write it down as a skill. The part I care about is the second half of the Perplexity description, though. Proposes, with strong evidence. An agent that rewrites its own playbook every night is how you end up with a wiki full of confident, slightly wrong procedures.

So this post builds the boring local version: a ~200-line, stdlib-only Python script that reads agent session logs, finds recurring tool-call sequences, and drafts skills/*.md pages into a proposals/ folder only when the evidence clears a bar. A human approves. It never touches an approved skill, and it tells you when an approved skill has stopped matching reality.

The last row is why I don't let the agent write skills directly: a wrong procedure fails the same way on every run.

Most harnesses can already dump a transcript. I normalized mine to one JSONL file per session: a start event with a task label, one tool event per call, and an end event with whether the result was accepted.

"Success" here just means a human accepted the output. It isn't a model grading itself, and it's the most valuable field in the log.

The fixture in this post is a sample I made up: 19 fictional sessions from a fictional team between Sep 24 and Nov 19, 2026. There are five recurring tasks plus two approved skills that already exist. I seeded it with the messy stuff real logs have: one run that retried wiki.search twice, one failed release, an FAQ workflow that gets rejected a third of the time, and a weekly-metrics skill the team quietly stopped following.

1. Count sequences per session, not per occurrence. Every contiguous run of 4 to 8 tool calls is an n-gram. If a session loops the same four calls three times, that's still one session of evidence. Repetition inside a single run is usually a retry, not a habit.

2. One decision per task, longest passing sequence wins. For each task label I keep the longest sequence that clears all thresholds: at least 3 sessions, at least 75% accepted, last seen within 30 days. If nothing clears them, the script prints the best candidate and the exact reason it was rejected. That turns out to be as useful as the proposals.

3. Confidence is a Wilson lower bound, not a success rate. 3 out of 3 is "100%" but it's thin evidence. The Wilson lower bound for 3/3 is 0.44 and for 4/4 it's 0.51, which matches how much I actually trust those numbers.

Core of skill_miner.py (candidates, pick, stale/contradicted check) def pick(cands, today, min_sessions, min_success, max_age): """One decision per task: the longest sequence that clears every threshold, or, if none does, the best-supported one and the reason it failed.""" groups = defaultdict(list) for c in cands: groups[c["name"]].append(c) out = [] for name, cs in groups.items(): ok = [c for c in cs if not judge(c, today, min_sessions, min_success, max_age)] if ok: out.append((max(ok, key=lambda c: (len(c["steps"]), c["support"])), None)) else: c = max(cs, key=lambda c: (c["support"], c["rate"], len(c["steps"]))) out.append((c, judge(c, today, min_sessions, min_success, max_age))) return sorted(out, key=lambda x: (x[1] is not None, -x[0]["support"], x[0]["name"])) def check_skills(skills, sessions, today, window): """Flag approved skills that recent sessions no longer follow.""" recent = [s for s in sessions if (today - s["date"]).days <= window] flags = [] for name, sk in skills.items(): if sk["meta"].get("status") != "approved": continue steps, task = sk["steps"], sk["meta"].get("task", name) matched = [s for s in sessions if contains(s["steps"], steps)] last = max((s["date"] for s in matched), default=None) same_task = [s for s in recent if s["task"] == task] hits = [s for s in same_task if contains(s["steps"], steps)] if same_task and len(hits) * 2 < len(same_task): variant, n = Counter(tuple(s["steps"]) for s in same_task if not contains(s["steps"], steps)).most_common(1)[0] flags.append(("CONTRADICTED", sk["path"], f"{len(hits)}/{len(same_task)} recent '{task}' runs match; " f"{n} use: {' > '.join(variant)}")) elif not same_task and not any(contains(s["steps"], steps) for s in recent): when = f"{last} ({(today - last).days} days ago)" if last else "never" flags.append(("STALE", sk["path"], f"last matched {when}, 0 runs in last {window} days")) return flags Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode

The write path has three guards, and each one has a unit test:

A second run changes nothing: all three proposals come back as KEEP.

Two choices here are deliberate. owner: human means the agent is never the owner of its own procedures. And the "why" section cites session ids, which gives you the SIM idea in miniature: when someone asks in February why the agent always reads the changelog page first, the answer is three linked sessions, not a vibe.

The review checklist at the bottom of every page ("nothing in the args is secret or one-off") matters more than it looks. Session args are where tokens, customer names and one-time paths leak into a doc that every future session will read.

A skills/ folder in a repo works for one developer. For a team, I'd put skill pages in the same place as the docs and decisions they depend on. A skill that says "read the changelog style page" should link to that page, so a reviewer sees the procedure and its inputs side by side.

In AFFiNE, this is how I would set it up. Skills become ordinary pages with properties (status, owner, evidence, confidence), in the same workspace as the docs and the whiteboard where the team sketches the process. The miner runs against a Markdown export and its proposals land in a review collection. Approving one would mean a person flips status to approved. If you're choosing knowledge base software for this, look for queryable page properties and backlinks, so "which approved skills cite this doc?" is one query when the doc changes.

The review flow is the same one teams already use for SOPs, just with better evidence attached. If you've written process documentation before, the shape will feel familiar: trigger, steps, owner, review date. The difference is that the first draft comes from what actually happened, not from what someone remembers happening. And if you're comparing tools for the human side of that loop, this rundown of SOP management software covers the approval and versioning features that matter.

I'd also keep this layer somewhere you control. Procedural memory says more about your team than the facts do: which systems you touch, in what order, and where you cut corners. That's an argument for an open source Notion alternative you can self-host, rather than one more SaaS that learns your workflows. It's also why I think the "agents write their own skills" trend belongs inside your AI knowledge base software, not in a side database owned by whichever agent vendor you use this quarter.

It needs a task label. Grouping by task makes proposals readable and keeps release notes from merging with postmortems. If your harness doesn't log intent, you'll need to cluster prompts first, and that's a harder problem.

Contiguity is strict. One retry and the run doesn't count. You could allow gaps (subsequence matching), but then the miner starts "finding" skills that are really just "every session reads a wiki page." I'd rather have strict and slow.

It only sees tool names. It can't tell that wiki.search for "changelog style" and wiki.search for "who owns sync" are different steps. The args shown on the proposal page are hints for the reviewer, not part of the match. A next version could bucket args. I'd still keep the human gate.

If you want the bigger picture of how this fits with the fact side, here's a good primer on what an LLM wiki is and how teams structure one.

Try it: export a week of your own agent transcripts to JSONL, run the miner with --dry-run, and read the SKIP lines before the PROPOSE lines. In my sample fixture, the skills it refused to write were just as informative as the ones it wrote.

#9765. 180B Parameters, 32GB of RAM: Pushing MoE Inference to the Limit with Transformers

Streaming MoE experts directly from SSD gets within 6% of Strata on token generation.

I've been trying to rely less on online models and run bigger ones locally. At home I have a PC with two RTX 4090s (let's call it Orthrus - the two-headed hound of Greek mythology), and for work I have a MacBook M5 with 32G of unified memory.

Orthrus runs on Windows 11, because my kids play games all the time. I had a dual boot with Ubuntu, but their games ended up taking most of the two terabytes of disk.

I am also a huge fan of RMD (rooms moving development): one hour in the kitchen sipping my coffee, two hours at my office desk, then the sofa. A fixed desktop tower is not for me.

My first experiment was to run Qwen 3.8 27B with llama.app on Orthrus and use it from my laptop through pi. That model does the coding tasks, an online model like Opus does the orchestration, and the second RTX runs a FIM model for auto-completion in Neovim.

When I talked about this on social networks, I got very strong feedback: use Strata with Qwen3.8-Flash-Next.

Strata is an inference engine for MoE models like Qwen. Only the hot experts stay in VRAM, the rest goes to RAM, or even to disk. Experts are 90%+ of a MoE model's weights, so a 180B model like this one can run on a GPU with much less memory. Like my RTX 4090!

It works on a laptop too, and I stumbled on this blog post doing exactly that: Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on a 32 GB Mac M4, faster than llama.cpp, at 13.5 tok/s.

That's too slow for how I use coding agents, but it's an interesting itch to scratch. A whole range of MoE models don't fit in a MacBook's unified memory and could run at a decent speed.

Before committing to Strata, I looked at what llama.cpp, vLLM and Transformers do when a MoE model doesn't fit. Three questions matter: where do the experts live, where does the expert matmul run, and what moves on each token?

llama.cpp maps the GGUF file with mmap and can keep the experts on the CPU (--cpu-moe, --n-cpu-moe N, -ot "exps=CPU", or --fit on to pick for you). Those experts are also computed on the CPU, so only the activations cross PCIe, never the weights. Great when the experts fit in RAM. When they don't, the page cache thrashes. A GPU expert cache (--moe-cache-mib) just landed, but it fragments the graph (2 splits per token become 50) and loses ~10% even when everything fits.

vLLM's --cpu-offload-gb N puts N GB of weights in pinned RAM, and kernels read them in place over PCIe. For a MoE layer, that's only the routed experts, but nothing is cached: a hot expert crosses PCIe again on every token, and there's no disk tier. By default the offloaded weights include dense layers, read on every token; --cpu-offload-params experts keeps it to the experts. That fits vLLM's big batches, which touch almost every expert anyway, less so one user on one GPU.

Transformers offloads through Accelerate (device_map="auto", offload_folder), one module at a time: hooks copy its weights to the GPU before forward. For a MoE, that module is a layer's whole expert bank, so every token copies every expert of every offloaded layer to use 8 or 10 of them. No cache, no notion of routing. And on a Mac, CPU and GPU share the same memory, so "offload to CPU" frees nothing.

I ran all of them on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on one A10G (24 GB), with plenty of RAM, and Harry Mellor reran vLLM with better flags:

Offloading only the experts doubles vLLM's speed, and FP8 helps on top (half the bytes per expert, more of the model on the GPU). vLLM's other offload backend, which copies groups of layers ahead of time, ran under 1 tok/s.

If the experts fit in RAM, llama.cpp is hard to beat. If they don't, you have to stream only what the router picks, through a bounded cache, fast enough that the SSD is the bottleneck and not Python, ideally reusing the model's fast expert kernels. That's Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on a 32 GB Mac, and Transformers couldn't do it out of the box.

Strata was already too slow for me on the laptop, and Transformers was not going to beat it anytime soon. But the Accelerate path was so far off that I wanted to try fixing offloading in Transformers itself, with the big model on my laptop as the target, knowing it would probably stay too slow for how I work.

All of the code was built with AI: the Transformers PR, the model-specific package and the Metal kernels. My part was choosing what to try, reading the profiles, and deciding what to keep. Everything is in a Space: tarekziade/moe-expert-streaming.

I started with OLMoE-1B-7B, which fits in memory, so I could compare every token with vanilla Transformers.

First version: experts on disk, an LRU cache on the device, and a Python loop running one expert at a time. With every expert already cached, it did 10.1 tok/s. Vanilla did ~32. The I/O was fine, my loop was not: vanilla uses grouped_mm, which runs all the experts of a layer in one kernel.

The fix, and the key idea of this project, was to turn the cache into a slot pool: one preallocated device tensor shared by all layers, plus a per-layer table from expert id to slot. Remap the router's expert ids to slots and the pool looks like a regular expert bank, so grouped_mm runs on it as is. No custom expert matmul needed. That got it to 34.6 tok/s, against 38.1 for vanilla.

I then turned the standalone loader into an option of from_pretrained, in huggingface/transformers#50717. To try it, install Transformers from that PR:

Then, moving from OLMoE to the real target, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next:

That repo holds the output of the project's conversion script: the dense weights, the experts quantized to 3 bits, and the n-gram table.

Experts mapped to "disk" go through the streaming path instead of Accelerate's offload: the loader skips their tensors and MoE layers switch to an offloaded implementation. Misses are read by 8 I/O threads, one contiguous read per expert. The next two layers' routers run early on the current hidden states to guess which experts to prefetch. Experts can be quantized offline so reads are smaller. It works for MoE models with the standard experts layout.

The API is still being discussed with the Transformers maintainers. The device_map form came out of that, and quantized experts will probably go through the per-layer quantization plan of #50245 rather than their own option.

Qwen3.8-Flash-Next has 48 layers of 512 experts (10 active), 121 GB in FP8. Streaming them isn't enough: there's also a 51 GB n-gram embedding table that needs its own disk path. So:

The conversion takes ~5 hours. After loading, it uses ~18 GiB, and a 6K prompt peaks at 25.4 GiB. That's about the limit: I have to close the browser, or macOS starts swapping.

The model-specific bits (the n-gram table, Metal kernels) live in a small package, moe-expert-streaming, on top of the PR. The first version ran at about 10 tok/s.

Then I installed Strata on the same M5, with the same prompts:

Strata 0.1.60 used IQ3_XXS experts. Both ran greedy, with thinking, MTP and speculative drafts off, and 1,024-token prefill chunks. The full setup and raw results are on the Space's details page.

I also tried vllm-metal, vLLM on Apple GPUs through MLX, which recently got expert offloading. It streams the routed experts from an MLX checkpoint through a bounded cache, like this project. But it can't run Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on 32 GB, for the n-gram reason above: only the experts are streamed, and the n-gram tables stay in memory. That's 32 GB in the MLX checkpoints on the Hub, before the ~5 GB of dense layers and any expert cache.

Most of the time wasn't spent on experts. Here's what helped:

Here's one MoE layer for one token, as it runs now:

These are the final results after these optimizations on the same M5 with the same prompts:

That's about 6% behind Strata on short decode, with slightly faster prefill, all through Transformers.

Most of what's left is host round trips, ~10 ms per token. Waking up after a sync is only ~1 ms of that. The rest is the GPU running dry while Python queues the next layer. Strata queues the whole token's work up front, and the GPU waits on a Metal shared event at each layer while the host reads experts. PyTorch doesn't expose that. I tried to fake it with a kernel spinning on a flag the CPU writes, and the GPU took anywhere from a second to never to see the write. The real fix would be a native op on PyTorch's MPS stream, with a risk of hangs, so I haven't built it.

It runs at ~14 tok/s, close to Strata, and it's still too slow for how I use coding agents. Orthrus keeps doing the real work.

Transformers didn't beat Strata, and closing the last ~6% would take deeper changes in the stack, starting with control over that per-layer sync, which PyTorch doesn't give you today. The interesting part is how it got that close: streaming only the routed experts, a bounded cache that grouped_mm runs on as is, and a few targeted Metal kernels. There's no C++ extension in the project: just Python, Metal kernels compiled at runtime with torch.mps.compile_shader, and prebuilt kernels from the Hub. All the Metal kernels written for this experiment are now published on the Hub, and the project loads them from there.

Beating Strata was never the only goal, though. Building this was a great way to learn how MoEs and LLMs work from a systems perspective: how sparse the routing really is, how much an expert cache buys you, where memory bandwidth goes per token, and how much time the host and the GPU spend waiting on each other. Transformers makes all of that easy to poke at, one module at a time.

The generic expert streaming implementation is in huggingface/transformers#50717, and the benchmarks are in the Space. Feedback on the approach and the API is welcome.

Thanks to Pedro, Lysandre and Arthur for their excellent feedback, and to Harry for helping test vLLM.

Finally, thanks to Niko Veit for Strata. Strata set the bar for what's possible with expert streaming on consumer hardware, and having those numbers to chase is what pushed this work as far as it went.

#9764. What is high-extraction flour, exactly?  : A baker’s guide to our new T85 Baker's Reserve Bread Flour.

High-extraction flour is a technical term that often prompts a lot of confusion from those unfamiliar with it. But with the debut of our new high-extraction flour, known as Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour, we’re breaking down just what it is and why it's a great choice for avid bread makers.

The extraction rate of a flour refers to how much of the original grain — the bran, germ, and endosperm — ends up in the final flour. A high-extraction flour typically has an extraction rate of about 80% to 90%, meaning some of the bran and germ have been sifted out, but it still retains much of the original grain. Our Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour is a T85 flour, meaning its extraction rate is 85%.

To put that in perspective, whole wheat flour has an extraction rate of 100%; it retains the entirety of the grain, including the bran, germ, and endosperm.

High-extraction flour falls between white and whole wheat flour. It’s lighter and less coarse than whole wheat flour because some of the bran has been sifted out, but it still retains more flavor, nutrients, and color than white flour, since it retains much of the original grain.

High-extraction flour is popular for artisan bread baking because it offers a balance of nutrition and good gluten development. It’s great for rustic loaves, baguettes, and pizza dough, and particularly well-suited for sourdough baking because it strikes a balance between flavor, nutrition, fermentation, and dough strength.

You can substitute our Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour 1:1 for bread flour (by weight or volume) in artisanal bread recipes; it can also be used 1:1 to replace the total flour in recipes that call for a combination of all-purpose and whole wheat flour. If you're subbing Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour for all-purpose flour in a bread recipe, you may find you need to add slightly more liquid to the recipe.

Bread bakers love high-extraction flour for artisan bread and sourdough because it offers the flavor and nutrition of whole grain flour; the stronger gluten development and more open crumb you get from white flour; and better fermentation from the minerals present in the bran and germ, which feed the wild yeast and lactic acid bacteria in sourdough starter, promoting more active fermentation.

If you want a loaf of bread that’s more flavorful and nutritious than bread made with exclusively white flour, but that still rises high and has an open crumb, high-extraction flour is a great choice.

Yes — in fact, it’s a great choice for feeding starter because of the sourdough-friendly minerals present in the flour, which boost activity in your starter.

Yes! T85 is a French specification that refers to the extraction rate (85%) of the flour. Our Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour is a T85 flour, meaning the extraction rate is 85%. If you have a recipe that calls for T85, this flour is the perfect choice.
