#9763. What Happens When AI Makes So Many Decisions That We Forget How?

Independent writer exploring science, space, AI, and emerging technologies. Curious about the future and the ideas shaping it.

Independent writer exploring science, space, AI, and emerging technologies. Curious about the future and the ideas shaping it.

Independent writer exploring science, space, AI, and emerging technologies. Curious about the future and the ideas shaping it.

A personal investigation into how AI is changing our reflexes, our tolerance for effort, and eventually the decisions we still call our own.

The most important thing AI may be changing is not what we know. It is what we do in the first few seconds after we realize we do not know something. That sounds trivial, but I think it may be the beginning of a much larger behavioral shift. For most of my life, uncertainty triggered a small sequence of actions: remember who might know, search for the right words, open several sources, compare them, decide what seems plausible, and only then act. Increasingly, one new reflex compresses that sequence into a single gesture: ask the AI.

A strange symptom. A recipe for whatever is left in the kitchen. The name of an actor I can almost remember. A confusing bill. A message I do not know how to phrase. A question about whether a laptop is actually worth the extra $300. These are not spectacular uses of artificial intelligence. That is precisely why I find them more interesting than the demos. Technologies change a society most deeply when they stop feeling like technologies and become habits.

Search engines did that once. They gave us the phrase “just Google it,” and eventually we stopped hearing how strange that sentence was. AI is producing a new version: “just ask it.” The next phrase may be even more consequential: “just let it handle it.” This essay is about what happens in the space between those three sentences.

For most of history, information had friction. You asked someone who might know. You checked a manual or an encyclopedia. You went to a library. You waited until you could speak to a doctor, mechanic, teacher, salesperson, or relative who had dealt with the same problem. Even when the answer existed, getting to it cost time, attention, and often a little embarrassment: you had to admit to another human being that you did not know.

The internet collapsed much of that cost. Search engines taught an entire generation a new cognitive skill: translate the messy question in your head into keywords, scan results, ignore obvious junk, open several tabs, compare sources, and assemble an answer from fragments. We outsourced access to memory, but we still did much of the interpretation ourselves.

A famous 2011 Science study by Betsy Sparrow, Jenny Liu, and Daniel Wegner found that when people expected information to remain available, they were less likely to remember the information itself and more likely to remember where it could be found. Later work on cognitive offloading described the broader pattern: humans routinely move mental work into notebooks, calendars, calculators, GPS, phones, and other parts of the environment. There is nothing inherently unhealthy about this. Civilization is, in part, a history of building tools so the brain does not have to carry everything alone.

But Google still left one important burden with us. It gave us routes to information. It usually did not decide which route deserved our trust. That distinction is where generative AI begins to feel different.

With conversational AI, I no longer have to think like a search engine. I can ask the question the way it exists in my head, incomplete and slightly confused. The system can ask a follow-up, infer what I am trying to accomplish, summarize competing possibilities, and turn scattered information into something that feels like an answer.

That changes more than convenience. It changes the first move. Instead of entering an information landscape and navigating it, I hand the landscape to an intermediary. The difference is subtle because the screen still looks like a place where I type words. Psychologically, however, the task has shifted from retrieval toward delegation of interpretation.

For readers who want the technical layer behind this shift, I have a separate explainer on how modern AI systems work.

Real-world usage already looks surprisingly ordinary. A 2025 NBER analysis of consumer ChatGPT use found that Practical Guidance, Seeking Information, and Writing made up roughly 77% of conversations in its dataset, while non-work use accounted for more than 70% of messages. The public story of AI is often about coding, corporate productivity, and frontier capabilities. A large part of the private story is simply people trying to get through Tuesday.

This is the first subconscious change I would watch: the destination of uncertainty. We used to send uncertainty outward to friends, books, forums, and search results. Now we increasingly send it to a single conversational system. Once that becomes automatic, the AI does not merely answer questions. It begins to occupy the position in our lives where questions go first.

I do not think the useful question is whether AI makes us “think less.” That framing is too crude. A calculator removes arithmetic effort but can free attention for a harder problem. GPS reduces route memorization but can make an unfamiliar city usable. The more interesting question is which kinds of mental friction disappear, and what those frictions were quietly doing for us.

In a 2025 CHI study, Microsoft researchers surveyed 319 knowledge workers and collected 936 examples of generative-AI use. Higher confidence in AI was associated with less reported critical-thinking effort, but participants also described a change in the location of that effort: less work generating a first answer and more work verifying, integrating, and supervising the output. That is not the same as thought disappearing. It is thought being reorganized.

Still, some mental work matters precisely because it is inefficient. Searching forces us to encounter disagreement. Comparing products can reveal that the feature we thought mattered actually does not. Writing a bad first draft can expose that we do not understand our own argument. Struggling to remember something can strengthen memory. A 2025 randomized study of undergraduates found lower long-term knowledge retention among students who used ChatGPT as a study aid than among those who used traditional methods, a result the authors linked to reduced effortful processing. One education study cannot be generalized to all everyday AI use, but it captures a principle psychologists have known for a long time: sometimes the work is part of the learning.

The phrase I keep returning to is cognitive friction: the interval between wanting an answer and having one. Some friction is pointless bureaucracy. Some is the resistance that makes a skill, a preference, or a judgment become ours. AI is extraordinarily good at removing the interval. The danger is not that every removed step makes us weaker. It is that convenience can erase the distinction between friction that was waste and friction that was formative.

It is easy to see why people reach for the language of addiction. The loop is unusually smooth. A question appears, the assistant responds immediately, and the response is often useful enough to justify another question. The system is available at midnight, it does not become irritated, and it does not make us feel foolish for asking something basic. Each successful interaction teaches the brain a very simple lesson: when uncertain, come back here.

But “it feels rewarding” is not the same as “it is a drug.” Current evidence does not justify treating ordinary or even heavy AI use as equivalent to substance addiction. Researchers have begun building scales for problematic ChatGPT use, conversational-AI dependence, and generative-AI dependency. One 2025 validation program across 1,333 participants in the United States and Singapore identified dimensions including cognitive preoccupation, negative consequences, and withdrawal-like experiences. At the same time, researchers writing in Addictive Behaviors have warned that the field risks pathologizing a new everyday technology before there is robust evidence of impaired control, distress, and functional harm.

I think that tension is more interesting than the headline “AI addiction.” There may be a large middle territory between healthy tool use and clinical addiction: dependency without obvious pathology. I depend on GPS, cloud calendars, and search in ways that would have looked extraordinary twenty years ago. If they vanish, I can still function, but I feel the missing scaffolding immediately.

AI could become a deeper kind of scaffolding because it does not only remember for us. It can compare for us, explain for us, draft for us, reassure us, and eventually decide for us. The warning sign may not be hours spent staring at a chatbot. It may be a growing irritation with any task that requires us to proceed without one. A ten-minute search feels too slow. Writing the first paragraph ourselves feels unnecessary. Calling three repair companies feels absurd. Uncertainty itself begins to feel like a technical problem that should have been removed.

That is why I would ask a different question: not “Am I addicted to AI?” but “Which abilities now feel unreasonably difficult when AI is unavailable?” The answer tells us more about dependence than screen time alone.

I doubt most people will ever sit down and make a philosophical decision to trust artificial intelligence. Trust will arrive much more quietly. The recipe works. The cable recommendation is correct. The summary saves twenty minutes. The hotel shortlist is genuinely better than the one we would have built ourselves. The assistant catches a fee we missed. Nothing dramatic happens — and that is exactly how a default is formed.

Research on algorithmic recommendations suggests that willingness to accept advice is strongly affected by perceived autonomy. In three experiments published in Computers in Human Behavior, people were more willing to accept algorithmic recommendations when they retained more choice, such as receiving several options rather than a single prescribed answer. Another 2024 study of purchasing delegation found that perceived decision autonomy significantly shaped willingness to let AI participate in buying decisions. We may accept machine judgment not when machines become perfect, but when the interface gives us just enough control to feel that the decision is still ours.

There is a paradox here. The better the system becomes at making good recommendations, the less often we have a reason to challenge it. And the less often we challenge it, the harder it becomes to know whether our trust is calibrated or merely habitual. A tool can earn trust through accuracy and still train us into passivity if the cost of checking it becomes higher than the perceived benefit.

This is where the question becomes philosophical for me. We usually imagine AI choice as a final step: there are ten televisions, and the agent picks number four. But a recommendation system has already made a more invisible decision before that. It decided which ten televisions entered the room.

Research on AI-assisted purchasing makes this point explicitly: recommendation systems narrow consideration sets and prioritize options before the consumer evaluates them. In other words, AI can shape not only the answer but the menu from which an answer becomes possible. If my agent shows me three hotels, I may feel fully autonomous while choosing among them. I may never see the twenty-seven hotels it excluded, or know which preference it assumed mattered most.

This matters because preferences are not always fixed objects hidden inside us, waiting to be discovered. We often construct them while choosing. Looking at cameras may teach us that weight matters more than zoom. Comparing three neighborhoods may reveal that we care about walkability more than an extra room. A system that becomes extremely good at predicting what I usually prefer can save me enormous time. It can also make it easier for my past behavior to keep selecting my future behavior.

That is one of the stranger possibilities of personal AI: convenience could turn yesterday’s self into tomorrow’s default. If my agent learns that I usually choose the quiet hotel, the reliable appliance, the familiar food, the cheapest morning flight, and the same kind of vacation, it may become excellent at protecting me from choices I would probably reject. It may also protect me from choices that would have changed me.

I do not mean that an AI agent will imprison us in a recommendation bubble by design. The point is more ordinary. Every good personal assistant needs a model of the person it serves. The better that model becomes, the more important a new question becomes: should the agent optimize for who I have been, who I say I want to be, or who I might become if it occasionally lets something unexpected through?

Today, most consumer AI still lives on the safer side of a line. It can recommend. We execute. An agent crosses that line by combining a model with tools, memory, accounts, and permissions so it can pursue a goal across several steps. The assistant does not merely tell me which action is sensible. It gets hands.

The design problem then changes completely. The question is no longer only “Is the model smart enough?” It becomes: What may it purchase? What may it cancel? What may it send in my name? How much money may it spend without asking? What is reversible? What is visible to other people? How quickly can I take control back?

A 2026 study of a general-purpose agent introduced the useful idea of delegation regret: people sometimes disliked an agent’s action not because the outcome was objectively bad, but because the system crossed a boundary they would have wanted to approve. The study was small — twenty university students — but its pattern is intuitively important. Participants calibrated trust by task, not by agent. They tolerated more autonomy for low-stakes advisory work and demanded more confirmation for actions that were externally visible or difficult to reverse.

That suggests that “Do you trust AI?” may eventually sound as crude as “Do you trust the internet?” We do not need one global answer. We need layers of trust. I may trust an agent to reorder detergent, prepare a tax checklist, compare insurance policies, or move a meeting. That does not imply that I want it to send a resignation email, approve a medical procedure, or transfer $15,000.

A recent HackerNoon essay makes a similar point from the system-design side: agentic AI changes who owns a decision, not merely how a workflow runs.

When I try to picture this future, I do not imagine a humanoid robot walking around the house. I imagine a normal weekday in which entire chains of tiny coordination disappear. The future becomes more believable when the examples are boring.

You are at work and remember that the guest-room television finally died. You tell your agent: “Replace it. Around 55 inches. Good for movies. Under $800. Avoid models with recurring reliability complaints.” That is all.

The agent checks current models, professional tests, owner complaints, the wall dimensions stored from a previous home project, the ports on your sound system, delivery times, return policies, and local installer availability. It knows from earlier purchases that you usually choose reliability over saving $100. Within the spending limit you already approved, it orders the television, schedules delivery, books the installer, sends the mounting details, stores the warranty, and updates the household calendar. You leave work. When you get home, the television is on the wall.

The striking part is that almost none of the individual capabilities are science fiction. Comparison sites, payments, delivery windows, calendars, contractor marketplaces, and product reviews already exist. The new thing is orchestration: one system carries intent across them without requiring the human to be the integration layer.

A refrigerator starts making a strange sound. Today, that can become a miniature project: find the model number, search the noise, read forums, decide whether it matters, find a repair company, compare reviews, call during business hours, explain the issue, and negotiate an appointment. In an agentic version of the same life, you record ten seconds and say: “Figure out whether this needs attention.”

The agent identifies the model from purchase history, checks the manual and known service bulletins, asks a safe diagnostic question, and — if service is warranted — finds an authorized technician who fits the calendar. It may be allowed to organize the visit freely but required to ask before any repair over $300. The intelligence is useful; the permission structure is what makes the intelligence livable.

Now imagine that on Friday morning the weather at your weekend destination deteriorates, the attraction you booked closes, and the hotel changes its cancellation policy. A future agent does not merely send three alerts. It notices that the original plan is collapsing, checks the rules you have given it, holds a refundable room somewhere else, proposes a revised route, and asks one meaningful question: “The original weekend no longer makes sense. I can switch everything to this alternative for $74 more. Want me to do it?”

I have explored that travel-specific version of agentic delegation in more detail in this article, where the same shift from planning to acting becomes especially easy to see.

That is a different kind of convenience. It does not reduce one search. It reduces the need to continuously monitor the world for changes that affect our plans. The agent becomes less like a search box and more like a background layer of attention.

The television example still begins with a command. But the most consequential future may begin when the command disappears. If an agent has enough memory, permissions, and context, it can notice needs before we articulate them: the warranty expires next month, the pantry is running low, the train is likely to be cancelled, the annual subscription quietly increased its price, the dentist has not been booked in a year.

At first, anticipation will probably feel like excellent customer service. Later it could become the normal relationship between person and software. We will not ask the system to solve every small problem because it will already be watching for the conditions under which a problem tends to appear.

This is where I think the psychological boundary becomes much more serious. Delegation says, “I have chosen a goal; please execute it.” Anticipation says, “Infer which goals deserve action from the pattern of my life.” The first transfers work. The second begins to transfer agenda-setting.

An assistant that reminds me that my passport expires is easy to welcome. An assistant that decides I should replace my car because maintenance costs crossed a threshold is still understandable. But what happens when the same logic reaches softer parts of life? It notices I have not seen certain friends lately. It decides I am overworking. It learns which invitations I usually regret accepting. At what point does a helpful model of my preferences become an invisible editor of my days?

There is another risk that is less dramatic than a rogue agent and probably more plausible: delegation debt. We delegate a task because the machine does it well. Then we stop practicing the task. Eventually the cost of taking it back rises, which gives us another reason to keep delegating it.

We already know this feeling in simpler technologies. Many people can navigate a city far less confidently without GPS than they once could. That is not necessarily a tragedy; navigation skill may be a rational thing to trade for time. But AI can reach skills that are harder to classify as disposable: comparing evidence, drafting an argument, negotiating a purchase, recognizing when an explanation sounds wrong, or even deciding what information is missing before a decision can be made.

This creates a strange loop. The more competent the agent becomes, the less competence I need to exercise. But the less competence I exercise, the harder it may become to judge when the agent is wrong. Trust then becomes partly self-reinforcing: I rely on the system because it is good, and I have fewer independent reasons to know how good it is because I rely on the system.

That does not mean we should preserve every obsolete skill out of nostalgia. I do not want to memorize phone numbers just to prove I can. The more useful principle may be to preserve the skills required to supervise the things we delegate. If AI writes, we still need enough writing judgment to know when the result is hollow. If AI compares products, we still need to understand which criteria matter to us. If AI acts, we need to retain the ability to recognize a boundary it should not have crossed.

The obvious response to all of this is to defend human choice. But I am not convinced that every choice deserves defending. Comparing twelve washing machines is not a sacred exercise in free will. Modern life contains enormous quantities of low-value administrative thought: passwords, forms, appointment windows, renewals, return policies, price comparisons, delivery coordination, and inbox triage. If AI removes that burden, it can increase human agency rather than diminish it.

The difficult part is that low-value choices and identity-forming choices are not separated by a clean line. Buying socks is probably trivial. Choosing where to live is not. But between them sits most of everyday life: what we eat, how we spend weekends, which news we encounter, which hobbies we continue, which purchases we postpone, which friends we make time for. Repeated small decisions are part of the texture from which a life is built.

So perhaps the real design problem is not maximizing automation. It is deciding where friction is worth preserving. We may want almost zero friction around changing a delivery time and considerable friction around sending a message that could end a relationship. We may want an agent to prepare three investment options but not choose one. We may want it to draft a medical question but never decide that a symptom does not require a doctor.

I suspect good personal agents will eventually need something like a moral map of permission: not only what they can technically do, but what kinds of decisions the user wants to remain consciously present for. The machine will need a model not just of our preferences, but of our preferred relationship to our own preferences.

I think we will trust AI in many domains, but that answer is almost meaningless on its own. We already trust machines constantly: elevators, card networks, spam filters, navigation software, recommendation systems. What matters is not abstract trust. It is calibrated trust — trust matched to stakes, reversibility, visibility, evidence, and the cost of failure.

That is why the healthiest future may not look like an agent that never asks permission or one that asks permission for everything. Constant confirmation can become its own failure mode; when every action produces another approval box, attention turns into ritual clicking. Anthropic reported in 2026 that experienced Claude Code users enabled broad auto-approval more often while also interrupting the agent more often, suggesting a shift from approving every microscopic step toward intervening when something actually looked wrong. In a separate engineering report, Anthropic noted that users approved 93% of permission prompts in Claude Code, illustrating how repeated confirmations can create approval fatigue.

HackerNoon contributors have made a related argument about human-on-the-loop governance: if every action requires approval, supervision can degrade into ritual rubber-stamping rather than meaningful control.

Consumer agents will need their own version of that balance. The safest relationship may be neither obedience nor independence, but negotiated autonomy: act freely inside well-understood boundaries, slow down around irreversible actions, expose uncertainty when it matters, and make it easy for the human to inspect and reverse what happened.

And this returns me to the psychological question. We may think we are deciding how much to trust AI, while the more important process is happening in reverse: repeated convenience is teaching us what no longer feels worth deciding ourselves.

There was a time when “just Google it” sounded like a remarkable promise. Then it became infrastructure. We stopped noticing that it had changed memory, social habits, expertise, shopping, travel, and even the way an unanswered question feels. AI is crossing the same threshold, but the shift is deeper: search changed how we reach information; generative AI changes how much interpretation happens before the information reaches us; agents will change how much action happens after the answer.

What unsettles me is not the idea that AI will suddenly take control of everyday life. It is the opposite: that it will become good enough at thousands of tiny tasks that handing them over feels obviously rational, one by one. No dramatic surrender. No single day when we decide to stop choosing. Just a growing collection of decisions that no longer seem worth the effort.

Some of that will be liberation. I would happily live with less scheduling, less paperwork, fewer comparison tables, and fewer hours spent coordinating services that should have been simple. But not all friction is waste. Sometimes friction is where judgment is built, where a preference becomes visible, or where we notice that the thing we usually choose is no longer the thing we actually want.

So the question I keep coming back to is not “How intelligent will AI become?” It is more personal: which parts of my life do I still want to be present for, even when a machine could handle them better? I am not sure I know where I would draw that line yet. That uncertainty may be the point — we should probably decide it before convenience decides it for us.

If I let AI make decisions for me, am I also giving it the power to shape who I become — or to prevent me from becoming someone different?

Independent writer exploring science, space, AI, and emerging technologies. Curious about the future and the ideas shaping it.

#9762. Three more tools, three more countries: the Philippines' health fund, Vietnam's social insurance and a Bangla calendar

This week's batch on RozKaTool — free, no sign-up, everything runs in your browser — is three tools from three countries, and each one answers a question people ask every payday: what is being taken off my salary, and is the number right? A health premium in the Philippines, social insurance in Vietnam, and — for something completely different — a calendar converter for Bangladesh.

RozKaTool is now at 90 free tools, and the map keeps growing: Nepal, Thailand, Bangladesh, the Philippines, Sri Lanka, Vietnam, Indonesia, Malaysia, Brunei, Mongolia, Bhutan, Cambodia, Laos, the Maldives, Myanmar — and now the Bangla calendar joins the set.

PhilHealth, the Philippines' national health insurance, charges a flat 5% of monthly basic salary, split equally between employee and employer. But the percentage is only half the story: the premium is calculated on a salary clamped between a ₱10,000 floor and a ₱100,000 ceiling. Earn ₱8,000 and you pay on ₱10,000; earn ₱150,000 and you pay on ₱100,000 — so the maximum monthly premium is ₱5,000, or ₱2,500 from your side. On a ₱30,000 salary the premium is ₱1,500, split ₱750 and ₱750.

The calculator handles the cases the flat rule hides: kasambahay (domestic workers), whose employer pays the full premium, and OFWs, who pay on a different schedule. It shows the employee share, the employer share, and the total — because on a Filipino payslip the PhilHealth line is one of the few deductions you can actually verify by hand.

Philippines PhilHealth Contribution Calculator — enter your monthly salary in pesos and see your PhilHealth premium, split between you and your employer.

Vietnam's compulsory social insurance (BHXH) under Law 41/2024, in force since 1 July 2025, is really three insurances bundled together: social insurance, health insurance, and unemployment insurance. The employee pays 10.5% of salary; the employer pays 21.5% plus a 2% trade union fee — so on a VND 20,000,000 salary the employee's share is VND 2,100,000 and the employer's is VND 4,700,000. The social and health parts are capped at a salary base of VND 46,800,000 a month, while the unemployment part has its own region-based cap — and foreign employees do not pay unemployment insurance at all, which is the toggle most calculators forget.

The calculator shows each fund separately, with the caps applied, so the take-home figure can be checked line by line instead of trusted on faith.

Vietnam Social Insurance (BHXH) Contribution Calculator — enter your monthly salary in dong and see your BHXH shares, with caps, and your take-home pay.

The Bangla calendar is not just the Gregorian calendar with different month names: its year starts in mid-April, its months have different lengths, and the official version follows the Bangla Academy 2019 revision. The converter works in both directions, shows Bengali numerals, the weekday and the season, and always knows today's Bangla date in Dhaka time — 20 November 2026 is 5 Ogrohayon 1433. It was checked against 3,626 round-trip dates, and every one came back exact.

Bangla Date Converter — convert between English and Bangla dates, both ways, with today's Bangla date included.

Two of these three tools are about deductions that look simple — a flat 5%, a single percentage — until the floor, the ceiling, the caps and the exceptions show up. The numbers on a payslip are only trustworthy when the working is visible, so every calculator on RozKaTool shows the working beside the answer. The third tool is a reminder that "everyday" depends on where you live: for 170 million people, the date on the wall is a Bangla date first.

If you get paid in pesos or dong, or you plan your year by the Bangla calendar, try the tool for yourself and tell me if the result matches. And if there's a tool your country needs that I haven't built yet, I'd like to hear about it.

All 90 tools are free at RozKaTool — PDF tools, image tools, calculators and Pakistan-specific tools like the bijli bill and salary tax calculators. No uploads, no sign-up, no server.

#9761. Time-Series Models in the Streamhouse: A New Frontier and Use Cases

Real-time forecasting, anomaly detection, and optimization, powered by IBM time-series models with more than 50 million downloads. Now available natively on Confluent, in the cloud and on premises, running on CPUs.

Every business generates a continuous record of change: a machine reading, a payment, a sale, an order, or a change in inventory. These observations form time series, and they carry signals that can help teams anticipate what happens next.

The challenge is turning those signals into decisions while they still matter. A forecast delivered after a production run, a stockout, or a payment authorization may be accurate, but too late to influence the outcome.

IBM and Confluent are bringing time-series foundation models closer to the data as it flows. With Apache Flink, teams can apply forecasting , anomaly detection and semantic intelligence to streaming data using SQL, making model outputs available to the applications and people responsible for the next action.

Foundation models have changed how organizations work with text, images, and documents. Time-series foundation models extend a similar idea to numerical data by learning general patterns from diverse historical data and then applying that knowledge to new series and tasks. The models can provide a starting point without requiring teams to train a separate model for every series. Depending on the task and deployment, teams can also fine-tune a model or combine its outputs with other data and business logic.

Figure 1. More than 50 million downloads, and the family of four models behind them

Now the time series foundation models run natively inside Confluent as built-in functions in the cloud and on premises. In Confluent Cloud they are fully managed, with nothing to deploy (documentation). On premises, the models can run within your own infrastructure using Confluent Platform for Apache Flink.(documentation). The models run on CPUs, without requiring GPUs.

The models can support a range of mission-critical use cases, from helping keep production lines in spec and detecting unusual store activity to improving product-level planning. They can also provide signals to assess card payments and forecast trading volume to help place large orders. These building blocks can be applied across manufacturing, retail, banking, and airlines, bringing insights closer to where decisions are made.

See how time series and real-time context come together to create value:

Businesses operate continuously. Orders are updated, payments arrive, shipments are delayed, and inventory changes throughout the day. Yet the information behind these events often sits across systems that update at different times or rely on periodic batch processes. When applications and AI agents act on outdated or inconsistent information, they risk making decisions that no longer reflect what is happening.

A Streamhouse addresses this by continuously capturing, processing, governing, and serving current business context. Confluent’s Data Streaming Platform brings together five capabilities—connect, stream, process, govern, and query—to make that context available to applications, analytics, and agents. Apache Flink transforms and enriches data as it flows, while Lightning Tables provide low-latency access to the current state.

Figure 2. The Streamhouse on Confluent: from existing data sources to current business context that agents, applications, analytics and lakehouses use anywhere.

Time-series models add predictive power to this architecture. Flink can prepare the data, invoke forecasting and anomaly detection, and make the results available alongside the events that produced them. Other models—including large language models, statistical models, and specialized machine learning systems—can contribute where appropriate.

Figure 3. The intelligence layer of the Streamhouse: time series models, large language models, and ML and statistical models, with orchestration across them.

This approach can help teams in four ways:

-Scale model development. A pretrained model can provide a common starting point across many time series, reducing the need to develop and maintain a separate model for each one.

-Refresh predictions as data changes. Forecasts can incorporate recent observations as part of a streaming workflow, subject to the model’s requirements and the pipeline’s configuration.

-Put signals closer to decisions. Forecasts and anomalies can be routed to operational applications sooner, where teams can combine them with business context, rules, and human judgment.

-Run compact models on CPUs. The models are small enough to run on standard CPUs alongside the streaming pipeline, in the cloud or on premises, which can reduce the need for dedicated GPU infrastructure and simplify deployment.

Figure 4. Stream native time-series intelligence on Confluent

The following scenarios illustrate how organizations could combine time-series models, streaming data, and application logic.

An ice cream line’s quality depends on overrun—the amount of air whipped into the mix. Today, the process engineer and operator rely on QA lab measurements taken after the tubs are filled. If a new cream lot or a warm, humid day changes the process, hours of production may already need rework by the time the team sees the result.

To get ahead of the problem, a pretrained TTM model reads SCADA telemetry and QA measurements every 10 minutes. It forecasts the share of tubs expected to be in spec four hours ahead, along with a likely range.

When the forecast falls below the plant’s target, an optimization process evaluates combinations of freezer draw temperature and airflow. Because the model takes these control variables as inputs, it can score each option before anything changes on the line. The operator approves the recommended setpoints, while routine adjustments can be automated within predefined guardrails.

The outcome is a more proactive process: less rework, lower energy use per tonne, and more consistent quality. The same approach can be applied to ovens, dryers, kilns, and mills.

Figure 5. A forecast of product quality helps the operator evaluate freezer setpoints before making an adjustment.

A store operations team monitors sales for thousands of products across hundreds of stores. Fixed thresholds often flag predictable weekend peaks while missing quieter changes, such as a product selling less than expected. As alerts accumulate, it becomes harder for the team to know where to focus.

AI_DETECT_ANOMALIES gives each sales series an expected range based on its recent history. Each new reading is compared with that range at a confidence level the team chooses, without training a separate model for every product and store.

When sales fall outside the expected range, the signal can be combined with inventory and store data to help identify a likely cause and recommend a next step—for example, checking the shelf or replenishing stock. The same approach can be applied to machine sensors, API telemetry, meter readings, and payment volumes.

Figure 6. Store sales are compared with an expected range. In the view shown, recurring peaks remain within the range and no anomaly is flagged.

A category planner and a replenishment team need to keep products available across every store without carrying excess inventory. But forecasts may be refreshed only once a week, often focusing on top-selling products, while the long tail is managed with simpler rules. When sales patterns change between planning cycles, one store can run out while another has too much stock.

With AI_FORECAST, a pretrained model can forecast demand across products and stores. In this example, it produces a 28-day forecast with a P10–P90 range, refreshed as new sales data arrives. The planning application combines the forecast with inventory, lead time, and the planner’s chosen service level to calculate a reorder point.

When stock is projected to fall below that point, an agent can draft a purchase order for review. The same approach can support planning for spare parts, staffing, ATM cash, and energy demand.

Figure 7. A store-level demand forecast informs a reorder point and a proposed purchase order for oat milk.

Fraud teams already rely on sophisticated rules and models to evaluate transactions. One continuing challenge is that a threshold applied across many cardholders may not reflect how each person normally spends.

A time-series signal can add that individual context. In this example, each payment is compared with an expected spending range based on the card’s recent history. A transaction outside that range is passed to the bank’s existing fraud systems as an additional input, alongside other signals and business rules.

The bank can then decide whether to approve the payment, request additional authentication, or investigate further. The decision and the signals behind it can be retained for review.

Figure 8.A payment outside the card’s expected spending range prompts a step-up authentication in an illustrative fraud workflow.

An execution desk needs to divide a large order into smaller trades while managing its effect on the market. Historical volume curves offer a starting point, but today’s trading activity may look very different from the average.

On each one-minute bar, PatchTST-FM forecasts trading volume for the next 30 minutes, with a P10–P90 range. The execution algorithm uses that forecast to pace the order within the participation limit set by the desk.

If a news event changes market activity, the algorithm can pause and replan. If trading is quieter than expected, it can reduce the size of each slice and signal that the order may take longer to complete. Each forecast and the resulting execution decisions can be retained in the audit trail.

Figure 9. Volume forecast informs the proposed execution schedule for a 100,000-share order.

A reliability engineer investigating an unusual sensor pattern may want to know whether similar behavior appeared elsewhere in the plant.

TSPulse can produce representations of time-series windows that support similarity search. In a separately built application, those representations could be indexed and used to retrieve historical patterns across equipment. An engineer could search for shapes such as a spike and recovery, a gradual rise, or a step change, then inspect the associated maintenance records and operating conditions.

This application requires an embedding pipeline, an index, and access to the relevant context. Similarity can help narrow an investigation; it does not establish a root cause by itself.

Figure 10. Time-series embeddings can support a search for similar patterns across equipment and other signals.

The same models and building blocks can support different workflows across industries:

Figure 11. The plant twin, from sensor to setpoint. A new cream lot pulls overrun off target. The forecast reads the line, the agent proposes a new draw temperature and air flow, the operator approves, and the tubs are back in spec. Simulated data.

Figure 12. The store twin, a store and its supply chain. A promo is coming for oat milk. The forecast prices in the promo and sets the reorder point, the agent raises a purchase order, the planner approves, and the shelf is full on promo day. Simulated data.

Banking: payments and the trading desk. The fraud lead wants to stop card testing without blocking good customers, and the trader wants a large order done without moving the price. Every card and every symbol is scored against its own expected pattern, event by event. Fraud and security holds the odd swipe before authorization, anomaly detection spots the unusual flow, and trading paces each order with the forecast volume.

Airlines: hub operations, fleet and network. Operations control wants to see a disruption coming while there is still time to act. Engine, gate and network streams are forecast and checked in real time. Anomaly detection catches the engine reading that drifts, production optimization rebalances gates and crews, and supply chain planning puts the spare part where the aircraft will be.

In every industry, the Streamhouse does the same work: Flink runs the Granite models to forecast, detect and optimize, Streaming Agents act on the live context, and people approve the exceptions.

#9759. F5 iRule Commands Put the BIG-IP Data Plane on the Critical Patch Path

F5 BIG-IP appliances often terminate TLS, balance production traffic, and enforce network policy. Two current iRule issues matter because exploitation occurs on that data plane, not in an optional reporting page.

That description still depends on configuration. The presence of BIG-IP is not proof that either vulnerable command is used. Defenders need both the appliance version and the virtual-server iRule inventory.

First identify internet-facing virtual servers and those that carry authentication, payment, or administrative traffic. Search iRule configurations for the affected commands. Apply the fixed release listed in each F5 advisory and follow the vendor's installation guidance.

Where immediate maintenance is impossible, reduce exposure through tightly scoped virtual servers, source restrictions, or disabling unused commands. These controls do not replace the vendor fix, and they may not stop every request path.

After patching, verify the running software version on every cluster member. Check standby devices and synchronization status. A patch list for one appliance does not prove that the traffic group is protected.

Review TMM restarts, unexpected traffic disruption, crash evidence, and process behavior around the time of alerts. Preserve iRule versions and deployment history. Determine whether an unfamiliar iRule appeared or an existing one gained a vulnerable command.

Restrict management access separately from data-plane access. Use source-controlled iRule deployment with approval and drift detection. Remove unused iRules and keep a tested emergency procedure for disabling a virtual server without losing all visibility.

#9757. Inside the Bitcoin Mining Bug That Traps Slow Machines

A software engineer... Tinkering across Bitcoin and Finance

A software engineer... Tinkering across Bitcoin and Finance

A software engineer... Tinkering across Bitcoin and Finance

Bitcoin is, at its core, a record of who owns what. To better explain, no one  is in charge of it. There is no bank behind it, nor is there a company sitting in the middle to oversee the activities. Instead, thousands of computers around the world, called nodes, each keep their own full copy of the record.

Think of a notebook that everyone in a town keeps a copy of. When you pay someone in Bitcoin, you are not necessarily handing over a coin, you are pretty much announcing a new line to the network, something like "this amount now belongs to Ada", and node who hears it checks it against the rules. Was the money really yours to spend? Have you already spent it somewhere else? If the line breaks the rules, they ignore it and do not pass it on. If it passes, they pass it along and keep it ready to be written down.

That is the whole point of the design. Everyone who runs a node can verify the record independently. You do not have to trust a bank to tell you what you own, because you can check the record yourself.

But there is a problem with having thousands of independent computers maintaining the same record. What happens when two people try to spend the same bitcoin at roughly the same time? Some nodes may hear about the first transaction before the second, while others receive them in the opposite order. Each node can only accept one of the conflicting transactions, but how does the network eventually agree on which one counts?

Without a bank to settle the disagreement, who decides which payment is valid? And why should anyone trust the answer?

Bitcoin's answer is proof of work. Rather than allowing anyone to decide which transactions make it into the record, the network requires participants to demonstrate that they have performed computational work. Transactions are collected into batches called blocks, which you can think of as pages in our notebook. Roughly every ten minutes, a miner proposes the next page, and other nodes check it against the rules before accepting it. Each new page also refers to the one before it, so the pages form a chain in a fixed order.

When two transactions conflict, the network eventually settles on the one included in the accepted chain. The other is rejected.

Putting a page together, however, is not free. If anyone could write the next page, they could include whatever transactions they wanted and expect everyone else to copy it. The rules therefore require miners to prove that they have spent real computing effort before their proposed block can be accepted. That proof of work is what mining produces, and the people doing it are called miners.

A miner takes a candidate block containing pending transactions, adds an extra number to it, and runs the entire thing through a hash function. This number, called a nonce, can be changed repeatedly. Each time the block is hashed, the result is a fixed-length string that looks random. Change even one character of the input and the output changes completely. There is no reliable way to predict which number will produce the result the network needs.

The network only accepts a block if its hash, interpreted as a number, falls below a target set by the protocol. The miner has to keep changing the nonce and trying again until it finds a result that meets the requirement. Mining machines do this trillions of times every second. That speed is called the hash rate.

It is a bit like rolling dice until a very rare combination turns up. Finding it takes an enormous number of attempts and a lot of luck. Checking the result, on the other hand, takes just one roll. Once a miner finds a valid block, other nodes can verify it independently. The successful miner receives newly created bitcoin as well as the fees from the transactions included in the block. At the time of writing, that reward is 3.125 bitcoin per block.

All that computational effort is also what makes rewriting the record so difficult. Anyone attempting to change an old block would have to redo the work for that block and every block that follows it, and do so faster than the rest of the network can keep adding new ones.

There is another mechanism that keeps the process predictable. Bitcoin adjusts its mining difficulty every 2,016 blocks, roughly every two weeks, to keep block production close to ten minutes. When more computing power joins the network, the target becomes harder to meet. When computing power falls, it becomes easier.

Suppose you buy a mining machine and plug it in. You are now racing everyone else who wants to find the next block. Some of these other miners run whole warehouses of machines for the purpose of mining. Ideally, your one machine has a very small chance of winning any given race. It could take years, and nobody can tell you when. Your electricity bill, meanwhile, still arrives every month.

That is why miners team up working together and combining hash rates in order to improve their chances to compete for the next block. A group of miners working together is called a pool. Everyone in the pool works on the same block, and if anyone in the group wins the race, the reward is shared out according to how much work each member did.

Every pool has an operator who runs it. The operator's server puts together the candidate block, chooses which payments go into it, and hands the same job to every member. Each machine then tries its own range of numbers, so nobody wastes effort repeating someone else's guesses.

How the reward gets split is up to the pool. Some pay a fixed amount for each unit of work, whether or not the pool wins the race, so that at the end of the day, the pool carries the luck when it finds a block. Others pay only when a block is found, split by recent work. You will see these called PPS and PPLNS. The details differ, but every scheme needs the same thing, an honest count of how much work each miner did.

That count is the hard part. The pool cannot see your machine, you could tell it you are running a hundred of them and it could not check, and it cannot simply trust you, because then anyone could claim a share of the pay without doing any work. All it ever gets is what you send back. If the only thing you ever sent back was a winning block, it would hear from you almost never, and a machine that was switched off would look exactly the same as an honest one that had been unlucky. So the pool needs a better way to measure you.

The trick is to ask for something smaller than a winning block. Remember that the network only accepts a block if its hash result falls below a very low target. The pool sets a second target of its own, one that is far easier to hit, and tells its miners to send in every guess that gets below it. Those guesses are called shares.

A die makes the idea easy to see. Landing a six a hundred times in a row almost never happens. Landing a single six happens frequently. The network asks for the first kind of luck, and the pool asks for the second. Every machine can produce shares over and over, so the pool starts hearing from everyone, constantly. And checking a share is cheap, because the pool only has to hash it once and compare the result with its target.

A share cannot be faked. Nobody can steer a hash function, so the only way to produce a result that beats the target is to actually make guesses, the same as when chasing a real block. A pile of shares is honest evidence that real work happened, and once in a very long while, one of those shares also beats the network's target, and that share is the block.

Now the pool has something it can count. If one machine sends ten shares a minute and another sends twenty, the second is doing about twice the work and earns about twice as much. Because shares come so often, that steady stream tells the pool two things at once: that you are still alive, and roughly how fast you are going.

The pool controls how often you find shares, the settings for this is called the share difficulty. A higher difficulty means a harder chance for shares, because the hash result has to land lower to count, so you find fewer of them. A lower difficulty makes shares easy and plentiful.

In the usual convention, a difficulty of 1 takes about 4.3 billion guesses on average, and a difficulty of 1,000 takes about a thousand times that. So to find how many shares a machine sends each second, take its hash rate and divide it by the difficulty times 4.3 billion.

Let’s try an example, say a machine running at 100 tera hashes a second, which means 100 trillion guesses every second. At difficulty 1 it would send about 23,000 shares a second, and the pool's server would have to check every one of them. At a difficulty of 100,000 the same machine sends about one share every four seconds, which is far more comfortable. Now take a much smaller machine running at 1 tera hash a second, with that same difficulty of 100,000. It sends a share only about every seven minutes. So the right difficulty is different for every machine, and machines differ in speed by huge margins. It also changes with the moment, because a single machine speeds up and slows down through the day as it heats up, cools down or loses power. No fixed setting suits everyone, or even suits one machine for long. The pool has to pick a difficulty for each miner, and keep picking it.

Pools handle this with something called variable difficulty, or vardiff. Instead of fixing one difficulty for everyone, the pool changes it for each miner while that miner is connected. It picks a target share rate, say one share every few seconds, and keeps adjusting the miner's difficulty to stay near it. A new miner starts at some initial difficulty, and the pool corrects from there.

It works like a thermostat in a house. A thermostat does not know what the weather will do. It reads the temperature, compares it with what you asked for, and turns the heating up or down. The pool does the same with shares. If a miner speeds up and shares start flooding in, the pool raises the difficulty. If a miner slows down and shares thin out, the pool lowers it. Engineers call the code doing this a controller, the miner is the thing being controlled, and the target share rate is the goal.

A thermostat has a thermometer, and the pool's equivalent is the shares themselves. That is a problem, because the pool cannot ask the machine how fast it is going. The shares arriving are all it can see, and they are noisy by nature. They come at random, like raindrops on a roof. Even in steady rain the gaps between drops are uneven, so one long gap does not mean the rain has eased. When shares come often, the controller can average over plenty of them and get a clear picture. When they come rarely, it has very little to average, and the picture is blurry.

This is the detail that the article is about. There are two ways to build a controller. One wakes up only when a share arrives, looks at how long it has been since the last one, and decides what to do. The research post calls this clockless, and ckpool is one pools that defines its controller this way. The other also has a timer, so it wakes up on a schedule even if nothing arrives. The Stratum v2 reference implementation, SRI, works this way. It sounds like a small difference, but it decides what happens when a miner goes quiet.

So what happens when a miner goes quiet? Picture a machine in a hot container, running fine all morning. The pool has settled on a difficulty that gives it one share every few seconds. Around noon the heat builds and the machine throttles itself down to a fraction of its speed. Nothing is broken. It is still hashing and still honest, just slower. And this happens all the time. Miners slow down when it gets too hot, when the power supply wobbles, when a fan fails, or when a site is asked to cut its electricity use for the grid.

The difficulty, though, was set for the old speed. Shares that used to show up every few seconds now take minutes. Think about what that does to a controller that only wakes when a share arrives. It is woken far less often, and when it does wake it has very little to go on. So it rarely acts, the difficulty stays high, shares stay rare, and the controller stays mostly asleep. Nothing in that loop ever breaks it.

A research post on Delving Bitcoin in July 2026 called this stranding a miner, and Bitcoin Optech picked it up in September.

A controller with a timer escapes the loop. Because it wakes on a clock, it notices that no shares have come in for a while and lowers the difficulty anyway. A research post, A clockless vardiff strands a slowing miner, tested this in a simulation where hash rate falls to zero over minutes 60 to 64. The SRI design, which has a timer, noticed the silence and kept lowering difficulty. The clockless design did not. It stayed stuck at a difficulty the slowing miner could no longer reach.

The obvious reaction is to say the controller is badly tuned. Make it react faster, shorten the window it looks at, tighten the thresholds. The Delving Bitcoin post, "A clockless vardiff strands a slowing miner", argues that none of this fixes the problem, because the problem is not in the settings at all.

Start with what the controller can actually know. To guess a miner's speed it counts shares over some stretch of time. When shares are plentiful, that count is a good guess. When there are only a few, it is a poor one, the same way two coin flips tell you almost nothing about whether a coin is fair. The post puts a number on it. The error in the estimate, as a fraction of the true speed, grows roughly as one over the square root of the number of shares you expect to see. As the shares dry up, that error has no ceiling, so the controller is not badly tuned. The information it needs is simply not arriving, and the post calls this "a correctness problem, not a tuning problem".

The post also separates two kinds of tolerance, because one of them is a trap that is easy to build by accident. A controller can decide that small errors in its measurement are not worth acting on. That is harmless, because the next reading will correct a slightly wrong one. A controller can also have a dead zone in what it does, a range of difficulties it will not move away from. That one is dangerous, because a miner that sits at the wrong difficulty inside it will never be moved out.

From this the post draws a simple test for any design. Ask where the controller comes to rest after hashrate drops, meaning the difficulty at which it stops changing anything. There should be exactly one such place, and it should be the correct difficulty. If there is a second one, at a difficulty that is too high, a miner can get stuck on it, and that is what happens in the loop above.

Silence is not the only way to get stuck. The second way works even while shares keep arriving, and it comes from how pools choose their difficulty values. Many of them allow only a short list, usually powers of two: 1, 2, 4, 8 and so on. Each value is a rung on a ladder, and the controller can move between rungs but never to a value in between.

On its own that is harmless. The trouble starts when it is combined with a weak push. Say the controller only steps down a rung when the measured share rate looks well below the target. A miner that has slowed a little, so that its rate is low but not low enough, sits in the gap between two rungs, and the controller does nothing. The post shows that you need both ingredients to trap a miner this way, the coarse rungs and the weak push. Either one alone does not do it.

Eric Price of MARA said on the Optech podcast that plenty of Stratum v1 pools behave like this, and that he traced the habit back to CGMiner. He also said Stratum v2 does not have this power of two quirk.

The idea did not stay on the forum. Bitcoin Optech covered the thread in newsletter 423 on 18 September 2026 and says Price agreed with where it was heading. Four days later, on the 22 September podcast, Price explained vardiff to Mark "Murch" Erhardt in plain terms.

Murch asked the obvious question: if a miner is declining, might it "starve before they reach" the lower difficulty? Price called that "the vicious cycle", and added that machines "live longer" when the share rate is pushed higher, which is one reason pools like to keep it up.

The guest PortlandHODL, a former MARA engineer, brought up two more cases. One was a startup flood, where a new miner sends a burst of shares before the pool has worked out its difficulty. The other was a proxy that combines several sites with curtailments, where one site stalling gets hidden inside the total.

A caution on my own sources. I could not open Optech's own pages, so the newsletter point comes from the podcast coverage and the Delving thread, and I did not read the last stretch of the podcast transcript. Check both against the originals before you publish.

The simplest fix is to give the pool a clock. If the controller wakes on a timer as well as when a share arrives, it notices when a miner has gone quiet and eases the difficulty, and the trap disappears. SRI, the Stratum v2 reference implementation, already works this way. The second fix is for the controller to lean less on the past. Some designs average everything since their last change, so a long healthy stretch makes them slow to notice that a miner has just fallen ill.

People in the discussion added their own ideas. Anthony Towns suggested that a proxy, the middleman that sits between a farm of machines and the pool, should halve the difficulty after 30 seconds of silence. The reply was that this only moves the problem, because the proxy then needs a watchful loop of its own, and there are now two controllers that both have to get it right. Eric Price's contribution was to treat easing and raising difficulty differently, and to count the absence of shares as an event in its own right.

That last idea sums up all the others. When a miner goes silent, the silence is information. A pool that waits for the next share before acting is waiting for exactly the thing it will not get.

The lesson is simple. A controller that only acts when it hears from the thing it controls goes quiet at exactly the moment the thing goes quiet. Miners that throttle for heat, power cuts or curtailment are the ones at risk, and as more mining sites sell flexibility to the grid, slowing down on purpose is becoming normal.

One caution before you take this too far. The evidence in the post is a simulation, a test proxy and a read through the source code, and two of the three designs it tests are small examples built for the test, not copies of pools running today. Nobody has yet surveyed real pools to see how many behave this way, or checked whether real miners have lost money to it. The most useful next step belongs to anyone with access to pool logs.

#9756. Why your fine-tuning job takes longer than the FLOPs say

Predicting end-to-end fine-tuning time on shared GPU clusters, from 272 production runs.

A preview of our upcoming paper, Predicting End-to-End Fine-Tuning Time for Generative Language Models. The full version will be on arXiv soon.

GPUs are among the most expensive and scarcest resources in AI today. Anyone running a shared cluster has to decide, every day, which jobs go on which GPUs and in what order. That plan is only as good as the estimate of how long each job will take. When a job finishes hours early, GPUs sit idle until the next one is dispatched. When it runs hours late, everything queued behind it slips, experiments wait and delivery dates move.

Better duration estimates turn this into planning instead of guesswork: what runs, when, and on how many GPUs, with less idle capacity in between. Yet the estimate most teams use is a back-of-the-envelope FLOP calculation. It says nine hours, and the job finishes the next afternoon.

We wanted to know how far off that math really is, and whether we could do better before a job is even dispatched. So we took 272 real supervised fine-tuning (SFT) jobs from our production pool of NVIDIA H200 GPUs, about 7,382 GPU-hours in total, and compared analytical estimates against learned predictors.

The short version: the usual FLOP-based estimate explains little of what we observed (R² = 0.31, MAE 12.41 h). A CatBoost regressor that only sees information available before dispatch reaches R² = 0.98, with a mean absolute error of 1.71 h and a median error of 0.51 h in 5-fold cross-validation. The gap comes from two things a closed-form estimate cannot do. The regressor sees more training-specific signals, such as evaluation cadence, checkpoint policy, per-GPU load and fine-tuning regime, and it learns the nonlinear interactions between them from past runs.

For a dense Transformer, training costs roughly 6·P·D floating-point operations, where P is the parameter count and D the number of training tokens. Divide that by what your GPUs can deliver and you get a training-loop time:

Here N_GPU is the number of GPUs, FLOPS_peak is the peak throughput of one GPU from its spec sheet, and MFU (Model FLOPs Utilization) is the fraction of that peak the training actually achieves. Real jobs never run at peak because of memory traffic, communication and kernel inefficiencies, so MFU typically sits somewhere between 30% and 60%, and the right value for a given job is not known in advance.

This is a good description of the optimization loop. A job is more than its loop, though. Before the first step there is environment setup, model download and loading, and tokenization. During training there are periodic evaluations and checkpoint uploads. At the end, the final model goes to object storage. On a multi-tenant cluster, all of it competes with other jobs for network and storage I/O.

These overheads depend on configuration, and they do not scale neatly with workload or GPU count. Two jobs with the same nominal compute can finish hours apart.

To keep the comparison fair, the FLOP baseline we test counts the scheduled evaluation tokens as well as the training tokens, and we sweep MFU over a wide range.

We treat end-to-end duration as a supervised regression problem. Given a feature vector built from the job configuration and model metadata, predict the wall-clock time between the moment the job gets its GPUs and the moment it is done. Queue time is excluded.

We compared Linear Regression, Ridge, XGBoost and CatBoost. Feature selection combined correlation filtering, mutual information and permutation importance across 18 candidate feature sets, followed by a grid search with MAE as the criterion. The final CatBoost model uses 24 features.

Distribution of end-to-end duration across the 272 runs. Mean 23.43 h, median 15.29 h.

All numbers come from stratified 5-fold cross-validation. The first four rows are analytical and involve no fitting.

No single MFU value fixes the FLOP baseline. We swept MFU from 0.25 to 0.65. The best setting, 30%, still leaves a mean error above 12 hours on jobs that last 23 hours on average.

A more detailed analytical model does not close the gap. As a second baseline we took Calculon (Isaev et al., SC '23), an analytical performance model for LLM training from prior work. It builds an explicit layer graph and accounts for compute, memory traffic and inter-device communication. We extended the public implementation to cover LoRA, grouped-query attention, fused attention, bfloat16 and SwiGLU. Its estimates still correspond to a median of only 11% of the observed wall-clock time. That says nothing against Calculon as a step-level tool, which is what it was designed for. It shows how much of a production job happens outside the optimization step.

Linear models help, and then stall. Ridge brings MAE down to 7.23 h. The relationship between configuration and duration is not well captured by a purely linear model.

Gradient boosting does the heavy lifting. CatBoost and XGBoost land within one standard deviation of each other on every metric. We carry CatBoost forward because it has the lowest mean error across the board.

CatBoost's feature importance concentrates in a handful of features. Model and workload variables are there, as expected, but so are evaluation and checkpoint variables. num_eval_data, the total number of samples processed in evaluation over the life of the job, ranks first, followed by num_trainable_params, batch_eval_size_percent, num_all_params and num_gpus*batch_train_percent, with num_params_saved close behind. SHAP values tell the same story: high evaluation volume consistently pushes the predicted time up, while trainable parameter count has a nonlinear effect that only becomes large for the biggest models.

Mean feature importance of the CatBoost model across folds (PredictionValuesChange).

Feature importance is not a causal claim. Still, the pattern lines up with how a job is actually spent. How often you evaluate, how large the evaluation set is and how many checkpoints you persist all shape the wall-clock time, alongside model and dataset scale. These are choices people often make by habit when writing a training config.

One caveat on reading the plots: larger GPU allocations show positive contributions to predicted time. In our data, bigger allocations go with bigger jobs, so num_gpus acts partly as a proxy for job scale. It does not mean adding GPUs makes a job slower.

Looking at all 272 out-of-fold predictions, the median absolute error is 0.51 h. 80% of predictions are within 2.20 h and 90% are within 4.31 h. Broken down by job duration:

Up to 60 hours, the median error stays at about one hour or less. The long tail is where the model struggles, and with only 13 runs above 60 hours we read that as a data limitation.

Out-of-fold absolute error against real duration, colored by duration range. Errors stay low up to 60 h and widen in the sparse tail.

More data should still help. On a fixed 20% holdout, MAE drops from 1.63 h to 1.50 h when going from 85% to 100% of the training partition, with no clear plateau.

In practice, the predictor gives a scheduler a duration it can plan around before a job starts: which jobs to run together, when GPUs will free up, and whether a run will finish in time for its deadline.

What does transfer is the method: overhead-aware features, multicollinearity-aware selection and the comparison protocol. The full paper will report the feature formulas, the selection procedure, the search spaces and the final hyperparameters in full, so the pipeline can be rebuilt on any execution-log dataset with a similar structure.

Next on our list: hardware-specific descriptors and validation on other GPU types, transfer learning for configurations with few observations, other training objectives, and more data on long runs.

The full paper is coming to arXiv soon. Follow the Dharma-AI organization on Hugging Face to be notified when it is out, and leave your questions in the comments below. We would like to hear how you estimate job duration on your own clusters.
