#9755. Granola vs Otter vs Fireflies: what the same 25 hours of meetings really costs in year one

Posted on Nov 20 • Originally published at theaistackguide.blogspot.com

Disclosure: this post contains affiliate links, including ElevenLabs and systeme.io. If you sign up through one of them this site may earn a commission at no extra cost to you, and that is how the site pays for itself. Every price below was read from the provider's own pricing page on 20 November 2026 and is a published list price, not an estimate. More detail on the about page.

Meeting notes are the one AI subscription most teams in 2026 already pay for, and almost nobody can price — including the engineers who own the data pipeline behind it. The reason is not that the tools are expensive. It is that they are metered three different ways, and the meter only starts to matter in month three, when the free tier runs out of the thing you did not know it was counting.

Take the three tools a solo builder or small team actually weighs: Granola, Otter.ai and Fireflies.ai. Read their pricing pages side by side on 20 November 2026 and a strange pattern appears. Granola charges by history — the free plan keeps 30 days of notes and the paid plan keeps all of them. Otter charges by transcription minutes — 300 a month on Basic, 1,200 on Pro, unlimited on Business. Fireflies charges by stored minutes — 400 per team on Free, 8,000 per seat on Pro, unlimited on Business, with transcription itself advertised as unlimited from the free tier up.

So the honest question is not which one transcribes better. It is: for the same 25 hours of meetings a month, for one person, for one year, which meter runs out first — and what does the plan that does not run out cost? Billed annually, the answer is $168 on Granola, $228 on Fireflies and $239.88 on Otter. Paid monthly, the same three plans cost $168, $348 and $360. That gap is the whole article.

A cost comparison only travels if the workload is stated, so here it is. It is deliberately unremarkable: a consultant or one-person software business whose sales, client calls and partnerships all happen on video calls.

Two things are deliberately left out of the totals and priced separately at the end: what happens to the recordings afterwards, and the fact that none of the three will send anything to a list. Both matter more than people expect, and both are where a “free” stack turns into a paid one.

Granola is the cleanest bill of the three, because it does not meter meeting minutes at all. The Basic plan is $0 and includes AI meeting notes, bot-free device-audio capture, speaker tagging, custom note templates, shared folders, voice typing and AI chat within and across meetings. What it does not include is time: the plan comparison lists 30 days of meeting history on Basic, against unlimited on the paid tiers. A free plan that deletes the meeting you need to quote three months later is a trial with a nice interface.

Business is $14 per user per month and it is the plan this workload needs, because it removes that one limit: unlimited meeting notes and history, advanced AI thinking models, pre-meeting briefs, follow-up emails, a workspace-wide dictionary, integrations with Attio, Notion, HubSpot, Affinity and Zapier, MCP across your apps, and API access. It also adds the thing people forget to price: it is not a per-seat multiplier for a solo user, so the first year is $168.

Enterprise is $35 per user per month and is a different product: SSO, HIPAA-compliant workspaces, org-wide auto-deletion periods, admin controls over sharing and API access, workspace usage analytics, an audit API and an org-wide notification that Granola is in use. For one person it is $420 a year spent on governance nobody audits.

Two details worth knowing before you compare it to the others. Granola's grid marks bot-free, device-audio capture as included on every plan — there is no participant joining the call, which changes how the tool feels to clients. And the page is explicit that you are responsible for consent: it recommends asking permission before transcribing others and ships an automated notice at the start of each meeting for that reason. That is a policy line, not a price line, but it is the kind of thing that decides whether you can use a recorder on a client call at all.

Otter's pricing page is the most conventionally generous-looking and the most arithmetic-sensitive. Basic is free with 300 monthly transcription minutes, a 30-minute maximum per conversation, the 25 most recent conversations kept, three lifetime file imports and 5 custom vocabulary terms — in other words, a plan that cannot hold a 45-minute client call, let alone a year of them.

Pro is $16.99 per user a month, or $8.33 a month billed annually (the page advertises 51% off the annual price, so roughly $100 a year). It brings 1,200 in-app recording minutes a month, 90 minutes per meeting, 10 monthly file imports, unlimited storage, unlimited history, advanced AI workflows and meeting templates, and Salesforce/HubSpot/Zapier integrations. At $8.33 it is by far the cheapest way to get a serious notetaker — for someone whose meetings fit in 20 hours a month.

That is exactly where this workload breaks it. 1,200 minutes is 20 hours, and the workload is 25. Otter's minute allowances do not roll over, and the page sells no overage or top-up route, so the only correct answer is the next tier up: Business at $30 per user a month, or $19.99 billed annually (the page shows a $24 first-three-months promotion and a 33% annual saving). Business removes the limits that matter here: unlimited meetings and in-app recordings, up to 4 hours per meeting, 6,000 imported minutes a month, custom AI workflows, activity logs, usage analytics, three concurrent meetings and 25 workspace members. Annual billing makes it $239.88 a year; paying monthly makes it $360.

Note what happened there: a 51% annual discount on Pro still lost to a $14 flat plan, because the tier the workload forced was never the discounted one. That is the most common way a “cheap” AI subscription turns out to be a $20-a-month subscription.

Fireflies is the one that reads as unlimited and is not, and the trap is subtle enough to be worth spelling out. On the pricing page, read with the annual switch on, Free is $0 with unlimited transcription, limited AI summaries, 400 minutes of storage per team, 20 AI credits, 2-hour recording limit, three public channels, and API access at 30 requests a minute.

Pro is $18 a seat a month, or $10 billed annually (annual billing takes up to 44% off). It adds unlimited AI summaries, video recording at 720p, a personal assistant, an email assistant, voice agents, unlimited integrations and 8,000 minutes of storage per seat. Transcription is unlimited here too — and that is the sentence people stop reading at, because the meter that fills up is the other one.

8,000 minutes is 5.3 months of the 25-hour workload. If you keep what you record, Pro reaches its ceiling around month six of twelve, which makes Business at $29 a seat a month, or $19 billed annually, the plan this workload actually needs: unlimited storage, 30 AI credits, multi-language mode, conversation intelligence, team analytics, private channels, 3-hour recordings and 1080p video. Annually that is $228 a year; monthly it is $348. Enterprise at $39 a seat a month is annual-billing only, adds rules engine, SSO/SCIM, audit logs and HIPAA-ready workspaces with a BAA, and is priced for companies with an IT department.

The free tier deserves one honest sentence, because “unlimited transcription” is real: 400 minutes of team storage is about nine 45-minute calls. Fireflies Free is a good way to try the product on a fortnight of meetings and a bad way to run a year of them.

Every figure below is from the provider's own pricing page on 20 November 2026, in US dollars, excluding tax. “Annual” means the per-seat monthly equivalent that the annual option actually charges, not a discount you have to ask for.

Read the annual column twice, because it is where the three products stop looking alike. Otter's discount is the steepest in the table and still lands above Fireflies' list price; Granola offers no annual option at all, which is unusual in 2026 and worth knowing before you budget for a discount that does not exist.

Now assemble the three stacks for the workload at the top. Annual billing throughout — the way you buy a tool you intend to keep — and the plan is the cheapest one that survives both the 45-minute call and the twelve-month history.

First, the discount is a decoy. Otter advertises 51% off and Fireflies up to 44% off, and Granola advertises nothing because it does not sell an annual plan. Yet the tool without a discount is the cheapest of the three, by $60 to $72 a year. A percentage off is a fact about the vendor's pricing psychology, not about your bill: what matters is which tier the workload forces you into, and both metered tools were forced up one tier while the flat one was not.

Second, the meters fail in the order you would not expect. You would guess the tool that bills by the minute runs out first. In practice Otter's Pro tier missed by 300 minutes a month — one extra call a week — while Fireflies' Pro missed by storage, which no one thinks of as a budget line. If you delete old recordings you could stretch Fireflies Pro to $120 a year; if you keep them, as the workload requires, you are on Business. That single habit is worth $108 a year.

Third, the yearly difference is small next to the monthly one. Between the cheapest and most expensive of the three, annual billing is a $72 spread over twelve months. Between paying monthly and annually on the same plan, Otter is $120 and Fireflies is $120. The billing cycle moves the bill more than the choice of product does — the opposite of what comparison shopping assumes.

All of the above assumes 25 hours of meetings, which is a lot of talking. Halve it and the ranking inverts, which is the most useful thing a metered competitor can do to a flat-priced one.

At 10 hours a month (600 minutes, 120 hours a year) Otter Pro's 1,200 minutes cover the workload with room to spare, so the $8.33 annual price applies: $99.96 a year, $0.83 per meeting hour. Fireflies Pro's 8,000 minutes of storage last thirteen months at this volume, so $120 a year works, at $1.00 per hour. Granola has no cheaper tier to drop to — the plan is $14 whatever you do with it — so the same $168 is $1.40 per hour, nearly three times Otter.

That is the actual shape of this decision: light meeting loads belong to the metered tools, heavy ones belong to the flat one. Somewhere around 20 hours a month Otter's Pro tier stops fitting and the arithmetic turns; above 25 hours, Granola's $168 is the cheapest credible answer and stays flat if your calendar gets worse. If you know your monthly meeting hours within a few, you can pick correctly in one line. If you do not, the flat plan is the one that will not surprise you in a busy quarter.

Free plans are where most people start and where most comparisons stop, so here is the same workload against all three free tiers.

None of the three free tiers is a scam; each is a fair sample. But the marketing sentences differ in how much they hide. “Unlimited transcription” is true of Fireflies Free and irrelevant, because storage is the limit. “AI meeting notes” is true of Granola Basic and expires. Otter's free plan is the most honest of the three about volume — it just tells you a number you will exceed in week one.

Two pieces of the job sit outside all three products, and leaving them out is how a $14-a-month tool becomes a $40-a-month one.

Getting the recording out as something other people will consume. A transcript is an asset only if it travels. The cheapest way to make it travel is audio: a five-minute recap of a client call sent as a voice note gets listened to, while a 6,000-word transcript gets archived. ElevenLabs Starter is $6 a month for 30,000 credits, and text to speech spends one credit per character, so that is roughly 30,000 characters of finished speech a month — about four or five call recaps. Annual billing is ten months' price, $60, and as of 20 November 2026 the Black Friday sale running to 1 December takes up to 55% off annual plans, with Creator quoted at $99 for the year. The end-to-end version of that pipeline is in the article-to-audio stack guide, and the per-hour cost of voice in the AI voice generator comparison.

Getting the notes to people who were not in the room. Follow-up emails are a Granola Business feature, but they send one email to one person; a list is a different tool. systeme.io's free plan carries 2,000 contacts, three funnels, one course, unlimited email sends and no transaction fees, which is enough to turn a weekly “what I learned this week” note into a list. The free-tier comparison, including where it stops being enough, is in the free funnel and email stack guide.

One structural point about where the notes should land. All three tools will push a summary into Notion or Slack; Granola's Business plan lists Notion, Zapier and HubSpot integrations and MCP access, Otter's Business plan lists Salesforce and HubSpot sync, and Fireflies lists unlimited integrations from Pro. If your notes end up in a second brain anyway, the notetaker's own search becomes the second-best search you own — which is what the second-brain cost comparison is about. And if you want the pipeline to run itself, the workflow automation comparison prices what that automation layer costs on its own.

Choose Granola if your calendar is heavy and you want a bill you can predict. $14 a month, no minute meter, no storage meter, no annual discount to chase — and the only wall is history, which the paid plan removes. It is the cheapest of the three for this workload at $168 a year and $0.56 per meeting hour, and it is the only one whose price does not move when a busy month arrives. The trade is the absence of the governance stack: no SSO, no audit API, no HIPAA until $35 a seat.

Choose Otter if your meetings are moderate and you like the transcript layer more than the notes layer. At $8.33 a month billed annually, Pro is the best value in this article for anyone under about 20 hours of meetings a month, and the editing, playback and search tools are the most complete of the three. Just measure your minutes before you commit: the tier above is $19.99 and the jump happens at 1,200 minutes, not at a price you choose.

Choose Fireflies if you record a lot of sales or customer calls and want the conversation analytics around them — sentiment, talk-time, topic trackers, team insights. It is the middle price of the three at $228 a year, with unlimited transcription on every tier including free, and the useful insight that its real constraint is storage, not minutes. If you are disciplined about deleting old recordings, Pro at $120 a year is the cheapest way into a paid notetaker of the three.

And whatever you pick, pay annually and know your meter. Moving Otter or Fireflies from monthly to annual saves $120 a year on the same plan — more than the entire spread between the three products. Knowing whether your plan counts minutes, stored minutes or days is worth another $60 to $108, and it takes ten minutes with your calendar.

Yes. Granola Basic is $0 and includes AI meeting notes, bot-free device-audio capture, AI chat within and across meetings, custom templates and shared folders. The limit is history: Basic keeps 30 days of meeting history, while Business ($14 per user a month) makes it unlimited. For anyone who needs to search a call from three months ago, Basic is a trial rather than a free tier.

1,200 in-app recording minutes per user a month, with a 90-minute maximum per meeting and no rollover. Otter Basic includes 300 minutes a month with a 30-minute per-meeting cap, and Business is unlimited with a 4-hour per-meeting cap. Otter Pro costs $16.99 a month, or $8.33 a month billed annually.

Not in the way people expect. Fireflies advertises unlimited transcription even on the free plan; what it meters is storage — 400 minutes per team on Free, 8,000 minutes per seat on Pro, and unlimited on Business. At 25 hours of meetings a month, 8,000 minutes is about five months of recordings, so a year of history requires Business at $19 a seat (annual) or $29 (monthly).

Granola Business at $168 a year billed monthly, which is also the annual figure because Granola publishes no annual discount. Fireflies Business is $228 billed annually ($348 monthly) and Otter Business is $239.88 billed annually ($360 monthly). At 10 hours a month the order reverses and Otter Pro at $99.96 a year is the cheapest.

Granola does not: its plan grid lists bot-free, device-audio capture on every plan, so nothing joins the call. Otter's feature grid describes a notetaker that joins Zoom, Microsoft Teams and Google Meet to write and share notes. Fireflies joins through its notetaker or, as its page notes, can record through a Chrome extension without the bot. The difference matters for client calls, where a visible bot is also a consent signal.

Multiply by seats on the same plans: Granola Business $504 a year, Fireflies Business $684, Otter Business $719.64. Above that, the products diverge into admin features rather than price — Otter's SSO starts with a 100-licence Enterprise plan, Fireflies sells SSO at $39 a seat a month with annual billing only, and Granola includes SSO from $35 a seat.

For the same 25 hours of meetings a month, one person pays $168 on Granola, $228 on Fireflies and $239.88 on Otter, billed annually — $0.56, $0.76 and $0.80 per meeting hour. Pay monthly and the last two become $348 and $360 for the identical plans.

The useful lesson is not that Granola wins. It is that the two tools advertising the biggest discounts were the two that cost more, because both meter something — minutes, or stored minutes — and this workload pushed both one tier up, past the discount. Granola charges a flat $14 and meters history instead, which is why it looks expensive next to a $8.33 promotional sticker and turns out cheapest at the end of the year.

So price your own calendar before you price a product. Count the meeting hours in a normal month, decide whether you intend to keep the recordings, and then buy the tier that survives both. That ten-minute exercise is worth $60 to $180 a year here, and it is the only part of this comparison that your own numbers can improve on mine.

#9754. DaisyRose-27B: Pushing the Frontier of Post-Training Efficiency

Today we are releasing DaisyRose-27B, RadixArk’s first model, built on Qwen3.8-27B and trained with reinforcement learning using Miles. We trained it on long-horizon agent tasks with sessions up to 1M tokens, with just 1,200 curated tasks in 18 days on 144 H200 GPUs. DaisyRose-27B improves Terminal-Bench 4.1 pass@1 from 5.6% to 12.0%. Beyond Terminal-Bench 4.1, it also delivers gains on a variety of other reasoning, instruction following, and coding benchmarks.

The checkpoints are available under Apache 2.0:

The model retains Qwen3.8-27B’s architecture, tokenizer, chat template, image understanding, and 256K-token context window. The longer training sessions use harness summarization to span multiple trajectories. See the model card for model properties and inference settings.

We recommend serving DaisyRose-27B with SGLang and DSpark speculative decoding. The SGLang cookbook provides launch configurations for different GPUs and checkpoint formats.

After starting the server with the served model name DaisyRose-27B on port 30000, you can send a request using the OpenAI Python client:

The model thinks before answering by default. Its reasoning is returned in reasoning_content, and its final answer in content. These settings follow the model card’s quickstart.

DaisyRose-27B scores higher than the original Qwen3.8-27B model on every benchmark above. The largest gain is on Terminal Bench 4.1, where pass@1 rises from 5.6% to 12.0%.

Scores use the higher of the BF16 and FP8 runs for each benchmark; the two differ by less than one point wherever both were evaluated. The model card includes comparison sources and evaluation settings.

Three parts of the training setup made this release possible: carefully designed tasks, an efficient training backend, and reliable sandboxes.

We built the tasks in partnership with Eigent AI, starting from its large pool of tasks in machine learning, software engineering, science, and other fields. Together we built thousands of candidates. About 1,200 made it into the final training set.

RadixArk trained DaisyRose-27B with Miles, our open-source reinforcement learning framework for large-scale model post-training, in fully asynchronous mode: the agent keeps working while the model learns, and neither waits for the other. While 128 H200s run the inference on agent tasks, 16 more run the trainer and learn from the trajectories. After every step, the updated model goes out to the 128 GPUs that run the agent. The learning runs on our internal training backend, which is built for agent training: each step learns from a handful of very long sessions, some as long as 1M tokens, folded into multiple trajectories via harness summarization.

57% lower training cost. On this release, 37% of each GPU’s peak compute went into useful training work (model FLOPs utilization, or MFU) on our backend. The open-source trainer, built on Megatron, reached 16% on comparable runs. So the same training needs 57% less GPU time. The gain is even larger on mixture-of-experts models: 6.2× on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, and more than 10× on the roughly 300B-parameter GLM-5.3-Flash.

2× faster end to end. Counting the time the agent spends on its tasks, the release run trained on about 16,800 tokens per second across its 144 GPUs. The open-source trainer reached about 8,300 on the same GPUs.

Stable over weeks. The release run trained for weeks on 144 H200s, 63,000 GPU-hours in total. From the first step to the last, its speed and efficiency held steady.

Every training step of the DaisyRose-27B release run on 144 H200s, plotted against total training time. Dashed lines: the open-source trainer on comparable runs.

Every training attempt runs in a sandbox: a fresh copy of the task’s environment where the agent runs commands, edits files, and is then graded.

Our service is built on the open-source AgentENV project, to which we also contribute fixes. Between mid-September and mid-November, it ran about 944,000 sandboxes for this project, with up to 1,566 running concurrently.

The service grew from one machine to as many as 12. We shipped ten upgrades to it, nearly all while training was running. Across all nine weeks, 99% of sandbox creations succeeded; since late October, that figure has exceeded 99.95%.

Cloud infrastructure costs for the project’s sandboxes were about 80% lower than running the same sandboxes with popular cloud sandbox providers. One way we keep costs down is to let each sandbox’s memory allocation grow and shrink with its actual usage, allowing more sandboxes to share each machine.

Download DaisyRose-27B, follow the SGLang serving guide, or use Miles to train your own agents.

We’d like to hear how DaisyRose-27B performs on your tasks, including where it falls short. Share your setup and results in the model’s Community tab.

We thank Eigent AI for working closely with us on training data, and the Qwen team for creating Qwen3.8-27B. We also thank the Miles and SGLang communities, along with other open-source projects including slime, AgentENV, and Harbor.

#9753. Your Backup Isn’t Real Until You’ve Restored It: A 15-Minute Drill

There’s an old saying in operations: a backup you haven’t restored is a hope, not a backup. Backup jobs can report success for months while writing empty files, skipping folders, or saving to a disc that’s already failing.

The fix is a restore drill: pick some real files, restore them somewhere safe, and check they match. It takes about fifteen minutes, and it’s the cheapest insurance in IT.

Here’s a simple way to do it, plus a small script that does the comparing for you.

The drill Pick a real dataset. Choose something that matters, like last month’s project folder, a database dump, or the accounting export. Not a test file you made up. Restore it to a scratch location. Never restore over live data. Use a separate folder or machine. Compare the results. Check that files exist, open correctly, and match the originals. Time it. How long did it take? This number is your real recovery time, and it’s usually longer than people assume. Write it down. Date, what you restored, what you found, and who did it. The script

For step 3, checking by eye doesn’t scale. This script picks random files from the original folder and checks that the restored copy exists and has an identical SHA-256 hash.

SRC="${1:?source dir}" DST="${2:?restored dir}" N="${3:-5}"

pass=0; fail=0 while IFS= read -r -d '' file; do rel="${file#"$SRC"/}" if [[ ! -f "$DST/$rel" ]]; then echo "MISSING $rel"; fail=$((fail+1)); continue fi a=$(sha256sum "$file" | cut -d' ' -f1) b=$(sha256sum "$DST/$rel" | cut -d' ' -f1) if [[ "$a" == "$b" ]]; then echo "OK $rel"; pass=$((pass+1)) else echo "DIFFERS $rel"; fail=$((fail+1)) fi done < <(find "$SRC" -type f -print0 | shuf -z -n "$N")

echo; echo "Checked $((pass+fail)) file(s): $pass ok, $fail problem(s) " [[ $fail -eq 0 ]]

bash chmod +x restore_check.sh ./restore_check.sh /data/projects /tmp/restore-test 10

Here’s the output from a quick test I ran, with one file missing from the restore and one changed:

text MISSING three.txt DIFFERS bids/two.txt OK bids/one.txt

The script exits with a non-zero code if anything is wrong, so you can drop it into a scheduled job or CI step and get alerted.

It samples, so it can miss things. A random sample of ten files can’t prove the whole backup is good. Raise the sample size for important data, and also spot-check by opening a few files by hand. It needs sha256sum and shuf. These come with GNU coreutils on Linux. On macOS you’ll want shasum -a 256 and gshuf (from brew install coreutils). Files that legitimately change will differ. If the source is live, files edited after the backup will show as different. Compare against a snapshot or a quiet period when you can. It can’t tell you the data is usable. A database file can match its hash and still be unusable if the app version has changed. For critical systems, open it in the real application. It’s not a full backup validator. Backup tools often have their own verify commands. Use those too. Turning it into a habit Schedule it quarterly at minimum, and after any major change (new server, new backup tool, new storage). Rotate what you test, so you cover different folders and systems over the year. Follow 3-2-1: three copies, on two types of storage, with one off-site and isolated from your main network, since ransomware tends to hunt for connected backups. Don’t assume SaaS is backed up. Many cloud tools protect their own platform, not your accidental deletions. Write down recovery targets, such as how long you can be without email, accounting, or project files. If you support non-technical teams

This is one of the easiest wins for small businesses, because nobody ever asks, “Have we tried restoring this?” I put together a plain-English guide on IT support for construction company job sites, laptops, and bid data that covers backups along with the rest of the basics if you need something to hand to a non-technical client or friend.

It’s from ZIA Networks, an IT services company in New Mexico. (Disclosure: I’m affiliated with them.)

When did you last run a real restore, and what did you find? I’d like to hear your stories, especially the “backup was fine on paper” ones, in the comments.

TechnologyWire (Technology Wire) is a tech newswire and press release distribution platform operated by MediaFuse LTD.

TechnologyWire (Technology Wire) is a tech newswire and press release distribution platform operated by MediaFuse LTD.

Amsterdam, Netherlands, November 19th, 2026/TechnologyWire/--G2A.COM, the world’s largest marketplace for digital entertainment, has polled just over 2,000 of its users to investigate whether Black Friday still plays a crucial role in the annual purchasing journey. The findings reveal that, beyond the appeal of discounts, players are making increasingly deliberate purchasing decisions, tracking prices and postponing purchases in anticipation of Black Friday. This follows a recent report by Newzoo and G2A.COM, titled Game purchasing behavior in an era of choice, which provided a detailed examination of how gamers are dealing with higher prices, their attitudes toward discounts, and the growing number of ways to buy games.

G2A.COM’s transactional data reinforces the commercial importance of this shopping period. During Black Friday–Cyber Monday 2025, total orders in the marketplace increased by 33% year-on-year, while video game orders surged by 87%, significantly outpacing overall growth.

G2A.COM’s survey findings reveal that, despite a growing trend of delayed purchases and consumer skepticism, Black Friday remains the peak value event for gamers. This data corroborates with the recent Newzoo report, which found that 73% of gamers feel AAA games are overpriced at launch and, on average, wait 4.9 months for a sale or discount. Together, the studies highlight how price awareness and patience increasingly influence purchasing decisions, with Black Friday proving a key opportunity for gamers to act on their plans.

"Black Friday is no longer just about impulse purchases. It has become a planned part of how gamers manage their entertainment budgets," said Paweł Wróbel, Chief Growth Officer at G2A.COM. "Players are increasingly willing to wait, track prices and prioritise the games they want most. Our findings show that getting the best value is becoming just as important as getting a game at launch."

The survey further reveals that 39% of respondents plan to spend more on gaming this Black Friday than last year, while 41% expect to spend roughly the same amount. These findings underline Black Friday’s continued importance as a major shopping period for gamers, increasingly shaped by preparation, informed decisions and the search for value.

G2A.COM is the world's largest marketplace for digital entertainment, serving over 35 million users from 180 countries with more than 200 million visits in 2025. As a true gateway to digital entertainment and a rapidly evolving digital ecosystem, G2A.COM gives access to over 125,000 digital offerings, including vouchers, games, DLCs, in-game items, and non-gaming items such as gift cards, subscriptions, software, or e-learning, sold by sellers from all over the world. A compliance-driven organization audited by Deloitte for over a decade, G2A.COM is a leader in online security, recognized by the prestigious American CNP Award alongside industry giants like Microsoft and PayPal. Today, the company is a key gateway for recognized global brands, leveraging its scalable infrastructure to drive the next phase of e-commerce through agentic AI and global M&A - continuously expanding its role as the Gate 2 Adventure in the digital world.

#9751. My Dark Factory Reinvented Sprint Planning

Posted on Nov 20 • Originally published at jduncan.io

As of last week, I had pushed roughly 40 billion tokens through Leaf, my local Level 5 dark software factory. Once the core build and review loops felt steady, I couldn't resist poking at what else an unattended fleet could catch on its own.

First, I added an SRE loop. Its job was to watch application health and performance over time: reading end-to-end test results, repository-declared performance benchmarks, and chronic CI/CD failures, then filing bugs whenever performance envelopes or reliability started drifting the wrong way.

That ran alongside my daily dreaming loop, which scans 30-day swaths of telemetry verdicts to catch slow-burn patterns that single-room Analysts miss, plus the single-room Analysts themselves and the Improve loop that looked for dead code and measured code complexity to make the next agent find the right work easier.

Within 24 hours, the factory handed me a surprise I didn't see coming.

Telemetry, SRE, and dreaming were all finding the same issues from different angles. Same root causes, just three different points of view on the same symptom.

That's normal in the real world. What wasn't normal was how my factory handled it. Because my planning room picked up issues one at a time, the factory would grab SRE's ticket, plan a fix, and ship it. Ten minutes later, it would grab Telemetry's ticket for the same underlying flaw and patch it from a slightly different angle.

I needed a process that could look across all the open issues for a repository, collate them, strip out the duplicates, set dependencies, and organize them into a coherent batch before any planning room opened.

Oh no. I needed a sprint planning meeting.

My first reaction was to laugh at myself. I spent months trying to strip unnecessary human ceremony out of agent workflows, and the factory's own failure mode walked me right back into backlog grooming.

When you stop and think about the mechanics, though, it makes complete sense.

Every loop was doing its job faithfully. The SRE agent's job wasn't to track performance across the repository; its job was to notice a drifting benchmark or a flaky deploy and file a clean defect report. The Telemetry Analyst's job was to explain why a pod burned 95 turns. The Dreamer's job was to connect three slow rooms over the last month.

Their goal wasn't cross-team coordination. Their goal was to report from their specific point of view.

Human engineering teams have the exact same problem. SRE files a latency alert, QA files a flaky test bug, and a developer files a tech-debt ticket. All three point at the same overloaded query. Sprint planning exists in human orgs because specialist roles naturally generate overlapping symptoms, and someone has to synthesize them before engineers start cutting branches.

Good process isn't always bureaucracy. Sometimes it's just the shape of the problem. Sometimes we have to sit and stare at the stickies on the whiteboard.

So on Monday, I built a Triage loop right in front of the planning room.

Instead of letting every newly filed bug wake up a PM and Architect on the spot (hotfixes still jump the line), issues now land in a waiting backlog. On a schedule or on demand, a triager agent opens a short sprint-planning pass for a repository. It reads the waiting issues together, closes duplicates, groups related tickets, wires up dependencies, and starts the coherent work as a batch. It only works on issue content and bodies. Just like a human would shuffling cards around a kanban board.

By Tuesday morning, I had staggered triage across repositories in 180-minute slots. Instead of a chaotic drip of single-issue fixes fighting over the same files, work moved in predictable bursts. My plan was to stagger projects across the clock: Project A during business hours, background repos in the evening, keeping the closet shelf humming without stepping on itself.

Adding the SRE loop, the Triage backlog, and smarter work ranking was the straw that finally snapped the back of Leaf v1's single-threaded Node.js backend.

By Tuesday, the v1 src/ tree had grown to 206 non-test TypeScript files all sharing one Node.js event loop: HTTP API routes, WebSocket streams to five worker hosts, synchronous SQLite queries, git subprocesses, container orchestration, and background admission passes for 60 concurrent pod slots.

The git history from ~/Code/factory preserves the exact smoking gun. The very last commit on the v1 TypeScript codebase (ba4a044e, Tuesday, November 17 at 8:39 AM Eastern) tells the whole story in four lines:

Look at the chain reaction in that commit message.

And when the supervisor got killed mid-flight, the restarts triggered secondary fallout (commit cc7f910e earlier that same morning had to patch dropped tech-lead commands and re-ask pods whose say calls hit an unreachable Factory API during a restart).

Restoring the cursor walk in ba4a044e stopped the bleeding for the afternoon. It didn't fix the real architecture problem. Running a multi-loop, multi-host orchestration engine on a single-threaded runtime where one heavy loop calculation can starve the API and trip the health check was living on borrowed time.

To be fair to Node.js and TypeScript, I'm not claiming JavaScript can't run backend services. Plenty of huge companies run Node at scale with worker threads, queues, and separate microservices. My factory is a single-binary, closet-shelf control plane where I want one simple process managing SQLite, git repos, host sockets, and a dozen background loops without me babysitting event-loop lag.

The very next morning (Wednesday, November 18), I cut the cord and landed the initial Factory 2.0 build.

It's going to have a better name (I think), and it's taking every hard-won lesson from those 40 billion tokens while ruthlessly deleting the ideas that didn't survive contact with reality. The architecture split is simple:

I'm pushing the first real workloads through v2 right now and shaking out the remaining bugs across the fleet. I hope to unveil the whole thing, new name and all, in the next week or two.
