#9741. REA: The Open-Source AI Tool That Can Reverse Engineer Almost Anything (2026 Guide)

What if you could ask your AI assistant how any app works and get a real answer, backed by evidence, without ever seeing the source code?

You use an app, tap a feature, and wonder how it was built. Maybe it is a fast search bar, a clever clipboard trick, or a mechanic in an old game. Until recently, finding out meant months of learning disassemblers and reading assembly code. A new open-source project called REA changes that. It has earned more than 430,000 stars on GitHub, and in this guide I will explain what it does, which problems it solves, and how you can start using it today.

In this guide

  • The problem with reverse engineering
  • How REA solves it
  • How REA works
  • What REA can analyze
  • Real examples
  • How to get started
  • REA at a glance
  • Using REA responsibly
  • Frequently asked questions

The Problem: Reverse Engineering Is Hard

Reverse engineering is the practice of studying finished software to understand how it works. It is powerful, but it has never been beginner-friendly. If you have tried it, or even thought about trying it, you have probably run into these obstacles.

1. A steep learning curve

Reading assembly code and pseudocode takes a long time to learn. Many curious developers give up before they get their first useful result.

2. Too many tools and no single workflow

An Electron app needs one approach. An Android APK needs another. A .NET assembly, a native binary, and a website each have their own tools, file formats, and tricks.

3. Slow, manual investigation

Even experts can spend hours following one function through strings, calls, and references just to understand a single small feature.

4. AI answers you cannot verify

If you ask a general chatbot how an app works, it may give a confident answer that is simply invented. Without evidence, you cannot tell what is real.

5. Painful setup

Connecting analysis tools to an AI agent usually requires custom scripts and configuration, and it is easy to break.

The Solution: REA (Reverse Engineer Anything)

REA is a free, MIT-licensed project that connects your AI agent to professional reverse engineering tools through MCP (Model Context Protocol). MCP is a standard way for AI agents to use external tools. In simple terms, REA acts as a bridge between your agent and the software you want to understand. Here is how it answers each problem above.

The Problem How REA Solves It
Steep learning curve You ask in plain English. Your agent runs the tools and explains the results.
Too many tools One MCP server covers native binaries, Electron apps, Android, .NET, websites, and dozens of other formats.
Slow and manual The agent traces code, references, and calls for you.
Answers you cannot verify Every result includes the evidence and limitations behind it.
Painful setup One command registers REA with your agent and backs up your existing configuration.

You do not need the app’s source code. You point your agent at the app, ask a question, and REA helps it trace the answer.

How REA Works

  1. You ask a question. For example, how a feature in a particular app works.
  2. The agent calls REA. It uses MCP to inspect the target and trace the relevant code.
  3. REA returns findings. These include code, references, and clearly marked unknowns.
  4. The agent acts on them. It can explain the behavior, ask follow-up questions, or write and test its own version of the feature.

The same workflows are available from the terminal, so you can also script them without an agent. Analysis runs locally on your machine. Your agent receives the tool results, and your AI provider’s own data policy applies to that part.

What Can REA Analyze?

The range of supported targets is one of REA’s biggest strengths. These are the main groups.

Native programs and binaries

REA returns pseudocode, assembly, strings, symbols, calls, and references. Deep native analysis uses an engine you already have, such as Hopper, Ghidra, IDA, or Kuna. It also supports GNU objdump and Rizin for offline inspection.

JavaScript and Electron apps

This is the easiest place to start, because static JavaScript analysis needs no native engine. REA recovers modules, imports, source maps, routes, IPC connections, and native add-on relationships.

Android apps and devices

REA can inspect APK manifests, classes, decompiled methods, signatures, and resources. Through adb, it can also look at packages, processes, and logs on an emulator or a real phone. Flutter apps and JEB projects are supported too.

.NET and managed code

For .NET assemblies, REA reads metadata, CIL instructions, and native dependencies without running the program.

Websites and network captures

REA can inspect page structure, scripts, and network activity using a Chrome-family browser. It can also read saved HAR and Fiddler SAZ files to examine requests, responses, and exposed payloads.

Specialist formats

The list continues with Go and Rust binaries, GPU code objects, GGUF and safetensors model files, Unity IL2CPP metadata, Godot PCK archives, PE imports and certificates, ELF notes, Linux kernel modules, WebAssembly, EVM bytecode, SQLite databases, firmware images, packet captures, and PyInstaller executables. Most of these use built-in static inspection, so no extra software is required.

Real Examples: What Has REA Done?

The project publishes several case studies on its website.

  • DX-Ball sound panning. REA followed a sound call into a helper function and turned incomplete pseudocode into C. The reconstruction passed 3,205 test cases against the original x86 code and matched all 63 compiled function bytes.
  • Notion’s clipboard bridge. REA traced how Notion’s Electron app moves clipboard data from the renderer through preload and IPC into the main process, including the rich clipboard format.
  • TH04 bullet patterns. REA recovered the angle calculations of a classic DOS game and compared the rebuilt C++ with the original compiler output.

Bonus: build RL environments from a web app

REA can record a web app session and turn its API calls into tools an AI agent can use. It then exports a runnable environment for reinforcement learning or for testing how well an agent completes tasks. With a saved HAR file, the command looks like this:

rea environment-build ./session.har ./my-env --name my-env --json

You then run the result with AgentEnv and Docker, and add your own tasks and reward checks.

How to Get Started With REA

You need Node.js and npm. The project lists supported Node versions as 22.x (22.23.4 or newer), 24.x (24.22.1 or newer), or 26.12.1 and above.

Step 1: Run the setup command

npx rea-agents setup

Step 2: Choose your agents and approve the changes

Setup supports Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI, Grok Build, and other agents. It shows you the proposed changes first and keeps backups of your existing configuration.

Step 3: Restart your agent

The new MCP server is loaded when the agent starts again.

Step 4: Ask your first question

Understand how search works in the Notes app, show me the evidence,
and build a similar feature for my project.

Prefer the terminal?

You can inspect an extracted Electron app or ASAR file directly:

npx -y rea-agents@latest analyze-javascript-application /absolute/path/to/app --json

To keep REA installed, run npm install --global rea-agents. REA changes quickly, so use rea update to stay current. Updating is also the first fix to try if you run into a bug.

REA at a Glance

What makes it special

REA combines the reach of dozens of analysis tools with the convenience of an AI agent. It helps you understand software you do not have source code for, and it backs each conclusion with evidence instead of guesses. The range of supported formats, from native binaries to Electron apps to Android devices, is unusually broad for a free tool.

Key features

  • Works through MCP with Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI, Grok Build, and other agents
  • Evidence and limitations attached to every result
  • Local analysis on your own machine
  • A full command-line interface for scripting
  • Support for dozens of file and app types
  • An RL environment builder
  • Guides and case studies on the official website

Pricing

  • REA itself: free and open source (MIT license)
  • Commercial engines such as IDA Pro, Hopper, and JEB: you must obtain these legally under their own licenses
  • Ghidra: a free option for native analysis; see the setup guide for details

Perfect for

Developers, security researchers, students, software preservationists, and anyone who wants to understand how an app works.

Using REA Responsibly

Use REA only on software you own or are authorized to examine.

The project is intended for lawful research, education, interoperability, software preservation, and analysis of software you have permission to study. It does not permit cracked tools, stolen license keys, or bypassing license restrictions. Read the project’s disclaimer before you start.

Also be careful where you download it from. The project warns that a similar repository name or a copied README does not make a download official. Use only these sources:

  • GitHub: github.com/morluto/rea
  • Website: rea.tools
  • npm package: rea-agents

Frequently Asked Questions

Do I need Hopper or Ghidra?

Only for deep native binary analysis. JavaScript and .NET inspection work without a native engine, and setup can install Hopper with your approval.

Does REA upload my app?

No. Analysis runs locally. Your agent sees the results, and its provider has its own data policy.

Which AI agents work with REA?

Any agent that supports local MCP servers can use it.

What should I do if I find a bug?

Update first, because a recent release may already include the fix. If the problem continues, open an issue on GitHub with your REA version, the target type, the steps to reproduce, and the error output.

Final Thoughts

The old problem was simple: understanding software without source code took too much skill, too many tools, and too much time. REA’s answer is just as simple. It gives your AI agent the tools to investigate, and it requires the agent to show its evidence. Whether you want to learn how a favorite feature works, study a classic game, or inspect an Electron app, REA is a strong place to start. Just make sure you use it only on software you are allowed to examine.

#9730. What is piloncillo? This sweetener makes great cookies, pan dulce, and more: Use this traditional Mexican unrefined sugar for a dash of flavor and history.

This article is part of our feature celebrating Pan Dulce. Find all things pan dulce here.

Categorically, piloncillo is a “non-centrifugal” cane sugar, meaning it is an unrefined sugar product and a true natural brown sugar. It’s mostly consumed in Mexico and Latin America, but a similar product can be found in Asia, known as jaggery in India. Though often lumped together, these unrefined dark sugars are very different from brown sugars on the market today, which have been refined to a large degree — in some cases, they’re actually just white sugar with coloring or molasses added.

Making piloncillo, on the other hand, involves an artisanal process that’s hundreds of years old. To make it, pressed cane juice is boiled to evaporate the water and deeply caramelize the sugar. The cooked cane is then poured into molds (often made of wood) and left to dry and harden. Traditional piloncillo is conical in shape and can vary in size from small to large cones but is most commonly found in a medium size that weighs about 200 grams. In Guatemala and Colombia, it is called panela, where it is cooked to a lighter degree and typically formed into a brick, rather than cone, shape. Other forms of piloncillo can be granulated or liquid (which is more rare).

Minimally processed and boldly flavored, piloncillo was historically a prized and respected foodstuff. As an unrefined cane sugar, piloncillo provides more complex vitamins and minerals than refined sugars, which undergo processing and whitening methods that also strip nutrients from the whole food. And piloncillo is also great for baking, providing notes of burnt caramel and hints of smoke. Plus, its rich molasses qualities keep baked goods moist and fresh for longer.

Always look at the ingredient label when purchasing piloncillo and make sure it says 100% pure cane juice or cane sugar. It is becoming increasingly common to find imitation products marketed as jaggery or piloncillo that contain coloring and corn syrup. You can find good piloncillo at specialty grocery stores or online at retailers.

In Mexico and throughout Latin America, piloncillo is an important ingredient in many traditional dishes. (Some will even say it’s not the “real dish” if you substitute sugar in these recipes due to the deep flavors and richness that only piloncillo can provide.) This deep, dark unrefined sugar lends its characteristic flavor and texture to popular foods and beverages such as capirotada, tepache, coyotas, atole, café de olla, calabaza al horno, coricos, and hojarascas, to name a few!

I love adding piloncillo when I’m making champurrado. In this warm and thick chocolate beverage, the piloncillo is chopped or grated and dissolved in the pot with water or milk before adding the chocolate and masa. In this recipe, the piloncillo’s intense sweet and smoky flavors pair well with the chocolate and corn masa.

While there are many dishes and uses for piloncillo, it’s not a simple substitution for granulated white sugar in recipes, but you can use it the same as you would brown sugar with a 1:1 substitution by weight.  Depending on how hard the cone is, it can be crumbled or grated for easier measuring. If it is very hard, try cutting it in half with a sharp knife and then placing it between parchment paper or a towel and beating with a rolling pin.

Find puerquitos and many more Mexican sweets in our feature celebrating pan dulce.

#9729. COVID-19 and Moral Injury: a Mental Health Pandemic for Frontline Health Care Workers

More than 2 years ago, the alarm and first warnings of a global pandemic sounded. Now with over 830,000 deaths caused by COVID-19 in the US, there looms on the horizon a second underlying curve with equally serious long-term consequences: a mental health pandemic.

The mental health fallout from the COVID-19 pandemic demands recognition, intervention, and mitigation strategies. Among the many at-risk populations are frontline health care workers who have been at the epicenter of the global pandemic, working long shifts with at times a tenuous safety net and limited support, and caring for COVID-19 patients with limited resources, mixed messaging, and uncertainty with regards to an end to the crisis. The psychological effects in some health care providers are akin to the moral trauma or moral injury that is recognized in combat veterans with posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD).

Mental health professionals and other health care providers caring for frontline health care workers who present with insomnia, depression, anxiety, panic attacks, PTSD, and suicidal thoughts should recognize and validate their experiences and moral injury. Intervention strategies including health promotion, resilience training, and ongoing multilevel support will play an important role in flattening the moral injury curve.

As a rule, the frontline health care workforce is considered capable, competent, resilient, professional, and persevering in the face of adversity. However, COVID-19 presented as an unprecedented crisis unlike any other unforeseen disaster, eliciting fear, uncertainty, and anxiety, coupled with grief and loss, both personally and professionally.1 As noted by Warren D. Taylor, MD, MHSc, and Jennifer Urbano Blackford, PhD1:

The pandemic created anxiety and fear in health care providers, from physicians and nurses to allied health professionals and first-line responders. We fear for the safety of our families and patients. We grieve for those who have died. We feel guilt for not being able to save all our patients, for getting sick ourselves, and for abandoning our families. Many adopted the phrase, “we will get through this together but none of us will survive unscathed.”

At the outset, the shortage of equipment and resources, changing practice guidelines, and unpredictability of the workload rendered health care workers with a sense of powerlessness and loss of control of the conditions under which they were able to deliver care. The emotional distress and social isolation from family and friends exacted an immeasurable toll on the physical health and emotional well-being of the workforce, setting the stage for the inevitable moral injury.2

Moral injury is a term that has been applied to veterans of combat. Moral injury or moral distress as experienced by frontline health care providers occurs when health care providers are forced to make decisions that transgress their professional commitment to patient comfort and care, and forcibly shift their moral compass. They are not able to meet the physical, emotional, and end-of-life needs of patients.3

Watson et al noted that moral injury in health care workers “can occur when someone engages in, fails to prevent, or witnesses acts that conflict with their values or beliefs.”4 Moral injuries may result from the following, according to Watson et al4:

The consequences of such experiences may include feelings of rage, guilt, shame, and anger and moral injury is the “lasting psychological, spiritual, behavioral or social impact that may result from these experiences.”4 The number of acutely ill COVID-19 patients and high death rate coupled with lack of resources and at times rationing of limited resources such as personal protective equipment (PPE) and ventilators added to the dilemma that frontline health care workers faced.

In a study of 448 Jordanian nurses during the COVID-19 pandemic, the majority of nurses (64%) reported experiencing acute stress disorder (ASD) and 41% reported significant psychological distress, with a predilection for younger nurses compared to older nurses.5 However, coping self-efficacy was a protective factor with the potential to mitigate the severity of psychological distress.5 An online survey of nonhealth care providers (N=976) found that individuals with previous trauma were at highest risk for increased symptoms of anxiety, depression, and PTSD related to COVID-19 compared with individuals with no previous history of trauma.6

The long-term mental health consequences of moral injury for frontline health care workers have important implications for workforce survivability and durability; however, research on this topic is lacking. In one of the few published studies on moral injury among health care providers, investigators looked at the thematic content of experiences reported by nurses following incidents meeting the contextual definition of moral injury (ie, events with unintended consequences, potentially causing patient harm or putting patients at risk for serious injury). The investigators found nurses reported experiencing “guilt, shame, spiritual–existential crisis, and loss of trust.”7

COVID-19 has presented difficult and untenable working conditions beyond the scope of the challenges frontline health care workers are prepared for professionally. Frontline health care workers have experienced conflict and distress over prioritizing patient care vs their own safety, protecting family members from infection, and the reality that the supplies, medications, and equipment needed to save a life were not always available or were being rationed. Because of high infectivity, morbidity, and mortality associated with the spread of the virus, frontline health care workers were often in the position to be the only person at the bedside at the end of life with patients who were separated from their families. This is not how families should experience the loss of a loved one.4

There is a body of research regarding the long-term effects of moral injury among combat soldiers.3 It is reasonable to expect that feelings of guilt, shame, anger, and self-recrimination stemming from moral injury in these soldiers may be similar to feelings experienced by frontline health care workers during the COVID-19 pandemic and that their experiences increase the risk for acute stress reactions with long-term consequences including increased incidence of depression, anxiety, substance abuse, PTSD, and suicide.4,8 Behavior changes including intrusive memories, avoidance of situations that are reminders of prior events, self-isolation, and potential triggers of traumatic memories are common in individuals suffering from acute stress disorder or PTSD. Additional responses to stress, trauma, and moral injury include disturbed sleep, emotional changes such as numbing, desensitization, depersonalization, and a decreased capacity for empathy and compassion. For some individuals, the consequences of moral injury may be an opportunity for reflection and reprioritization of values and an existential inner process of reflecting on what is important in life.4

Given the consequences of moral injury, it is important for mental health professionals and health care providers treating frontline health care providers to recognize and identify those experiences that have the potential for promoting resilience.9

An analysis of data from 2,579 frontline health care workers in New York City early on in the pandemic showed that key factors predictive of psychological resilience were positive emotions, self-efficacy, purpose in life, strong social support, and not engaging in maladaptive coping strategies (eg, substance abuse).9 Psychological resilience was described by the authors as, “the capacity to adapt and thrive while facing adversity or challenging circumstances,” leading to the question of how can institutions promote psychological resilience in frontline health care workers?9

Initiativespromoting psychological resilience are critical.10,11 Interventions identifying those at high risk for moral injury and in need of support in the form of psychological first-aid and psychotherapy have the potential of improving resilience. Kameno et al administered the short-form of the Kessler Psychological Distress Scale with 4 additional questions, 2 regarding sleep, 1 on appetite changes, and 1 on alcohol misuse, in health care workers during the pandemic.12 The researchers found that women and nurses had higher rates of affective symptoms compared to men and other medical staff, respectively. The researchers noted that early identification and psychotherapy may improve psychological resilience and reduce psychological distress in nurses at high risk for maladaptive coping.12

The need for institutional support, leadership support, education, and training is equally important. Leadership and management are challenged to identify those practices that address the needs of their respective health care workers.10 Survey findings on the expectations and needs of health care workers (physicians, nurses, advanced practice clinicians, residents, and fellows; N=69) during the first week of the pandemic at a single hospital identified the following 5 requests of their organization: hear me, protect me, prepare me, support me, and care for me.13 Management and leadership have the opportunity to promote resilience and show visible support for the health care workforce with unique initiatives to help reduce and mitigate the long-term consequences of moral injury and acute stress response.

Similar to triage protocols and models to meet emergent health care systems demands from unexpected disasters, there is a need for a multilayered mental health care response for frontline workers. Self-care and wellness initiatives have the potential to reduce the long-term consequences of moral injury. Ongoing support, skills training, psychoeducation, and wellness education regarding strategies to address and process the experiences of frontline health care workers are critical for healing the wounds of moral injury. Empathic sensitivity on the part of mental health providers and primary care providers is essential. Listening to “the story” and having the opportunity to process and reflect on the self-talk related to the experience of moral injury can lay the groundwork for healing.

Self-care needs should include the opportunity to seek out and have available a support system of peers and colleagues. All too often the experience of shame, guilt, and self-condemnation are obstacles to seeking self-help and lead to self-isolation. If allowed to process and reflect on those experiences, health care workers may be provided an opportunity for experiential growth and a redefinition of priorities personally and professionally.

Leaders in health care have the opportunity to create and foster a culture of open, nonjudgmental communication. In the face of unpredictable events such as the COVID-19 pandemic, natural disasters, and social and political unrest that impact health care delivery, strategies are available to promote mental health recovery and return to stability and wellness among frontline health care workers.

Catherine R. Judd, MS, PA-C, CAQ-Psy, DFAAPA, is an assistant clinical professor in the Department of Physician Assistant Studies at the School of Health Professions, The University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center, Dallas, Texas.

1. Taylor WD, Blackford JU. Mental health treatment for front-line clinicians during and after the coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic: a plea to the medical community. Ann Intern Med. 2020;173(7):574-575. doi:10.7326/M20-2440

2. Hossain F, Clatty A. Self-care strategies in response to nurses’ moral injury during COVID-19 pandemic. Nurs Ethics. 2021;28(1):23-32. doi:10.1177/0969733020961825

3. Borges LM, Barnes SM, Farnsworth JK, Bahraini NH, Brenner LA. A commentary on moral injury among health care providers during the COVID-19 pandemic. Psychol Trauma. 2020;12(S1):S138-S140. doi:10.1037/tra0000698

4. Watson P, Norman SB, Maguen S, Hamblen J. Moral injury in health care workers. Accessed January 4, 2021. https://www.ptsd.va.gov/professional/treat/cooccurring/moral_injury_hcw.asp

5. Shahrour G, Dardas LA. Acute stress disorder, coping self-efficacy and subsequent psychological distress among nurses amid COVID-19. J Nurs Manag. 2020;28(7):1686-1695. doi:10.1111/jonm.13124

6. Lahav Y. Psychological distress related to COVID-19 — The contribution of continuous traumatic stress. J Affect Disord. 2020;277:129-137. doi:10.1016/j.jad.2020.07.141

7. Stovall M, Hansen L, van Ryn M. A critical review: moral injury in nurses in the aftermath of a patient safety incident. J Nurs Scholarsh. 2020;52(3):320-328. doi:10.1111/jnu.12551

8. Pappa S, Ntella V, Giannakas T, Giannakoulis VG, Papoutsi E, Katsaounou P. Prevalence of depression, anxiety, and insomnia among healthcare workers during the COVID-19 pandemic: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Brain Behav Immun. 2020;88:901-907. doi:10.1016/j.bbi.2020.05.026

9. Pietrzak RH, Feingold JH, Feder A, Charney DS, Peccoralo L, Southwick SM, Ripp J. Psychological resilience in frontline health care workers during the acute phase of the COVID-19 pandemic in New York City. J Clin Psychiatry. 2020;82(1):20l13749. doi:10.4088/JCP.20l13749

#9721. Forget Expensive Ribeye: A Cheaper Cut For Delicious Beef Stroganoff

Indulgently and immensely comforting, beef stroganoff is one of those low-effort meals you make when you just want to feel good. But one thing that might not lift your spirits is the price. Classic stroganoff starts off with strips of thinly sliced beef, with cuts like ribeye being among the best picks. We're not here to fault ribeye, which has earned its price for a reason, but if you want to knock a few dollars off your next batch, try swapping in ground beef instead.

While it may not satisfy the purist, and might even horrify a Russian (the dish's country of origin), we'd argue that ground beef is a worthy alternative to any traditional whole cut of steak. The texture is bound to be different, and you'll need to adjust how you cook it, but good-quality ground beef still has the rich, beefy flavor that pairs so well with the tang of sour cream, earthy mushrooms, and the sweet depth of cooked-down onions, all at a significantly lower cost.

Another reason ground beef works so well here is its cooking time. Traditional beef stroganoff relies on expensive cuts that are prized for their tenderness and quick-cooking nature. Cheaper, tougher cuts like chuck or round usually need hours of braising to soften, which doesn't suit a dish that's meant to come together quickly. Ground beef, however, is often made from those same economical cuts, and the grinding process does all the tenderizing mechanically. That means you're getting all that mouthwatering flavor without the waiting, guaranteeing a tasty, Boomer-approved meal.

If you make the switch from ribeye to ground beef, you'll want to do a few things differently. First, check out the numbers on your ground beef packaging. You're looking for a blend that doesn't shy away from fat, something like an 80-to-20 lean-to-fat ratio, or even 70-to-30. Like ribeye, these fattier blends are packed with rich flavor, and the fat that'll render out will elevate the sauce, just in a different format. Go any leaner and you risk dry, chewy beef pebbles floating in your sauce.

With ribeye, standard practice is to slice the beef ultra-thin, give it a quick sear, then let it simmer in the sauce for a few minutes. The process for ground beef is similar, albeit with a few caveats. For starters, there's no slicing, so you're already saving time. Like ribeye, you want to get the meat nicely browned. Our personal advice is to add the beef to the pan in small handfuls and flatten each one with the back of a spoon, which allows it to brown without overcrowding the pan.

Remove the beef from the pan once it's seared, which isn't usually done with ribeye. Even in a fattier blend, ground beef has far more exposed surface area than your average slice of steak, so it risks drying out if it's left to simmer for too long. For the most tender results, build your sauce first, then add the beef back in and stir once you're just about ready to serve. Don't worry about the flavors not melding, since the fat and fond left behind from searing will be doing most of the heavy lifting.

#9719. 16 pumpkin recipes, from cakes and cookies to bars and bread: We've got a marbled pumpkin cake, chewy pumpkin cookies, and even pumpkin milk bread.

It’s that time of year when pumpkin spice everything starts appearing on store shelves — candles, lip balm, air fresheners, beer, and of course, the ubiquitous PSL (pumpkin spice latte). That means fall is here, and more importantly, that pumpkin should make a grand return to your kitchen! Pull out your canned pumpkin — or better yet, make your own pumpkin purée — and stock your pantry with pumpkin pie spice, because we have the best pumpkin recipes to bake this fall.

This Pumpkin Swirl Cake takes my breath away every time I unmold it from its intricate loaf pan. The anticipation keeps building until I slice into the pound cake-like loaf and reveal the swirled pattern inside, marbled with both vanilla and spiced pumpkin batter. (Don’t fret if you don’t have the specialty loaf pan — this can also be baked in a standard loaf pan and adorned with a simple confectioners’ sugar icing.)

To make this recipe, you'll need: Patch O Pumpkins Loaf Pan and Pure Vanilla Plus

To make this recipe, you'll need: Pumpkin Pie Spice and Sparkling Sugar

A cousin of Belgian-style Liège waffles, these Pumpkin Sugar Crunch Waffles have caramelized edges and a pleasant chew that’s reminiscent of brioche. The yeasted batter has pumpkin in it for flavor and color, plus Swedish pearl sugar that melts into pockets of crispy sugar. The best part? The batter rests overnight, so if you prepare it the night ahead, all you have to do the next morning is scoop and cook the batter for hot, crispy waffles in just a few minutes.

Get the recipe: Pumpkin Sugar Crunch Waffles

To make this recipe, you'll need: Swedish Pearl Sugar

I used to make the same pumpkin pie recipe for years, and it always left me wanting a little more excitement. Then I found this Smooth and Spicy Pumpkin Pie and never looked back! The generously spiced filling uses nutmeg, ginger, cloves, and Vietnamese cinnamon to create a more flavorful pie than traditional versions. The secret to its silky-smooth texture? Corn syrup, which is an invert sugar and keeps the custard from becoming grainy. Substitute another invert sugar like honey or maple syrup if you like; I use maple syrup.

Get the recipe: Smooth and Spicy Pumpkin Pie

To make this recipe, you'll need: Vietnamese Cinnamon, Ginger, and Nutmeg

Whenever I have these tender, golden scones on hand, I look forward to getting out of bed the next morning because I know they’re waiting for me. They can be easily customized to use a range of mix-ins, depending on what you have in your pantry. My personal preference is a mix of crystallized ginger and Cinnamon Sweet Bits.

Get the recipe: Harvest Pumpkin Scones (or Gluten-Free Pumpkin Scones)

To make this recipe, you'll need: Mini Diced Ginger and Cinnamon Sweet Bits

If you’re looking for a way to make your whole kitchen smell like fall, these one-bowl, easy pumpkin muffins deliver — and fast. They’re ready in under an hour, so you can spend less time measuring, mixing, and cleaning and more time tackling your autumn bucket list.

To make this recipe, you'll need: Standard Muffin Pan

Making banana bread is an almost weekly activity in my house — except during fall, when we pivot to pumpkin bread instead. This is a quick, easy bake that satisfies my craving for something pumpkin-y, and it uses a simple trick to concentrate the pumpkin flavor and ensure the loaf is perfectly textured: The pumpkin purée is reduced on the stovetop to cook off excess moisture. (The process is similar to browning butter.) As a result, the final loaf is packed with pumpkin flavor.

Get the recipe: The Most Pumpkin Pumpkin Chocolate Chip Bread

To make this recipe, you'll need: Ginger and Semisweet Chocolate Chips

These bars have all the cozy, spiced goodness of the classic dessert in a portable, crowd-friendly form. The buttery, brown sugar crust gets pressed into the pan (no rolling out pie dough!), and the silky pumpkin filling comes together with just a handful of ingredients. The (optional but highly recommended) sour cream whipped topping brings a slight tanginess and completes the traditional pumpkin pie experience.

To make this recipe, you'll need: Pumpkin Pie Spice

This Pumpkin Milk Bread is exceptionally soft, squishy, and feather-light, while also packing in a lot of pumpkin. Pumpkin can often weigh down baked goods, but here the combination of a tangzhong, bread flour, and a long mix makes this bread simultaneously moist and high-rising.

To make this recipe, you'll need: Instant Yeast

This tender pumpkin crumb cake is for people who double the chocolate chips in pumpkin bread and the streusel on coffee cake. Atop the thin layer of spiced pumpkin cake lays a heavy blanket of buttery crumbs with a bold chocolate flavor, thanks to Dutch-processed cocoa powder.

Get the recipe: Chocolate-Pumpkin Crumb Cake

To make this recipe, you'll need: Black Cocoa

These Pumpkin Cupcakes, with their piped swirl of cream cheese frosting, are the ideal way to celebrate fall birthdays. The cupcakes are super tender, thanks to the addition of cake flour and oil. Sour cream and brown sugar add tanginess and molasses-y sweetness while also preventing the cupcakes from being dry.

For more cupcake decorating ideas, see our YouTube video: Decorate Cupcakes Better Than Ever.

To make this recipe, you'll need: Cake Flour (or Gluten-Free Measure for Measure Flour)

My husband’s favorite fall dessert is Pumpkin Whoopie Pies, hands down. He can’t resist these subtly sweet cakes sandwiching rich cream cheese filling. This recipe has a few extra bells and whistles to take it over the top: Bread and Cake Enhancer to keep the cakes extra soft and fresh, xanthan gum in the filling to give it a smooth mouthfeel, and diced crystallized ginger for a bit of extra zing in the filling.

To make this recipe, you'll need: Bread and Cake Enhancer, Xanthan Gum, and Mini Diced Ginger

The next time there’s a rainy weekend, I’m taking on a project bake: our Pumpkin Cream Cheese Danish. It’s a multiday process and laminating dough is a labor of love, but the final product is worth the effort: buttery, crisp pastries filled with pumpkin and sweet cream cheese.

Get the recipe: Pumpkin Cream Cheese Danish

To make this recipe, you'll need: Baker’s Special Dry Milk

To make this recipe, you'll need: Pumpkin Pie Spice

This Pumpkin Layer Cake with Cream Cheese Frosting is a show-stopping dessert featuring spiced layers of cake, not-too-sweet cream cheese frosting, and a blanket of melted caramel poured over the top. Will it be slightly messy to serve? Yes. Will anyone mind? Absolutely not.

Get the recipe: Pumpkin Layer Cake with Cream Cheese Frosting

To make this recipe, you'll need: Pumpkin Pie Spice and Offset Spatula

The pumpkin spice recipe I’m most excited to bake this fall is a mash-up of greats: Part-coffee cake, part-Bundt cake, part-pumpkin bread, this Pumpkin Espresso Bundt Cake deserves a category all of its own. It has two layers of espresso swirl tucked within a moist, spiced cake. Make it in your favorite Bundt pan or serve it as a loaf if you’re more of simple-is-better person. Either way, it’s great for snacking all day long.

Get the recipe: Pumpkin Espresso Bundt Cake

To make this recipe, you'll need: Espresso Powder and Bundt Pan

#9716. This Chain Serves The Best Old-School Italian Sub, According To Customer Reviews

You might not expect it, but sandwich chains are holding it down when it comes to Italian subs. Of course, there is no denying the appeal of a small, locally owned shop, but there are many reasons why you might opt instead to head into a chain to get your Italian hoagie fix, the most obvious of which is proximity. But there is also the fact that some chains just make darn good food. Food Republic did its research and compiled a list of the best chain Italian subs based on customer reviews, and each entry brings its own unique flavor to the table. But only one, the No. 13 Original Italian from Jersey Mike's, can claim to be the best old-school version of this particular sub.

"They do it right," one Reddit user said, referencing the Original Italian. They continued by stating that if they had a classic Italian deli near them, they'd go there, but since they don't, "it's Jersey Mike's without question." Another user in that same thread agreed, writing, "I love this sub and am always a little amazed [it comes from] a chain" and not, presumably, from a traditional deli. And over on Google, a reviewer shared that the Original Italian reminded them of a sub they'd had during their childhood and expressed their gratitude that "there is a place that can make a real Italian hero like the old days."

It's worth noting that an old-school-style Italian sub owes it all to the Italian immigrants who populated this country throughout the 19th and 20th centuries. There are a few stories about how the hoagie came to be, including one based in Philadelphia (where it's the official sandwich of the city) involving shipyard workers and their distinctive lunches. There is another version that describes how Giovanna Amato sold filling sandwiches to dockworkers in Maine. Whatever its origins, the classic Italian sub came to be characterized by Italian meats and cheeses, a variety of fresh, crisp vegetables, a savory dressing, and an oily, vinegary drizzle.

Jersey Mike's Original Italian proves a chain can still honor those old-school roots. It checks every box, from five different Italian meats to provolone cheese to the default setting, Mike's Way, which includes onions, lettuce sliced super-thin, and tomatoes, as well as red wine vinegar and an olive oil blend, plus two impactful seasonings: salt and oregano.

But of course, Jersey Mike's serves 21st-century customers who like having options, so the sandwich, in addition to scratching an old-school itch, can also serve as a jumping-off point for some. You might, for example, upgrade your Original Italian sub by choosing the rosemary parmesan bread instead of plain white. There are a number of additional toppings available as well, such as jalapeño peppers, dill pickles, and hot chopped pepper relish.

#9714. What are flour enzymes?: Understanding a common flour ingredient.

If you look closely at a bag of King Arthur flour, you may see an unfamiliar ingredient listed there: enzyme.

We’re extremely thoughtful about every ingredient we use, across all King Arthur products and recipes. Our Food Philosophy guides every decision to ensure the quality of what we create, and that includes the enzymes in our flour.

Here’s exactly what flour enzymes are and why they’re included in flour.

Enzymes are found naturally in wheat, and thus are already present in flour. An enzyme is a protein produced by a living organism that acts as a catalyst to bring about a specific biochemical reaction.

The amount of enzymes in flour can vary based on growing conditions from harvest to harvest and year to year, so we add natural enzymes to correct for any variance and make sure our flour bakes more consistently — in other words, to make your baking even better. Those enzymes make up a very small portion of the total flour: less than 1%.

The enzyme we use in our flour is technically called fungal alpha-amylase. That’s a pretty technical name, so it is commonly labeled simply as “enzyme” on ingredient labels. “Alpha-amylase” is the actual enzyme, and “fungal” refers to the fact that the living organism that produces the enzyme is a fungus, not unlike yeast or a mushroom. Amylase may sound unfamiliar, but your body makes and uses it every day. When you eat, it begins breaking starch into smaller carbohydrates so you can draw on it for energy. Amylases added to flour perform a similar function.

Note: Though fungi are technically living organisms, enzymes are considered vegan, as they are not animal based.

Malted barley is an alternative source of enzymes that King Arthur has used in the past, but we found the efficacy can vary batch to batch. By swapping malted barley for straight enzymes, the flour produces more consistent results for our bakers.

Another reason we made the switch? Enzymes require less water and energy to produce than malt barley. As a Certified B Corporation, we're committed to being good stewards of our planet, so pivoting to a responsibly sourced ingredient with a smaller environmental footprint makes sense.

To put it simply, enzymes are added to flours to improve baking performance — they do not change the flour's nutritional value. More specifically, they help create the foods that feeds yeasts. The enzymes break down complex starches into simpler sugars; this, in turn, provides yeast with readily available fermentable sugar (food!), which enables yeast to work continuously and supports both fermentation and crust browning. This results in improved bread volume and crumb texture. Most other manufacturers of flour and yeasted mixes use enzymes for the very same reasons.

Ultimately, enzymes are yet another way for us to provide you with the most consistent flour — which means even better baking.

Cover photo and food styling by Liz Neily.

#9712. Skip Gruyère: This Norwegian Cheese Boasts Nutty Flavor & Fewer Calories

Cheese is one of life's greatest pleasures, but no two varieties are quite the same. Knowing your way around your mozzarella and parmesan is a useful skill that won't just impress your dinner guests but will also transform the way you use cheese in the kitchen. Take Gruyère, for example. If, say, a French onion soup recipe calls for it, and you've had no luck finding it at the store, any cheese connoisseur will tell you that Norwegian Jarlsberg makes an excellent substitute. The two share a similar nutty flavor and melt beautifully, with Jarlsberg also serving a lower-calorie option.

Jarlsberg is instantly recognizable thanks to its large, round holes, and while traditional Swiss Gruyère might lack these holes, it matches Jarlsberg's intensely nutty flavor — although how the two cheeses develop their respective flavors is very different. Jarlsberg gets it from a proprietary bacterial culture called Propionibacterium shermanii, a sub-sect of Propionibacterium freudenreichii. During fermentation, this culture consumes lactic acid to produce propionic acid and carbon dioxide. The acid contributes to the cheese's nutty profile, while the carbon dioxide becomes trapped in the cheese, creating those large holes. Gruyère takes a different approach, developing its signature flavor through a combination of factors, including the unique composition of the high-altitude Alpine milk, its bacterial cultures, and a longer aging process.

Despite sharing a similar taste, their nutritional profiles tell a different story. Jarlsberg contains around 100 calories per ounce, compared with up to 120 calories for Gruyère. That's a modest saving of 20 calories per ounce, which can quickly add up if you're using a generous amount in a grilled cheese or fondue. So if you're looking for a slightly lighter alternative to Gruyère without sacrificing flavor, Jarlsberg makes for a wonderful swap.

As is the case with Gruyère, one of Jarlsberg's biggest selling points is its versatility. You can always enjoy it as is, pairing it with grapes, crackers, and cold cuts as part of an elegantly presented charcuterie board, or keep things simple and serve it alongside a glass of wine; Jarlsberg goes particularly well with chardonnay and sweet rieslings, as well as low-tannin reds like pinot noir. While there are plenty of ways to enjoy the cheese without cooking it, we think the best way to get the most out of Jarlsberg is to take advantage of its meltability.

Jarlsberg's flavor is comparatively milder than that of sharper Gruyère, making it an excellent substitute if you're after a nutty, creamy cheese that won't overpower everything else, which makes it a great contender for a grilled cheese. If you still want some of Gruyère's intensity, simply combine the two. Their complementary flavor profiles mean neither cheese should overpower the other, giving you a nutty filling with plenty of depth. In a nod to Jarlsberg's Norwegian roots, add in some fresh dill, pickles, and a generous helping of cold-smoked salmon for a Scandi-inspired twist.

Another great way to put Jarlsberg to work is as a pizza topping. Its mild, buttery flavor and excellent meltability make it an obvious fit. Rather than tomato sauce, pair it with mushrooms, caramelized onions, and fresh thyme to let the cheese shine. If white pizza isn't your thing, swap the dough for Danish rye bread to create your own smørbrød, a charming Scandinavian open-faced sandwich. Simply take the buttered bread and add your toppings of choice, layer the Jarlsberg on top, then blast it in the broiler until creamy and gooey.

#9708. Two Personality Traits Linked To A Sharper Mind

How you respond to beauty may have more in common with your thinking skills than you realise.

How you respond to beauty may have more in common with your thinking skills than you realise.

Intellectual curiosity and an appreciation of beauty are both linked to stronger thinking skills.

People with these qualities tend to perform better on tests of literacy, numeracy and problem-solving.

The findings suggest that a person’s interest in ideas and aesthetic experiences may offer clues to their cognitive abilities.

Curiosity could encourage people to seek out opportunities to learn, while stronger thinking skills could make exploring complex ideas more rewarding, with both processes reinforcing one another.

Intellectual curiosity involves enjoying ideas, wanting to understand things and being drawn to questions that require thought.

Aesthetic sensitivity describes an appreciation of art and beauty.

Both qualities belong to the broader personality trait of openness to experience, which captures how receptive people are to unfamiliar ideas and experiences.

However, openness also includes creative imagination, and this aspect showed no significant independent association with cognitive performance.

Imagination, curiosity and an appreciation of beauty may overlap in everyday life, but their relationships with thinking skills differ.

The conclusions come from an analysis of almost 68,000 people across 12 countries, including Canada, Germany, Italy and New Zealand.

They completed personality questionnaires alongside assessments of literacy, numeracy and the ability to solve problems as circumstances change.

Intellectual curiosity and aesthetic sensitivity were linked to better performance across all three assessments, even after accounting for other personality traits.

The connections between personality and cognitive skills also varied between countries.

Educational systems and cultural practices could help explain such differences, although the reasons remain uncertain.

Overall, the findings link both a desire to understand the world and an appreciation of its beauty with stronger thinking skills.

The study was published in the journal Large-scale Assessments in Education (Rammstedt et al., 2026).

#9707. Heavy cream vs. whipping cream: What's the difference?: Understanding the right cream for your baking.

If you’re baking a recipe that calls for heavy cream, or picking up a carton to turn into whipped cream to finish a dessert, you may be confused when you hit the dairy aisle. There’s “heavy cream” — but also “heavy whipping cream” or, in some cases, just “whipping cream.”

So when it comes to heavy cream versus whipping cream, is there truly a difference?

Aside from being delicious, there are very specific definitions and standards that must be met in order for something to be labeled as heavy cream. It is made by separating the fatty top layer from the base milk layer during processing. The FDA states that heavy cream is cream that contains no less than 36% milk fat.  Comparatively, milk has 0% to around 3% milk fat, as well as a higher water concentration. Because of its fat content, heavy cream retains a rich taste and, when whipped, it excels at creating stiff peaks that hold their shape for a long time.

Whipping cream — sometimes called “heavy whipping cream” — is made using a similar process as heavy cream and is also the milk fat removed before milk is homogenized. However, whipping cream can contain somewhere between 30% and 35% milk fat content, according to FDA regulations. Because of its slightly lower fat content, it whips into a softer, more billowy cream, and it will deflate more quickly than whipped cream made with heavy cream.

Luckily, the difference in taste and performance between the two types of cream are not very discernible. This means you can use them interchangeably in recipes — and it's okay if you accidentally buy the "wrong" one. Both can yield a delicious bowl of homemade whipped cream. (Can’t justify buying a whole carton of either one? We’ve got you covered with an easy homemade heavy cream substitute.)

A note on King Arthur recipes: The King Arthur Test Kitchen prefers heavy cream in most instances, particularly when making whipped cream, because of the higher fat content. That said, you can substitute heavy whipping cream 1:1 in any King Arthur recipe that calls specifically for heavy cream without any issue.

As a general rule of thumb, use heavy cream for making stable whipped cream for topping pies, layered desserts like tiramisu or banana pudding, and any sweet where the structural integrity hinges on the cream really holding its shape. Heavy cream can also be handy for making cream scones and drop biscuits, where the richness of the dairy can shine through. For more heavy cream baking inspiration, check out these 12 recipes that call on heavy cream.

#9705. Give Tuna Salad A Flavorful Protein Boost With An Ingredient You Have Stocked In The Fridge

Tuna salad typically already comes with plenty of protein and flavor, but boosting these virtues can give you something even more delicious and nutritionally dense. This is especially true if you use boiled eggs, an easy-to-prepare ingredient that's highly compatible with whatever recipe you prefer.

Exact needs vary based on body type and medical history, but most adults need a minimum of about 0.36 grams of protein per pound of body weight daily. Beginning a recipe with canned tuna, which hovers around 22 grams of protein per 3-ounce serving, is a good start, but it can be better. A single boiled egg contains roughly 6 grams of protein and is rich in umami, no matter what texture you cook it to. The whites add a lovely, soft chew to counteract the density of fish meat, while the yolks themselves sort of disappear into the mayonnaise to boost its richness.

If you use the best mayo for tuna salad — Kewpie, which is packed with MSG — you'll get an extra umami bomb. Between the fish, egg, and MSG, you have all the makings of a hearty, satisfying meal, whether you eat it straight or heat it up in a melt. The end result is something that tastes more decadent than it does nutritious, full of velvety textures and rich flavors that make it seem like you spent quite a bit of time perfecting your recipe. Combine it all with minced veggies and pickles, and you get something comprehensively nourishing that's ready in a flash.

Eggs can be so much more than simply hard-boiled, so you've got plenty of options when it comes to the exact tastes and textures you want your tuna salad to have. Some bulk out a bowl, some focus on the sauce, and still others can add delightful new textures, but all are quite easy.

If you want something with an unobtrusive texture but a great amount of flavor, then boil your eggs for a jammy yolk. The runnier center diffuses through the mayonnaise, infusing it with flavor before it coats every piece of fish. If you're looking for something different, you can pan-fry hard-boiled eggs to crisp up the exteriors and add a touch of roasted flavor to a comparatively fresh and cool dish. If you use a flavored oil, like chili oil or one infused with herbs, this is an easy way to add new seasonings to the overall dish.

Eggs can either introduce a dichotomy of textures or disappear into the meal, depending on your preference. Leaving your eggs whole or cut in half lets you spoon them into individual bites, preventing your meal from being too one-note. On the other hand, finely dicing them into crumbles is the best way to get their flavor into every nook, cranny, and ingredient. Using an egg slicer can give you the best of both worlds, creating thin slivers of white while the yolk dissolves into the mayonnaise.

#9701. How to clean cast iron  : It’s simpler than you think.

Despite what you may have heard, cleaning and maintaining a cast iron skillet or Dutch oven isn’t difficult. It’s practically impossible to ruin a well-seasoned skillet, and despite your best efforts, sometimes food will stick. If your cast iron is covered in stuck-on bits of cheese from a batch of Crispy Cheesy Pan Pizza, here's how to clean it.

We can settle the debate once and for all: Yes, you can use soap to clean your cast iron. Dishwashing soap will not damage the seasoning that makes your skillet non-stick. Polymerized oil creates the layer of seasoning through heat, and dish soap isn’t strong enough to break that bond.

No, you cannot clean a cast iron skillet in the dishwasher. This will degrade the seasoning layer and cause it to rust.

You should not soak a cast iron pan either; the water will cause it to rust. If you do end up rusting your pan, you can still rescue it by scrubbing off the rust then re-seasoning the pan.

Using warm, soapy water, scrub the pan with a stiff-bristled brush or sponge to remove any food residue. Avoid harsh, abrasive scrubbers like steel wool or metal pads, which can strip the pan of its seasoning.

Once cleaned, fully dry the pan with a kitchen towel, or place it onto a burner over low heat so the water fully evaporates. Don’t walk away from the pan — it can quickly get smoky once the water has evaporated.

Regardless of which method you prefer, it’s imperative that the pan is fully dry. Water (not soap!) is the enemy of cast iron, which can cause it to rust. Once dry, add a few drops of neutral oil and spread all over the pan with a towel.

#9700. 7 Best Chain Restaurant Roast Beef Sandwiches, According To Customer Reviews

Roast beef sandwiches are one of the most hearty and heartening meals there is. That's why we think this comfort food deserves to be served year-round, not just on those brisk, rainy days when fall-apart-tender beef on a toasted baguette can be the most delicious way to warm up. Luckily, these chains' roast beef sandwiches are widely praised for their taste, texture, and consistency, so you can be sure you're getting a good-quality meal whenever you'd like to try one.

And you won't be alone when you do. According to the latest dedicated study on the subject, a 2019 survey by YouGov found that around 71% of adults across the country enjoyed roast beef sandwiches. That's one reason why the restaurants chosen for this list have the sandwich on the menu anytime you want it, and a few even overlap with the chains that have the best French dips. In the end, whatever place you choose to stop at will feed you well with homey, warm roast beef slices on toothsome bread.

Roy Rogers was once famed for its roast beef sandwiches, and today, people still line up for them whenever they get to visit one of the nearly 40 remaining locations. While it's been in business since the late 1960s, the chain has massively downscaled from its height of almost 650 stores in the 1990s. But the roast beef remains consistently delicious, thanks to the USDA Top Inside Round Roast Beef being slow-cooked for hours for maximum tenderness.

The sandwich has a hardcore fan base, who often say the beef here is tastier and juicier than other national competitors. One Reddit commenter said, "Roy's Roast beef is much better than Arby's. It actually tastes like real roast beef." Online reviewers suggest using the chain's barbecue and horseradish sauces to complete the experience. It helps that many of the remaining locations are in Maryland, where you can always grab some Baltimore tiger sauce for any leftovers.

And customers are willing to accept the limited regional footprint of the restaurant, although they're still hoping for an overall comeback for the brand. Those lucky enough to have an open Roy Rogers nearby have reported being overjoyed at the discovery.

Arby's is a nostalgic favorite for many people for a reason – the perfectly textured and easy-to-chew beef. The global fast food chain began operations in 1964 but has since circled the globe with over 3,500 locations without forgetting that fact. That's why the roast beef Arby's uses has had the same four ingredients since it opened — beef, water, salt, and sodium phosphates. The meat is slow-cooked before being thinly sliced and added to a toasted sesame seed bun the diner can customize however they'd like.

People have called Arby's classic roast beef sandwiches their preferred fast food order, adding they rarely try anything else because the meal is so consistently good. Other fans have echoed that consistency is also what brings them back, with one person saying they've always enjoyed their items from the restaurant. A Facebook user posted about their first time trying Arby's, saying, "Tried Arby's roasted beef sandwich. It is pretty tender and flavorful. It's like a poor man's prime rib." And customers love that they can choose how much meat to have put on the sandwich, with some noting they've enjoyed half-pound versions, with and without cheddar sauce.

The smallest chain on this list is a Missouri powerhouse that's crossed over into Illinois. Even though that means most people will have to travel a bit to reach the nearest Lion's Choice, fans say the trip will be worth it. That's because the chain's roast beef sandwiches are made from the top round cut and are roasted in-house for freshness. Then there's the company's proprietary blend of seasoning that's used to finish off the beef after it moves to the bun. The gluten-free mix helps set the meal apart from competitors, just like the secret roasting method does.

Fans of Lion's Choice are quick to recommend the establishment to newcomers, and those who've moved away look forward to the eatery being one of their first stops upon returning. Guests suggest getting extra seasoning on the beef, with some advising buyers to add cheese as well. The brand's horseradish sauce is also praised for being flavorful, although the beef is always the star of the show.

Black Bear Diner is an up-and-coming chain operating almost 170 locations across 14 states at the time of writing. Founded in 1995, the brand is dedicated to making comfort foods that taste as if they came straight from the best cook in the family's kitchen. The restaurant's Pot Roast Melt is certainly living up to that expectation. The meal is made with jack and cheddar cheeses, grilled onions, horseradish aioli, and slowly simmered pot roast. The sandwich also comes with au jus and is served on garlic- and Parmesan-crusted sourdough bread for a bit of crunch.

The melt gets consistent praise from customers, whether it's the diner's first time trying the sandwich or if they've come back just for another one. One Facebook user posted about the meal, saying, "Black Bear Diner knocked it out of the park with their Pot Roast Melt! Pot Roast, onion and cheesy goodness on grilled parmesan/garlic bread. On top of that – you get to dip it in au jus!" Others have called it yummy, delicious, and so good, cementing the elevated status of the sandwich for Black Bear Diner fans.

Like Lion's Choice, Culver's is another Midwest favorite for beef sandwiches. But Culver's is a little different because it's one of the only fast food chains that serves shredded pot roast instead of sliced beef. That creates a big difference in the taste and texture of the premium chuck roast the brand uses, so it's no surprise that Culver's Pot Roast Sandwich is praised for its rich flavor and lack of fat. One person was so impressed with the meal that they made it their go-to item from the menu.

Other diners point out the generous size of the sandwich, as well as how juicy and tender the meat is. Fans suggest adding gravy and/or grilled onions to finish off the sandwich, but barbecue sauce is another popular way to add spice to the roast. Some people add Swiss cheese and mushrooms, too, although you might need to eat it quickly to keep the bun intact.

Firehouse Subs is one of the largest fast food sandwich franchises in the U.S., with over 1,300 stores. It started in the mid-1990s and has always been dedicated to making filling meals that each diner could customize exactly as they'd like. The large menu includes hot and cold subs, as well as in-house sides and desserts. One of the most popular hot sandwiches is the Smokehouse Beef & Cheddar Brisket, which fans praise for its melty cheddar cheese, strong beefy flavor, and the incredibly tender brisket.

People agree that Firehouse Subs is a pricier option than many other sandwich shops, but the quality of the ingredients and the generous portions make up for the higher cost. One Facebook user said, "Trying Firehouse Subs for [the] first time. Large smokehouse beef and cheddar combo, with small fries. Pricier than Subway at $32.42, but bloody delicious!!" Others agree about the taste, saying the sandwich is one of their favorites and that they've had consistently good experiences eating one.

Portillo's is a Chicago-based chain that's best known for its Italian-style roast beef sandwiches, although there are several kinds of roast beef subs on the menu. Served either dipped in au jus or dry, the meaty Italian Beef Sandwiches have a nice kick of spice from the Italian peppers that come atop the layered protein. The meal is so sought after that the business ships kits nationwide to make the Italian beef sandwiches.  The set comes with all the elements needed to re-create the meal at home, and it serves up to 10 people.

Reviewers note the hot peppers that come on the sub add a spicy crunch that works nicely with the richness of the juicy meat. One Facebook user posted about the item, saying, "...I had a Portillo's beef yesterday with hot and sweet peppers and dipped twice. It was a pretty darn good beef sandwich."

Like that Facebook poster, many fans prefer to have the sandwich dipped, saying the flavor is worth the extra napkins you'll need. Some people even make long drives just to visit the shop. And who could blame them? The hot beef Italian subs offer great taste and value for some of the most tender meat you'll find at any chain restaurant.

To build a list of the best roast beef sandwiches, we first searched for chain restaurants with more than 24 locations that served the meal. We then looked through social media and message board posts and comments, user review sites, and professional reviews for each chain's roast beef. We ultimately chose the restaurants whose customers had praised the meal for its taste, value, and consistency across multiple platforms to be represented on this list.

#9695. How to proof bread in the oven: Common challenge, simple solution.

During proofing, bread and other yeasted doughs do best in a temperature-controlled, humid, draft-free environment. Your kitchen counter may not cut it (especially in colder months), but is there a corner of your kitchen that fits that description? Yes, your oven — and you don’t even need to fire it up!

Yeast dough is happiest when rising at temperatures between 75°F and 78°F. It will certainly rise in cooler or warmer temperatures. But for most doughs, that range is optimum for both yeast development and bread flavor.

Your oven’s interior will pretty much mirror room temperature. And depending on the time of year (or how much you use air conditioning), that temperature could be pretty cool—too cool for yeast’s comfort.

To get the oven up to that ideal proofing temperature, people often turn to a couple of different methods. I decided to try a bunch of them to see which is best — and helpfully, there was a clear winner.

It’s tempting to simply preheat the oven for a minute or so to warm its interior; but not only is this hit-and-miss (How long should I leave it on? Will the oven get too hot?), it’s ineffective; the heat quickly dissipates once you turn the oven off.

Enter your oven light. When turned on, your oven light’s slow, gentle heat will gradually warm the oven to the desired temperature. After trying a number of different methods for proofing bread in the oven, including several listed below, this was my clear favorite because it created the ideal temperature (not too hot, not too cold), maintained that temperature for several hours, and was essentially failproof (no overshooting the temp, for example!).

It can take your oven a while to reach the desired temperature, especially if your kitchen is cold to begin with. With so many variables — season, climate, kitchen, oven — you’ll want to do a simple experiment to determine your own best method for turning your oven into an effective, efficient proof box:

Take your oven’s temperature before turning on the light. Then turn on the light and measure the temperature again at 15-minute intervals, to see just how quickly the light warms things up. For reference, the light in my electric oven takes about an hour to raise the oven’s interior temperature by 10 degrees, and another hour to raise it an additional five degrees; your results will probably vary a bit.

Warm your oven to about 80°F before turning off the light. Over the next couple of hours, the temperature will gradually drift down by about 10 degrees, giving your rising dough plenty of time in and around that 75°F to 78°F sweet spot.

Once you know how to warm your oven using only its lightbulb, think about maintaining humidity: Dry dough can develop a tough skin, which inhibits rising.

If you’re proofing dough in a bowl (or later, a shaped loaf in a pan), cover it with a clear plastic shower cap or reusable plastic bowl cover. Whatever you use, make sure it's large enough to form a “poof” on top, so the cover doesn’t touch the rising dough.

For shaped rolls (or anything else in a large, flat pan), use an extra-large shower cap; or simply drape the pan with well-greased plastic wrap, waxed paper, or parchment.

What if your oven doesn’t have a light, the lightbulb only lights when you open the oven door, or it’s a “cool” LED bulb?

Then your best bet is a pan of boiling water set on the lowest rack, which will both warm and humidify your oven’s interior. Place the bread dough on the oven’s middle rack; no need to cover it.  Set a shallow pan (e.g., 9" x 13" pan) on the lower rack, and add four cups of boiling water. Quickly close the oven door.

Your oven’s temperature will immediately rise by about 30 degrees, which will probably be warmer than you want. Cool it down by opening the door wide for about five minutes; the temperature should drop about 15 degrees.

As the water in the oven cools, the air around it cools, too. But it happens so gradually that your oven should still remain sufficiently warm for the one to two hours your bread typically needs to rise. For longer-rising breads, simply switch out the cool water with another pan of hot water, if necessary.

Some ovens actually have a proof setting or proofing drawer. I don’t always love using this setting, though: Most are programmed to temperatures ranging from 90°F to 100°F, far warmer than yeast dough’s optimal 75°F to 78°F. For best results, figure out how long it takes to reach about 80°F, then turn it off.

Tip #1: If you have to open the oven door to check your rising dough, don’t worry. Unlike the huge 15- to 20-degree drop you experience when opening a fully heated oven, the temperature inside your light- or steam-warmed oven will only drop by a degree or two.

Tip #2: Typically, you don’t preheat your oven with rising dough inside. So when your dough is close to fully risen, remove it from the oven and set it somewhere safe. (If there’s room, the top of your fridge is both warm and out of harm’s way.) Timed just right, your bread will be perfectly proved by the time the oven finishes preheating.

Tip #3: To prevent someone from killing your rising dough by turning on the oven (say, to warm their leftover pizza), write “NO!” on a sticky note and affix it to the oven’s start button. Really!

For the highly passionate bread baker (or a small baking business), an electronic proof box like the Brod & Taylor Proofer Pro is a step up from proofing dough in the oven. It controls temperature with exquisite precision, from cold-proofing (down to 41°F) for those overnight ferments up to 122°F for an express warmup, all while ensuring perfect humidity. Wi-Fi and programmable timers let you control your dough’s development for up to eight days. It’s literally set it and forget it — the process is simple, but the results are simply amazing.

Still looking for a warm, draft-free spot for your rising bread dough? Think beyond your oven to other major appliances: Both your clothes dryer and dishwasher can double as a proof box!

#9691. Speaking Faster Can Make You More Persuasive — Until This Happens

Your best argument may lose its edge if listeners struggle to keep up with how quickly you deliver it.

Your best argument may lose its edge if listeners struggle to keep up with how quickly you deliver it.

Speaking at a lively pace can make a strong argument more convincing, but rushing can weaken its impact.

Very fast speech makes it harder for listeners to weigh up what they hear, reducing the advantage that good reasons have over weak ones.

The findings suggest that persuading someone depends partly on giving them enough opportunity to think.

The conclusions come from six experiments involving almost 4,000 people who listened to persuasive messages delivered at different speeds.

Across the experiments, increasing the pace from very slow speech initially improved impressions of the speaker’s confidence and encouraged closer consideration of the message.

However, these benefits eventually weakened or reversed as the delivery became faster.

This helps explain why simply telling someone to speak more quickly is incomplete advice.

A faster delivery can make an argument easier to engage with until the listener begins struggling to keep up.

Crucially, the consequences depend on whether the reasons being offered stand up to scrutiny.

In the two main experiments, listeners heard a proposal that would allow university students to pay lower tuition fees in exchange for working part-time.

Some heard strong arguments emphasising benefits such as smaller classes and better services.

Others heard weak arguments that included reduced leisure time and superficial improvements to the campus.

The recordings were digitally altered to change speaking speed while keeping other vocal features, such as pitch and intonation, unchanged.

Participants then rated their support for the proposal, with some also recording the thoughts that had occurred to them while listening.

The combined results showed that strong arguments gained an increasing advantage over weak ones as speech became faster, but lost some of that advantage at higher speeds.

In other words, delivery affected how effectively listeners distinguished a convincing case from an unconvincing one.

A central part of persuasion is how carefully people consider the reasons they are given.

When listeners examine a message closely, they have more opportunity to recognise its strengths, spot its weaknesses and form their own reactions.

This benefits a strong argument, while exposing the shortcomings of a weak one.

Very fast delivery can interfere with that process, making the merits of the message less influential.

The analyses suggested that changes in how easily listeners felt they could follow the reasoning helped explain this pattern.

Although speaking speed also affected how confident the speaker sounded, confidence alone did not adequately explain the overall pattern.

One possible reason very slow speech is less effective is that it makes sustaining attention more demanding, while excessively fast speech leaves too little time to absorb the content.

The experiments tested seven speaking speeds, ranging from 113 to 218 words per minute, but did not establish one ideal pace.

The most effective delivery is likely to depend on factors including the complexity of the message, the audience and the presence of distractions.

The findings also concern recorded persuasive messages, so they do not establish a universal rule for every conversation or public speech.

For someone presenting a strong case, the findings suggest keeping the delivery lively while giving listeners time to follow the reasoning.

Rushing may reduce the very scrutiny that would otherwise make a good argument convincing.

The study was published in the Journal of Nonverbal Behavior (Guyer et al., 2025).

#9690. Does β‑Blocker Use Increase Depression Risk?

The association between β-blocker use and depression was investigated in a population-based observational study recently published in the journal Drug Safety.

While depression is often cited as an adverse effect of β-blocker use, there is limited evidence supporting this causal relationship. To better understand the association between beta blockers and the risk of new-onset depression, the study authors analyzed data from the UK population-based Clinical Practice Research Datalink (CPRD) GOLD database.

“We identifed patients aged 18-80 years with an incident depression diagnosis between 2000 and 2016, and matched controls, and estimated the risk (odds ratio [OR]) of depression in association with use of β-blockers,” the study authors explained.

Findings of the analysis revealed an increased risk of developing depression among short-term users of β-blockers compared with no use at all (adjusted odds ratio [aOR], 1.91; 95% CI, 1.72-2.12).

Among short-term users, increased risk of depression was mainly restricted to patients with a neuropsychiatric disorder taking propranolol (aOR 6.33, 95% CI 5.16–7.76).  Patients on propranolol for a cardiovascular indication were found to be at slightly elevated risk of depression (aOR 1.44, 95% CI 1.14–1.82). Apart from propranolol, no other lipophilic β-blocker or hydrophilic β-blocker was found to increase the risk of depression.

Additionally, no association was observed between long-term use of β-blockers and the risk of depression (aOR, 0.85; 95% CI, 0.85-0.94).

“Our findings suggest that the reported association between use of β-blockers and depression may not be causal but rather a result of protopathic bias,” the study authors concluded.

Bornand D, Reinau D, Jick SS, Meier CR. β‑blockers and the risk of depression: A matched case–control study. Drug Safety. Published online January 19, 2022. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40264-021-01140-5.

Psychiatry Advisor, a trusted source of medical news and feature content for healthcare providers, offers clinicians insight into the latest research to inform clinical practice and improve patient outcomes.
